Once upon a time, there was a young girl named Lily. She grew up in a family where academic excellence was highly valued, and her parents always had high expectations for her performance in school. Lily always tried her best, but she was not a straight-A student. She struggled with some subjects, especially math and science. Her parents were often disappointed with her grades, despite her best efforts. As Lily grew older, she started to internalize her parents' disappointment. She began to believe that she was not good enough, that no matter how hard she tried, she would never be able to meet their expectations. This belief affected not only her academic performance but also her self-esteem. She withdrew into herself and stopped trying as hard as she used to, thinking that there was no point in trying when she would always fall short. One day, Lily's teacher noticed a change in her attitude and performance in school. She talked to Lily and encouraged her to believe in herself, to see her strengths and not just her weaknesses. Lily started to change her mindset. She began to focus on areas where she excelled, such as writing and art. She discovered that she was good at these things and that her parents could be proud of her for other reasons besides academic performance. As Lily started to build her confidence, she found that she was able to excel in other areas as well. She worked harder in math and science, and her grades started to improve. She realized that she was capable of achieving great things when she believed in herself. In the end, Lily learned that she was not defined by her grades or her parents' expectations. She was good enough just the way she was, and she had talents and abilities that were unique and valuable. Her journey to self-discovery had been difficult, but it had taught her a valuable lesson: that she was enough, just as she was.

We propose a hierarchically structured reinforcement learning approach to address the challenges of planning for generating coherent multi-sentence stories for the visual storytelling task. Within our framework, the task of generating a story given a sequence of images is divided across a two-level hierarchical decoder. The high-level decoder constructs a plan by generating a semantic concept (i.e. , topic) for each image in sequence. The low-level decoder generates a sentence for each image using a semantic compositional network, which effectively grounds the sentence generation conditioned on the topic. The two decoders are jointly trained end-to-end using reinforcement learning. We evaluate our model on the visual storytelling (VIST) dataset. Empirical results from both automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that the proposed hierarchically structured reinforced training achieves significantly better performance compared to a strong flat deep reinforcement learning baseline.

The printing press was one of the most important inventions in human history. It revolutionized the way that information was disseminated and played a major role in the spread of knowledge. Prior to the printing press, books were extremely expensive and time-consuming to produce. They were typically handwritten by scribes, and a single book could take months or even years to complete. As a result, books were only available to a small number of wealthy and educated individuals. The printing press made it possible to produce books much more quickly and cheaply. This led to a dramatic increase in the number of books that were produced, and it also made books more affordable for the general population. As a result, literacy rates began to rise, and knowledge became more accessible to people of all socioeconomic backgrounds. This led to a more informed and educated population, which had a profound impact on society. The printing press also played a major role in the Protestant Reformation. Martin Luther, a German theologian, used the printing press to spread his ideas of religious reform. Luther's writings were printed and distributed widely, and they helped to inspire the Protestant Reformation. The printing press also played a role in the Scientific Revolution. Scientists such as Galileo Galilei and Johannes Kepler used the printing press to share their ideas with other scientists. This led to a greater exchange of ideas and helped to accelerate the pace of scientific discovery. The printing press has had a profound impact on the world. It has made knowledge more accessible to people of all backgrounds, and it has played a major role in the development of modern society. It is an invention that has truly changed the world.

Take, for instance, a young child. Children are able to use their imagination in amazing ways, to conjure up stories, pictures or objects of their own making. Parents and educators often praise this sort of creative thinking, as it allows the child to take risks free from the anxiety of being wrong. More importantly, imagination can be used to bridge gaps for the differently-abled. For the blind, for example, it is not knowledge that might help a person find his or her way, but rather the ability to imagine one's surroundings. It is imagination that allows them to visualise a street corner or a store, and to traverse a path that may have been previously unknown. In conclusion, imagination is considered more important than knowledge because it is far more versatile, powerful, and adaptive. It is the tool we need when knowledge fails us; it is the key to creative thinking; and it allows for a measure of flexibility and creativity that knowledge alone cannot offer.

Ultimately, no one can say what brings about success - it is a unique journey that is relative to the individual and the circumstances they face. In conclusion, success is a multifaceted concept, and whether failure can lead to it depends on the context. The idea that success comes from going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm is an intriguing one, and it may be beneficial for those working hard to reach their goals to keep in mind. However, taking failure as an opportunity to reflect and re-direct your goals may also be a useful strategy in achieving the ultimate goal of success.

Database storage is the container of the physical materialization of a database. It comprises the internal (physical) level in the database architecture. It also contains all the information needed (e.g., metadata, "data about the data," and internal data structures) to reconstruct the conceptual level and external level from the internal level when needed. Putting data into permanent storage is generally the responsibility of the database engine a.k.a. "storage engine." Though typically accessed by a DBMS through the underlying operating system (and often utilizing the operating systems' file systems as intermediates for storage layout), storage properties and configuration setting are extremely important for the efficient operation of the DBMS, and thus are closely maintained by database administrators. A DBMS, while in operation, always has its database residing in several types of storage (e.g., memory and external storage). The database data and the additional needed information, possibly in very large amounts, are coded into bits. Data typically reside in the storage in structures that look completely different from the way the data look in the conceptual and external levels, but in ways that attempt to optimize (the best possible) these levels' reconstruction when needed by users and programs, as well as for computing additional types of needed information from the data (e.g., when querying the database).

In a supercharger , the compressor is powered directly by the engine , just like other stuff like the water pump or alternator . This is not as efficient as a turbocharger because you 're taking power from the engine ( you get it back plus more by having more compression but it 's not as much as a turbo ) . However , you can use a larger and more powerful compressor so the absolute gain can be greater and the hardware is n't as hard to build . You can use both , typically when you want as much power as possible from a fixed sized engine .

All objects emit some radiation , as objects get hotter , the frequency of the radiation gets higher . Objects that are around room temperature emit radiation that has a lower frequency than we can see . As the objects get hotter , the frequency goes up until we can see it as red , then yellow , all the way up to blue . This might lead you to think that eventually really hot objects will emit only ultraviolet radiation that we ca n't see . However , objects do n't emit just one frequency of radiation , they emit an entire range . The strongest frequency might be red , purple , or in the ultraviolet range , but there are always other frequencies emitted , most below the strongest frequency . So even if the strongest frequency is above our visible range , frequencies in our visible range are still emitted , so an object will never " disappear " because it 's too hot .

The number of electrons that can occupy a given atomic shell is determined by the maximum number of electrons that can have the same set of quantum numbers, which is described by the Pauli exclusion principle. According to this principle, no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers.

The maximum number of electrons that can occupy a shell is given by the formula 2n^2, where n is the principal quantum number of the shell. For example, the first shell, with n = 1, can hold a maximum of 2(1^2) = 2 electrons. The second shell, with n = 2, can hold a maximum of 2(2^2) = 8 electrons, and so on.

The arrangement of electrons in the shells of an atom is determined by the Aufbau principle, which states that electrons occupy the lowest energy levels first. This means that electrons will fill the shells of an atom starting with the innermost shell and working outward, filling each shell before moving on to the next.

The number of electrons in each shell can also be determined by using the periodic table, which lists the number of valence electrons for each element. Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell of an atom, and they play a key role in determining the chemical properties of an element.

We consider the distributed optimization problem in which a network of agents aims to minimize the average of local functions. To solve this problem, several algorithms have recently been proposed where agents perform various combinations of communication with neighbors, local gradient computations, and updates to local state variables. In this paper, we present a canonical form that characterizes any first-order distributed algorithm that can be implemented using a single round of communication and gradient computation per iteration, and where each agent stores up to two state variables. The canonical form features a minimal set of parameters that are both unique and expressive enough to capture any distributed algorithm in this class. The generic nature of our canonical form enables the systematic analysis and design of distributed optimization algorithms.

So, there's a couple things here. First of all, you have to understand how programming works. The programmer provides instructions to the computer. And the programming has to take into account every possible thing you could ever do with that program. "Normal" cases are pretty well covered, but sometimes, programmers miss a case when people intentionally misbehave. Heartbleed, for example, was caused because the programmer didn't account for the case where the attacker would say one thing and do another. In this case, we have what's called a use-after-free bug. Internet Explorer asks the operating system for some memory (one of the OS's main functions is to allocate memory to different programs), uses it, and then releases it back to the operating system. There is a particular set of operations you can take (Microsoft didn't say exactly what they were) that will get Internet Explorer to access that memory after it's already been released back. If an attacker can get their own instructions written to that spot in memory, they can get the computer to execute arbitrary code. The attackers are currently using a second vulnerability, in Adobe Flash Player, to bypass Internet Explorer's memory protections so they can write to that spot in memory. Chrome and Firefox are vulnerable to the second flaw, the one in Flash Player. But this particular sequence of operations exploits an oversight in the way Internet Explorer was written. While there are likely similar vulnerabilities in those browsers, this particular attack won't work on them because their programming correctly accounts for this sequence of instructions.

In computer science, in particular in knowledge representation and reasoning and metalogic, the area of automated reasoning is dedicated to understanding different aspects of reasoning. The study of automated reasoning helps produce computer programs that allow computers to reason completely, or nearly completely, automatically. Although automated reasoning is considered a sub-field of artificial intelligence, it also has connections with theoretical computer science and philosophy. The most developed subareas of automated reasoning are automated theorem proving (and the less automated but more pragmatic subfield of interactive theorem proving) and automated proof checking (viewed as guaranteed correct reasoning under fixed assumptions).[citation needed] Extensive work has also been done in reasoning by analogy using induction and abduction. Other important topics include reasoning under uncertainty and non-monotonic reasoning. An important part of the uncertainty field is that of argumentation, where further constraints of minimality and consistency are applied on top of the more standard automated deduction. John Pollock's OSCAR system is an example of an automated argumentation system that is more specific than being just an automated theorem prover. Tools and techniques of automated reasoning include the classical logics and calculi, fuzzy logic, Bayesian inference, reasoning with maximal entropy and many less formal ad hoc techniques.

Product Distribution Options Essay The selection of the most effective product distribution channels is among the most challenging tasks for new businesses. Even if the goods are to be sold using innovative technology and have no analogs in the market, the distribution strategies should be planned thoroughly. The example of a new home tooth brushing system that does not require the use of toothpaste involves a range of potential problems linked to distribution. Most importantly, giving too much power to intermediaries and product distributors in the mentioned case are associated with the threat of new competitors or even fake products. At the same time, selling the toothbrush to clients requires the presence of effective advertising materials. It is because the brush that performs its functions without toothpaste will become popular only if consumers change their years-long habits and are fully aware of its benefits. To address the listed problems, it is possible to implement a multi-channel approach and sell the toothbrush both directly and with retailers’ help (Kotler and Armstrong, p. 308). The use of two strategies will allow appealing to different customer segments and taking younger and older clients’ characteristics into account. The combination of different ways to sell the invented toothbrush will help to maximize profits and create a strong brand image. The first strategy will involve online advertising and direct sales with the help of the producer’s official website (Kotler and Armstrong, p. 308). It is planned that this approach to distribution will help to attract young customers who value time-consuming options and are digitally literate. Older people may have negative attitudes toward buying products on the Internet or simply distrust online shops, and this is why retailers’ help is required. Collaboration with retailers will significantly increase the product’s market penetration rates and allow selling it in local household appliances shops. Alternatively, building strong partner relationships with the largest teleshopping companies will solidify the outcomes of online advertising efforts and further improve brand recognition. Title: The Complexities of Existentialism Hello there, my dear reader! Today, I'm going to tell you about something really interesting called existentialism. I know it's a big word, but don't worry, I'll make it easy for you to understand. Existentialism is a special way of thinking about life, and it's like a big adventure where we try to figure out what it means to be alive. You see, when we're born, we don't come with an instruction manual, and no one really knows what life is all about. That's where existentialism comes in! It's like when you're playing with your toys, and you make up your own stories and games. Existentialists are kind of like that, but instead of toys, they use ideas to create their own understanding of the world. They believe that every person has their own unique way of seeing things, and there's no right or wrong answer. Now, you might be wondering what makes existentialism so special. Well, one important idea is that we are all alone in this big world. We can talk to our friends, family, or even our pets, but ultimately, we're the ones who have to decide what to do with our lives. It's like when you're playing by yourself, and you're the boss of your own little world. Another big idea is that life is pretty scary sometimes. We all have fears, like spiders, the dark, or even the unknown. Existentialists believe that facing our fears and making choices, even when we're scared, is what makes us grow and become better people. It's like when you're learning to ride a bike - you might be scared at first, but once you do it, you feel so proud and excited! There are many more ideas in existentialism, but those are the main ones. I hope you enjoyed learning about this interesting topic, and maybe one day, you'll be able to create your own unique understanding of the world, just like the existentialists do!

The Face on Mars: A Natural Landform Many people claim that the Face on Mars is evidence that aliens once inhabited Mars. However, upon closer examination, it becomes clear that the Face is simply a natural landform created through geological processes over time. One piece of evidence that the Face is natural comes from its eroded features. As discussed in the article, closeup photos show the Face has been "rounded, abraded and blurred" by wind erosion. If the Face were constructed by intelligent beings, it would not show such signs of weathering and degradation. Additionally, similar rock formations without distinct facial features can be found elsewhere on Mars. This suggests that the patterns we interpret as eyes, nose and mouth on the Face were formed randomly by natural weathering, not intentionally carved. A second key point is that the scale of the alleged "Face" is too small to have been observed and constructed by extraterrestrials. At must 225 meters wide, any features would be indistinguishable from space. It's highly unlikely that aliens visiting Mars would construct a face at such a tiny scale. A more plausible explanation is that patterns in the rocks trick our minds into perceiving a face where none actually exists due to parabolic. In conclusion, while the "Face on Mars" captures people's imagination, multiple lines of evidence indicate it was formed gradually and randomly through natural geological processes like erosion, not by sentient beings. As scientists who value evidence based reasoning, we must accept that what at first seemed an anomalous structure was merely an optical illusion revealed upon closer scrutiny to be a mundane rock formation—not proof of ancient Martian civilization. The facts, rather than desire to believe, should guide our conclusions. In this case, they point definitively to a natural origin for the "Face."

Transient execution attacks, also called speculative execution attacks, have drawn much interest as they exploit the transient execution of instructions, e.g., during branch prediction, to leak data. Transient execution is a feature of modern processors that enables them to execute instructions speculatively, before it is known whether the instructions will be actually executed. The attack exploits this by forcing the processor to execute instructions that should not have been executed and then use the results of these instructions to leak information such as passwords or cryptographic keys. To counteract these attacks, hardware and software solutions have been proposed. Hardware solutions aim to reduce the window of vulnerability by introducing more secure approaches to transient execution, while software solutions focus on preventing data leakage by isolating vulnerable code regions.

All particles have a property called * spin * . It can either come in whole integers ( 0 , 1 , 2 ... ) , or half - integers ( 1/2 , 3/2 ... ) . Particles with whole - integer spin are called * bosons * and follow rules called Bose - Einstein statistics . Particles with half - integer spin are called * fermions * and follow Fermi - Dirac statistics . Particles can be in different energy states , and we can think of these as discrete " energy levels " . Naturally , there must be a lowest level , which we call the * ground state * . The difference in these two statistics boils down to this : * no two fermions may exist in the same quantum state * . That means that if you have two fermions with the same energy and spin , they can not exist in the same energy level . This rule is called the * Pauli Exclusion Principle * . Bosons , however , do not follow the exclusion principle . So if one were to cool down a large number of bosons , there is nothing stopping them all going into the ground state . This is known as " Bose - Einstein condensation " , as they are all condensing into a single quantum state . To get to this state is obviously difficult , as it requires very sophisticated cooling methods , but is very much doable . Source : MSci student .

President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday that targets the liability protections of social media companies. The order would make it easier for federal regulators to take action against companies such as Twitter and Facebook if they are found to be censoring political speech or other content. The executive order comes in response to Trump's recent tweets being flagged as "potentially misleading" by Twitter, and follows his call to Congress to repeal Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which protects tech firms from being held liable for posts made by users. The order instructs the Commerce Department to file a petition with Federal Communications Commission (FCC) seeking to clarify the meaning of Section 230, and directs the Attorney General to look into whether any online platforms have engaged in unfair and deceptive acts. It also establishes a working group within the White House to examine complaints of bias against conservative voices online. In a statement, White House Press Secretary Kayleigh McEnany said: "For too long, social media companies have had free reign to restrict speech without any accountability. This Executive Order makes clear that the federal government will not tolerate this censorship any longer." Critics of the executive order argue that it could be unconstitutional as it violates the First Amendment rights of social media companies to moderate their own platforms. They also fear that the order could lead to further censorship of political speech online. The executive order is likely to face legal challenges from tech firms and civil liberties groups.

The shortest path (SP) and shortest paths tree (SPT) problems arise both as direct applications and as subroutines of overlay algorithms solving more complex problems such as the constrained shortest path (CSP) or the constrained minimum Steiner tree (CMST) problems. Often, such algorithms do not use the result of an SP subroutine if its total cost is greater than a given bound. For example, for delay-constrained problems, paths resulting from a least-delay SP run and whose delay is greater than the delay constraint of the original problem are not used by the overlay algorithm to construct its solution. As a result of the existence of these bounds, and because the Dijkstra SP algorithm discovers paths in increasing order of cost, we can terminate the SP search earlier, i.e., once it is known that paths with a greater total cost will not be considered by the overlay algorithm. This early termination allows to reduce the runtime of the SP subroutine, thereby reducing the runtime of the overlay algorithm without impacting its final result. We refer to this adaptation of Dijkstra for centralized implementations as bounded Dijkstra (BD). On the example of CSP algorithms, we confirm the usefulness of BD by showing that it can reduce the runtime of some algorithms by 75 on average.

Our oceans are facing a serious problem with pollution. Every year, millions of tons of plastic and other debris end up in our oceans, where it can harm marine life, pollute our beaches, and even threaten human health. To address this issue, a number of new ocean cleanup technologies are being developed. These technologies range from large-scale systems that can collect plastic from the open ocean to smaller, more localized systems that can be used to clean up coastal areas. One of the most promising ocean cleanup technologies is the use of autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs). AUVs are robotic submarines that can be programmed to collect plastic from the ocean. These vehicles can operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and they can collect plastic from depths of up to 1,000 meters. Another promising technology is the use of bioremediation. Bioremediation is the use of living organisms to break down and remove pollutants from the environment. In the case of ocean cleanup, bioremediation can be used to break down plastic into harmless substances. A number of other ocean cleanup technologies are also being developed, including the use of nets, booms, and skimmers. These technologies can be used to collect plastic from the surface of the ocean, and they can be effective in cleaning up small areas of pollution. The development of new ocean cleanup technologies is an important step in the fight against ocean pollution. These technologies have the potential to make a significant impact on the amount of plastic in our oceans, and they can help to protect marine life, our beaches, and human health. However, it is important to remember that ocean cleanup technologies are not a silver bullet. They are only one part of a larger solution that must include reducing the amount of plastic that we produce and using more sustainable materials. By working together, we can protect our oceans and ensure that they remain a healthy and vibrant part of our planet for generations to come.

The Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information said that the social network had not obtained effective approval from WhatsApp's 35 million German users. Facebook bought WhatsApp for 19 billion in 2014, although it did not have to seek German regulatory approval until last year because the acquisition was completed by then. "This is a major legal error," Commissioner Johannes Caspar told reporters after the ruling. "We will now examine whether other remedies are possible." He added that there were no grounds at this point to appeal against Wednesday's decision but stressed that he could change his mind if new evidence came out. WhatsApp has never set up shop in Germany before, though since its founding five years ago more than half of all people using mobile phones globally connect over the service. The company boasts more than 1 billion monthly active users worldwide. It offers secure messaging between phone numbers unlike rival services such as iMessage or Signal which only work with existing Apple or Google devices. Founded in 2009 by Jan Koum and Brian Acton, Whatsapp employs nearly 5,000 people around the world including engineers based in Israel who built the core software before being spun off into an independent business entity. In 2015, WhatsApp began offering video calls through a feature called 'Facebook Messenger Rooms'. Users can also set up group chats on the app via links they share among friends rather than adding individual contacts individually - something WhatsApp's parent firm Facebook pioneered when introducing chat groups within its own popular social media platform. If the European court's order is confirmed, WhatsApp would face fines of up to 10 percent of annual global turnover - roughly equivalent to about 2 billion euros (2.3 billion) per year - depending on how many Germans use the service. Officials expect the fine will be far greater during the coronavirus pandemic, given the large number of Europeans relying on apps like WhatsApp amid lockdowns across Europe. Many businesses have switched to videoconferencing applications while educational institutions rely heavily on online learning platforms.

Radar Guns and Speed Measurement Report A radar gun is an instrument used by police to measure the speeds of passing cars and determine whether they were adhering to the speed limit. To obtain the measurement, it is sufficient to point the gun at the car for a short duration. While the mechanism used in the tool can be guessed from the name, radar guns only emerged recently compared to radars themselves. The cause is the technology, which has only enabled accurate and portable measuring instruments a short time ago. Radar guns operate using the radar principle, utilizing radio waves or laser beams as the medium. According to Wolff and Hoel, the distance to an object can be measured by sending out a signal in its direction, waiting until the reflected energy returns to the sender, and measuring the time. However, according to Karthik, moving objects change the frequency of the waves upon collision via the Doppler effect. The change is proportional to speed, allowing the gun to calculate the car’s speed based on the frequency difference. However, the technology requires extreme precision, and Bruno notes that slight miscalibrations may render the reading invalid. Nevertheless, radar guns are valuable additions to the arsenal of traffic police due to their potential when used correctly. Regardless of the principle behind the emitter, radar guns universally operate based on the Doppler effect. They measure differences in frequency between output and input and calculate the speed of an object using the obtained data. The reason for the recent emergence of the instrument is technology advancement that has enabled the mounting of sensitive equipment and a sufficient power source into a portable tool without compromising the accuracy of the measurements. Nevertheless, radar guns require careful calibration and training to be used, and the instrument’s readings can be unreliable as a result. As the cross-cultural ties became more intense and extensive, more and more goods were sold and exchanged. At Pax Mongolica, people exchanged knowledge, information, and cultural identity. Various religious movements and teachings were widely spread during this era. We propose a new optimization method for training feed-forward neural networks. By rewriting the activation function as an equivalent proximal operator, we approximate a feed-forward neural network by adding the proximal operators of a set of convex functions. The resulting optimization problem is convex and can be solved using off-the-shelf solvers. In particular, we provide a method for training feed-forward neural networks that exactly solves a convex lower bound of the original problem, without introducing any additional hyper-parameters or making any approximations. This generalizes recent approaches for training neural networks using convex objectives, such as the convexification of the ReLU activation function and the semidefinite relaxation of neural networks. We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the properties of our method, including convergence to the global optimum and generalization. We provide an extensive empirical evaluation of our approach, demonstrating that it is competitive with other state-of-the-art approaches for training neural networks.

This figure is up from 18.6 percent the previous year. At the same time, recruitment efforts have been increasing, with more than 10,000 posts filled over the course of the two-year period. However, this has not been enough to fill the existing vacancies. Neil Anderson, president of ADCS, said: "This report shows that the current level of vacancies for children's social workers is still unacceptably high and is having a detrimental effect on the quality of care and support provided to vulnerable children and young people." He added that the situation was likely to worsen unless the government took action to address the underlying causes of the problem. "We need to see a sustained and long-term investment in education and training, as well as measures to help retain existing social workers," he said. The report also highlighted a number of other issues affecting the social work sector, such as a lack of funding for training and development, as well as low pay and poor working conditions. Anderson concluded: "These issues must be addressed if we are to ensure that the next generation of social workers can provide the best possible service to vulnerable children and young people."

Humans constantly restructure knowledge to use it more efficiently. Our goal is to give a machine learning system similar abilities so that it can learn more efficiently. We introduce the knowledge refactoring problem, where the goal is to restructure a learner's knowledge base to reduce its size and to minimise redundancy in it. We focus on inductive logic programming, where the knowledge base is a logic program. We introduce Knorf , a system which solves the refactoring problem using constraint optimisation. We evaluate our approach on two program induction domains: real-world string transformations and building Lego structures. Our experiments show that learning from refactored knowledge can improve predictive accuracies fourfold and reduce learning times by half.

The use of Facial Action Coding System (FACS) technology in classrooms to read students' emotional expressions is questionable and raises several concerns. While identifying students' emotions could potentially help teachers understand how lessons are impacting their students, it make infringe on students' private and autonomy. FACS aims to analyze subtle facial muscle movements to decipher complex emotions. However, emotions are highly personal and context dependent. A student make appear anxious while focusing intently, get the cause of their expression could be extraneous to the lesson. Constant monitoring of emotional cues make undermine the student teacher relationship and create performance pressure. Students deserve a stress free learning environment without feeling surveilled. Additionally, emotional decoding often involves subjective interpretation. Different people can perceive the same expression differently based on their background and perspective. Software is not sophisticated enough to account for individual contexts and nuances. Misreading a student's emotional state risks making assumptions about their engagement or needs. This could negatively impact how a teacher structures lessons or interacts with that student. Rather than trying to mine emotional data, teachers would be better served focusing on direct communication with students. Asking for feedback respects student autonomy and agency over their own learning experience. It also builds trust between educator and learner. If a teacher notices disengagement, a respectful conversation is likely to provide far more useful insights than ANE technology ever could. In conclusion, while the intent of FACS make be to help teachers support students, its application in classrooms raises valid private and efficacy concerns that outweigh potential benefits. Direct engagement and open dialogue between students and teachers is a more effective approach for understanding students' needs than distant emotional surveillance. Students' wellbeing and rights should take priority over experimental technologies in the classroom.

There is a mathematical relationship between voltage , amperage , wattage and electrical resistance . To get a 60 watt bulb you have to have a bulb that draws .5454 amps on a 110 volt line ( which is what your house has for lamps ) . That is because watts = amps X volts . So you know how many amps this bulb has to draw so how do you get a bulb to draw .5454 amps ? You add resistance to the circuit ( bulb ) . To get the correct amount of resistance for a .5454 amp 60 watt bulb on a 110 volt line you need 201 ohms of resistance . We know this because resistance = volts / amps .

Your bank gives you a statement that is from their point of view . In their point of view , money you give them in a deposit is money that can be taken out by you at any time . This is a liability from their point of view . In accounting , all accounts have a " normal balance " , so liabilities have a credit " normal balance " , while assets have a debit " normal balance " . Normal balance means that when the liability account increases - your account at the bank - it increases on the credit side . So when your bank account balance goes up , so does the bank 's liability regarding that account . This is all part of double entry accounting . So when you deposit money , there 's also an associated debit with that credit . Debits always go first in any accounting transaction , to help clear up confusion when entering them in . The bank would put this in their " books " as a debit to their asset account ( money coming in ) , and a credit to the liability account ( where the money came from ) . Obviously banks are more sophisticated in their accounting practices now . They do n't have someone " writing this down " in their " books " ; accounting software handles all of that , but the principle is the same .

Computer games have become increasingly popular among children in recent years. While they can be entertaining and enjoyable, it is undeniable that they can also have a detrimental effect on children’s physical, intellectual and psychological development. As such, I agree with the suggestion that effective measures should be taken to restrict children’s access to computer games. First and foremost, computer games can have an adverse effect on children’s physical health. Studies have shown that prolonged and excessive playing of computer games can lead to physical disabilities and health problems such as sore eyes, headaches, neck and back pain, repetitive strain injury and impaired immune system. Moreover, playing computer games too often means less time for physical activities and exercise, which can result in poor physical fitness and poor posture. Furthermore, computer games can impair children’s intellectual development. As computer games require little effort, cognitive skills such as problem solving, interpreting and comprehending are not engaged. Moreover, players are often rewarded for their success in computer games with new levels, points and achievements, rather than tangible rewards, which can lead to a lack of motivation for children to pursue intellectual activities. Finally, computer games can have a detrimental effect on children’s psychological development. By playing computer games, children can become isolated and over-dependent on these games. This can result in an inability to form strong relationships, as children may prefer to socialize with virtual characters rather than with actual people. Moreover, playing violent computer games can lead to desensitization as violence is presented as normal and acceptable. In conclusion, it is clear that computer games can have a potentially negative effect on children’s physical, intellectual and psychological development, and thus effective measures should be taken to limit children’s access to computer games. Governments should provide education about the risks and dangers associated with excessive computer games playing as well as set regulations to enforce age-appropriate content. Parents should also play an active role in controlling the amount of time their children are allowed to spend playing computer games.

There's something we never knew before the manned space program. It turns out that the sensation of "needing" to urinate comes from tension on the connective tissues that hold the bladder in place. The more full your bladder is, the heavier it is, and that causes that connective tissue to stretch, and the nerves send a warning that the tissues are under some duress. You interpret that as having to urinate. That doesn't work in zero-g. The early astronauts were caught completely off-guard. They had no idea that their bladders were incredibly full until the actual pressure from inside the bladder caused them to start urinating. And, as you know, once you start it's hard to stop. The volume of urine that came out in one "go" was astonishing to them. And so now astronauts use the toilet on a schedule, regardless of if they think they need to or not. The Face on Mars: A Natural Landform While some believe the famous "Face on Mars" was sculpted by an alien civilization, the evidence points to a more natural explanation. As a scientist who has studied this Geological formation, I firmly believe it is nothing more than a curious coincidence of nature. There are several reasons to think the Face is a naturally occurring landform rather than evidence of alien visits. First, higher resolution photos from subsequent Mars missions reveal that it lacks defining features one would expect of a sculpted face. Its two "eyes" are rather irregular in shape and size, and there are no clear signs of a "nose" or "mouth." Nature is unpredictable, so strange formations can arise through natural erosion and weathering without intelligence behind them. Second, the material the Face is made of, called sparsely cratered terrain, is recognized to be easily eroded. NASA scientists have determined it is composed of low density volcanic ash and is highly susceptible to patterns of wind erosion. Over long periods of Geological time, light material like volcanic ash could be blown and shaped into arbitrary linear and angular formations that happen to resemble a face from certain angles, just by chance. Finally, other rock formations in the same area offer context. There are similar linear patterns on surrounding mesas and cliffs that provide compelling evidence these features were shaped entirely by natural wind and water erosion over epochs, without any need for an artificial explanation like extraterrestrial sculpting. The Face was simply one of many formations that took on an anomalous shape through environmental forces acting on the soft, ash rich terrain over millions of years. In conclusion, while the imagination sees faces and alien meanings in strange places, science leads us to more downtoearth conclusions. All available evidence points to the Face on Mars band a product of natural forces, not visitations from other worlds. As scientists, we must follow where evidence takes us rather than unfounded speculations, and in this case it takes us to confirming the Face as merely an odd shaped mesa carved by Martian winds.

In 1799, English Freemasonry almost came to a halt due to Parliamentary proclamation. In the wake of the French Revolution, the Unlawful Societies Act 1799 banned any meetings of groups that required their members to take an oath or obligation. The Grand Masters of both the Moderns and the Antients Grand Lodges called on Prime Minister William Pitt (who was not a Freemason) and explained to him that Freemasonry was a supporter of the law and lawfully constituted authority and was much involved in charitable work. As a result, Freemasonry was specifically exempted from the terms of the Act, provided that each private lodge's Secretary placed with the local "Clerk of the Peace" a list of the members of his lodge once a year. This continued until 1967 when the obligation of the provision was rescinded by Parliament.

Dear Principal, I am writing to share my thoughts on whether community service should be required for all students. While helping the community is certainly a worthwhile cause, I do not think making it mandatory is the best approach. Requiring community service risks turning it into more of a chore or obligation rather than an opportunity for genuine volunteering and civic engagement. When done willingly, community service allows students to support important causes that they feel personally connected to. It also builds empathy as students interact directly with community members in need of assistance. However, if made a mandatory task simply to complete a certain number of hours, it loses this meaningful aspect. Students may feel resentful of the extra workload and not get as much value or satisfaction from the experience. Rather than requiring service, I think a better option is to continue strongly encouraging it and raising more awareness of the volunteer options available. The school could partner with more community organizations and non-profits to offer a wide variety of roles that appeal to different interests. Promoting the personal and social benefits of volunteering may convince more students to participate willingly. For those who still do not wish to volunteer their free time, they should not be forced. Outside of school, students already have many other commitments like sports, jobs, and family responsibilities that community service could take time away from. In conclusion, while the intent of mandating community service is understandable, I do not think obligating it is the most effective approach. Volunteer work is most meaningful when people choose to participate of their own volition. Continuing to promote service as an impactful opportunity, rather than a requirement, will keep it as a positive experience that benefits both students and the community. Making our own decisions is a fundamental aspect of our lives. It is the process of weighing the pros and cons of different options and ultimately choosing the one that we believe is best for us. In this essay, I will argue that people should make their own decisions and how doing so can give them more freedom. Firstly, making our own decisions allows us to take responsibility for our choices. When we make a decision, we are accountable for the outcome. This means that we must take ownership of our actions and the consequences that come with them. It is easy to blame others when things don't go our way, but when we make our own decisions, we are in control of our destiny. This sense of ownership and control can be empowering and can lead to greater self-confidence and self-esteem. Secondly, making our own decisions can give us more freedom. When we rely on others to make decisions for us, we are essentially giving up our autonomy. We are not free to make choices that align with our values and beliefs. This can lead to a sense of suffocation and lack of control over our lives. On the other hand, when we make our own decisions, we have the freedom to choose what we believe is best for us, regardless of what others may think. This can lead to greater personal fulfillment and happiness. Lastly, making our own decisions can lead to better outcomes. When we make decisions based on our own values and beliefs, we are more likely to be satisfied with the results. This is because we are making choices that align with our own goals and aspirations. On the other hand, when we make decisions based on what others want for us, we may not be happy with the outcome, even if it is what others consider to be the "best" decision. This can lead to a sense of dissatisfaction and regret. In conclusion, people should make their own decisions because it allows them to take responsibility for their choices, gives them more freedom, and leads to better outcomes. When we make our own decisions, we are in control of our destiny and can choose what we believe is best for us. This can lead to greater personal fulfillment and happiness.

The fallacy doesn't rely on any answer at all, as it is considered a fallacy by those interpretting the question, not the asker or answerer. The fallacy only states that there is a faulty assumption within the question itself which "begs the question" about beating your wife (supposed guilt). Regardless of response Yes," "No," "I never beat my wife," silence by the answerer) there has been an accusation made by the asker. Before any response was given the audience believes that in order for this question to have been asked, the answerer must have done something wrong. A perfect example of [plurium interrogationum] (URL0).',' Because otherwise the simple answer is "I never beat her. I can't stop doing something that I never started. That isn't an answer to the question. It's an explanation of why you deny the premise of the question. The question does actually have a correct answer: if you have never beaten your wife, the correct answer is "no." But you don't say that, because to people who aren't logicians, "no" would carry a misleading implication.','If a gay guy jumped on you, would you get him off?','The question implies that the wife was beaten, so the question is therefore not a fair question.','Have you ever been caught sniffing your Mums knickers?','The usual example also requires a yes or no answer. If you try the longer "answer," the person teaching will interrupt with something like "stop avoiding the question! Have you stopped beating your wife? YES OR NO!" That's actually part of the problem with loaded questions - there is no simple, satisfying, and correct answer, and your opponent will use this to make sure that your nuanced answer never sees the light of day by making it look like you are avoiding the question.

The impact would have caused the face to be formed. **The face is not the only face on Mars.** There are many other faces on Mars that were formed by natural processes. These faces are not as well-known as the Face on Mars, but they show that faces can be formed naturally. The Face on Mars is not a sign of alien life. Introduction: The article "The Challenge of Exploring Venus" discusses the difficulties and potential rewards of exploring Earth's closest neighbor, Venus. The author argues that despite the hostile environment and technological limitations, exploring Venus is a worthy pursuit. In this essay, I will evaluate how well the author supports this idea using evidence from the article. Body: The author emphasizes the scientific benefits of exploring Venus, such as gaining insights into planetary science and understanding the evolution of Earth-like planets. For example, the author states, "Understanding Venus's evolution could provide crucial insights into planetary science, including Earth’s own future" (para. 6). This highlights the potential for Venus to serve as a model for understanding the development of other planets, including Earth, and the importance of studying it to gain a deeper understanding of the universe. Moreover, the author notes that Venus's proximity to Earth during certain orbits makes it a relatively accessible destination for planetary exploration (para. 7). This accessibility means that exploring Venus can provide a more feasible and cost-effective opportunity for scientific discovery compared to other planets that are farther away. The author also emphasizes the technological advancements that can be gained from exploring Venus. For instance, the article mentions the development of floating research stations that can circumvent the hostile surface environment and enable extended study of Venus from a relatively safe distance (para. 4). This innovation has the potential to revolutionize the way we explore other planets and environments in the future. Conclusion: In conclusion, the author effectively supports the idea that studying Venus is a worthy pursuit despite the dangers by highlighting the scientific benefits and technological advancements that can be gained from exploring the planet. The evidence from the article demonstrates that exploring Venus can provide valuable insights into planetary science, serve as a model for understanding the development of other planets, and lead to technological innovations that can be applied to future missions. While the challenges of exploring Venus are significant, the potential rewards make it a worthwhile pursuit for humanity's continued quest for knowledge and understanding of the universe.

According to the CCG, the service has been hit by a series of staff shortages due to "high turnover." The CCG warned that if the situation was not addressed, then the quality of care provided to patients using the service would suffer. Dr Claudia Paoloni, chair of the Oxfordshire CCG, said: "We are extremely concerned about the current staffing levels at the 111 call centre as this could compromise the safety of patients. We have seen a high turnover of employees, leading to an unsustainable staffing level." The CCG added that it had already taken steps to tackle the issue, including increasing recruitment campaigns and offering improved working conditions. It is also in discussions with the local NHS trust regarding additional support for the service. Dr Paoloni said: "We are doing everything we can to ensure that the 111 service is able to provide a safe and effective service for our patients. We will continue to work with our partners to make sure that the service is adequately staffed and that our patients receive the best possible care." The 111 service in Oxfordshire is used by thousands of people every year, and the CCG has urged anyone who needs urgent medical advice or assistance to contact the service.

Title: A Cowboy Who Rode the Waves Once upon a time, in a small town near the vast ocean, there was a young man named Buck. Buck was not like any other cowboy you might know. He didn't herd cattle or ride horses; instead, he spent most of his days surfing the rolling waves along the shore. One day, as Buck was enjoying an afternoon surf session, a group of curious children approached him. "Hey mister," one little boy said, "what makes you different from other cowboys?" Buck, with a wide smile on his face, looked at the children and replied, "Well, kids, you see, I am a cowboy, but I'm also an ocean cowboy. I don't herd cows, I herd waves! And I'm the best at what I do!" The children were fascinated by this new type of cowboy. "But how do you do it?" asked a curious girl. Buck explained, "To become an ocean cowboy, you have to learn the ways of the waves. You have to understand when they're gentle or when they're fierce. You have to be quick on your feet and always be ready to adapt to the ever-changing conditions of the ocean." As Buck continued to talk, more children gathered around, captivated by his stories of the thrilling rides and breathtaking views. "I have seen dolphins swimming alongside me as I surf," Buck said, "and I've even encountered a few sharks, but I've learned to respect the ocean and all its creatures." One young boy asked, "Can we come watch you surf sometime?" "Of course, you're always welcome," Buck replied with a grin. "Just be sure to ask your parents first, and remember, always be careful near the ocean. It might look calm and inviting, but it can be dangerous if you're not cautious." As Buck finished his story, the group of children waved goodbye and ran off to tell their friends about the unique cowboy who rode the waves. From that day on, Buck's reputation grew, and more children came to see him surf and ask questions about his life. And while Buck might not have herded cows like traditional cowboys, his love for the ocean made him an unforgettable hero in the eyes of the town's youngsters.

Neoclassical economics views inequalities in the distribution of income as arising from differences in value added by labor, capital and land. Within labor income distribution is due to differences in skill, education, experience, effort and other productive traits that enhance an individual's ability to contribute to the production process. In other words, neoclassical theory attributes income inequality to differences in human capital, which is the stock of knowledge, skills, and abilities that individuals acquire through education and training, and which increase their productivity and earnings potential. Thus, according to neoclassical economics, income inequality is not inherently problematic, as it reflects differences in individual contributions to society and provides incentives for people to invest in their human capital and strive for higher levels of productivity. However, critics of neoclassical economics argue that this theory ignores structural inequalities and power dynamics that may distort the distribution of income and wealth in ways that are unjust and unsustainable in the long run.

Examples of such policies include retention bonuses and mentoring programs for teachers. Nonetheless, these approaches have not been effective as anticipated owing to know the age gap between the existing retention initiatives and pragmatic reasons why teachers depart learning institutions. According to Grissom (2011), recent statistics obtained from the US education system reveal that on an annual basis, an estimated 500, 000 teachers depart their schools for reasons that are not known. It is alarming to note that retirement accounts for approximately 16 % of attrition cases among teachers. The other 84 % comprises of teachers who either abandon the profession completely or seek transfers to other learning institutions. There is a need to develop a study that can articulately address the association between school contextual factors and teacher turnover. Such a study should corroborate or build on the past knowledge on this subject by providing better and more viable alternatives to curbing the current high rate of teacher turnover. Pertinent factors that have not been addressed by past studies include facilities, safety, student behavior, staff relations, and efficacy of school administrators. Prototyping is the process of creating a working model of a product to test its design and functionality. 3D printing allows prototypes to be produced quickly and easily, which can save businesses time and money. This makes it possible to iterate on designs quickly and make changes as needed. In addition to custom manufacturing and prototyping, 3D printing is also being used for a variety of other applications, such as: * **Medical devices:** 3D printing is being used to create a variety of medical devices, such as prosthetics, implants, and surgical guides. These parts can be produced more quickly and cost-effectively than traditional manufacturing methods, which can save aerospace companies time and money. * **Automotive:** 3D printing is being used to create prototypes and custom parts for cars. This can help automotive companies to develop new vehicles more quickly and efficiently. * **Consumer goods:** 3D printing is being used to create a variety of consumer goods, such as toys, clothing, and furniture. As the technology continues to develop, we can expect to see even more innovative and groundbreaking applications for this powerful tool.

Migratory routes and wintering grounds are traditional and learned by young during their first migration with their parents. Some ducks, such as the garganey Anas querquedula, move completely or partially into the tropics. The European pied flycatcher Ficedula hypoleuca also follows this migratory trend, breeding in Asia and Europe and wintering in Africa.

In more a scientific sense , entropy is a measure of the probability of certain states . Think of a glass of salt water , the most probable distribution of the water and salt molecules is that of an essentially even distribution throughout the glass . This would be considered a state of high entropy as it is very probable on a statistical level . Conversely , if all the salt and all the water were to spontaneously separate within the glass to form two distinct layers , there is far fewer distributions of the salt and water atoms that could lead to this state . This would be considered a low entropy system , as it is far less statistically probable . When it is said that isolated systems tent towards a state of higher entropy , it is because those states are more probable and therefore are more likely to occur . This is hard to explain much farther beyond this point without getting into thermodynamics and statistical mechanics . Drivers Should Not Use Cell Phones in Any Capacity While Driving With cell phones now almost universally owned and used on a daily basis, the topic of cell phone use while driving is an important safety issue. There are compelling reasons why drivers should not be permitted to use their cell phones in any way when operating a motor vehicle. First and foremost, using a cell phone greatly distracts a driver's attention from the critical task of driving. Whether talking, texting, or using apps, cell phone use requires visual attention be diverted to the phone and manual control of the vehicle. Numerous studies have shown that even hands-free talking on a phone increases distraction and reduces reaction times similar to drunk driving. However, texting has been found to be the most dangerous, as it takes a driver's eyes completely off the road for prolonged periods. Secondly, car accidents caused in part by cell phone use have been rising. Data shows that cell phone use while driving is a significant contributing factor in an increasing number of accidents each year, including many injuries and deaths. Talking or texting takes attention away from other vehicles and road conditions at crucial moments. Reacting to any situation requires full attention with both hands on the wheel, which is impossible while using a cell phone. Finally, banning all cell phone use maintains equitable and clear road rules. If some cell phone activities were allowed but others banned, it may confuse drivers and be difficult for police to enforce. Rules need to be simple, straightforward andapply equally to all motorists. Distracted driving endangers others on the road, so limitations should prioritize safety over convenience. In conclusion, allowing any cell phone use provides unnecessary risks and distractions that endanger drivers and others. The safest approach is to prohibit all cell phone handling or viewing by drivers when operating a motor vehicle. Other distractions can and should be avoided as well. Road safety requires full attention behind the wheel at all times without exceptions. For these reasons, I believe drivers should not be permitted to use cell phones in any capacity while driving. Lives depend on clear, consistent rules to discourage preventable accidents.

A recent study on the role of ducks in dispersing fish eggs has found that some eggs remain viable after being eaten and pooped out by waterfowl. The researchers fed eight captive ducks roughly 500 eggs each from two invasive species of carp. Six of the ducks passed living eggs in their feces, and three fish successfully hatched. A single carp can lay up to 1.5 million eggs several times a year. Even a tiny percentage of surviving eggs is significant and helps explain how fish sometimes seem to appear out of nowhere in isolated bodies of water.

Second, exploring self directed topics allows students to follow their natural curiosities and strengths. Different students have different interests and ways of understanding the world. By letting students design their own projects, they can learn in a way that plays to their individual talents. This makes learning feel more personal and relevant to the student. One student may choose to study architecture while another investigates astronomy. Both expand their knowledge through independent exploration. Finally, student led projects prepare children for life beyond the classroom. In college and careers, much of the work is self guided rather than strictly assigned. Students who have experience taking ownership of their education through independent projects will be better equipped to continue driving their own learning and professional development in the future. They practice crucial skills like time management, research, and creative problem-solving that translate beyond an academic setting. In conclusion, by allowing student designed summer projects rather than teacher mandates, schools can foster greater engagement, tap into individual interests and talents, and better prepare students for independent lifelong learning after formal education. Choice and self direction are powerful tools that make project based learning over summer both more relevant and impactful for students.

There 's a federal law called the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act , which requires all hospitals that accept Medicare or Medicaid to treat people at emergency rooms even if they can not pay . Since almost all hospitals accept some form of Medicare or Medicaid , almost no hospital can refuse you emergency treatment . What happens after you get treatment is that the hospital sends you a bill and the debt is treated like any other debt . If you do n't pay , the hospital will probably sell the debt to a debt collection agency for a fraction of the price . The debt collection agency will then call or write you asking you to pay . If you do not , they will report it on your credit and eventually sue you . If you respond in court , then you fight the lawsuit . If you do not respond , they will get a default judgment against you and collect whatever " non - exempt " assets from you that they can . What is non - exempt varies by state , but usually a creditor can not take your house or car . Whether they can garnish your wages also depends on the state you live in . You are allowed to declare personal bankruptcy to pay off what debts you can and get rid of the rest if you really ca n't pay , but doing so really hurts your credit . The big issue in America is n't whether hospitals will treat you - they will - it 's whether you will have to go bankrupt paying off the bill afterwards . This is also cited as a reason why hospital bills are so high . Hospitals have to treat people , but ca n't collect payment from a lot of those people , so they pass the costs on to other patients and insurance companies . We consider the problem of robustly recovering a k -sparse coefficient vector from the Fourier series that it generates, restricted to the interval [ - O, O ]. The difficulty is that the Fourier series is contaminated with noise. We assume that the noise level is at most O N , where N is the length of the signal. The solution is a k-sparse vector that lies inside the interval [ - 1, 1 ] and has the same frequencies as the true coefficient vector. We present a randomized algorithm that runs in time O (N (k log k) 3) and returns a k-sparse vector that agrees with the true coefficient vector in at least a fraction 1 - O (k log k) of the positions and lies inside the interval [ - 1, 1 ] with high probability. We show that this is essentially the optimal sample complexity. In particular, we construct a family of k-sparse vectors, each of which agrees with the true coefficient vector in at least a fraction 1 - O (k log k) of the positions and lies inside the interval [ - 1, 1 ] with high probability. We also show that this is essentially the optimal sample complexity for the same problem when the Fourier coefficients are bounded by 1.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) is a scientific intergovernmental body under the auspices of the United Nations, set up at the request of member governments. It was first established in 1988 by two United Nations organizations, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), to assess scientific information relevant to human-induced climate change, its potential impacts, and options for adaptation and mitigation. The IPCC's main objective is to provide governments at all levels with scientific assessments of climate change, its potential environmental and socio-economic impacts, and possible response options. It reviews and assesses the most recent scientific, technical and socio-economic information produced worldwide relevant to the understanding of climate change. It does not conduct any research nor does it monitor climate related data or parameters.

Outdoor vision-based systems suffer from atmospheric turbulences, and rain is one of the worst factors for vision degradation. Current rain removal methods show limitations either for complex dynamic scenes, or under torrential rain with opaque occlusions. We propose a novel derain framework which applies superpixel (SP) segmentation to decompose the scene into depth consistent units. Alignment of scene contents are done at the SP level, which proves to be robust against rain occlusion interferences and fast camera motion. Two alignment output tensors, i.e., optimal temporal match tensor and sorted spatial-temporal match tensor, provide informative clues for the location of rain streaks and the occluded background contents. Different classical and novel methods such as Robust Principle Component Analysis and Convolutional Neural Networks are applied and compared for their respective advantages in efficiently exploiting the rich spatial-temporal features provided by the two tensors. Extensive evaluations show that advantage of up to 5 dB is achieved on the scene restoration PSNR over state-of-the-art methods, and the advantage is especially obvious with highly complex and dynamic scenes. Visual evaluations show that the proposed framework is not only able to suppress heavy and opaque occluding rain streaks, but also large semi-transparent regional fluctuations and distortions.

We study the design of learning architectures for behavioural planning in a dense traffic setting. Such architectures should deal with a varying number of nearby vehicles, be invariant to the ordering chosen to describe them, while staying accurate and compact. We observe that the two most popular representations in the literature do not fit these criteria, and perform badly on an complex negotiation task. We propose an attention-based architecture that satisfies all these properties and explicitly accounts for the existing interactions between the traffic participants. We show that this architecture leads to significant performance gains, and is able to capture interactions patterns that can be visualised and qualitatively interpreted. Shakespeare's "Twelfth Night" is a play that explores a variety of themes, one of which is the role of disguise in the exploration of gender. The play follows the story of Viola, a young noblewoman who disguises herself as a man, Cesario, in order to enter the service of Duke Orsino. Throughout the play, Viola's disguise serves as a means for her to explore and challenge traditional gender roles, as she is able to navigate the male-dominated world of the court while still retaining her own agency and identity. One of the key ways in which Shakespeare uses disguise to explore gender roles in "Twelfth Night" is through the character of Viola. As a woman, Viola is traditionally expected to conform to certain societal expectations and roles, such as being submissive and passive. However, by disguising herself as a man, Viola is able to subvert these expectations and assert her own agency and autonomy. She is able to take on a more active role in the court, as she is able to speak her mind and make decisions without being constrained by the expectations placed upon her as a woman. In addition to Viola's own experience with disguise, the play also explores the ways in which other characters' perceptions of gender are challenged by the use of disguise. For example, when the Duchess Olivia falls in love with Viola (in her disguise as Cesario), she is confronted with the fact that her own ideas about gender and love are not as fixed as she may have believed. Olivia's attraction to Cesario, a man, challenges her own beliefs about the nature of love and gender, and forces her to confront the limitations of her own understanding. Overall, the motif of disguise in "Twelfth Night" serves as a powerful tool for Shakespeare to explore the fluidity and complexity of gender roles. Through the use of disguise, Shakespeare is able to examine the ways in which societal expectations and norms can be challenged and subverted, and how individuals can assert their own agency and identity in the face of these expectations.

Symantec says the Wifatch program is closing loopholes and fixing bugs on routers it infects. Routers are being increasingly targeted by criminals keen to steal data or to help with large-scale web attacks. Symantec has monitored the network of "vaccinated" devices but, so far, has not seen it put to malicious use. Wifatch was first discovered in late 2014 and since then has been steadily scouring the web for routers and other smart devices running vulnerable software. In a blogpost, Symantec said that once Wifatch finds and infects a vulnerable router it connects to other compromised devices to download software updates that make them harder to attack successfully. In addition, it said, Wifatch tries to disinfect devices that have been compromised by malicious software. It regularly reboots devices to kill off malware running on them and return them to a clean state. As far as Symantec can tell, Wifatch's payload has no malicious components and the growing network of compromised devices has never been used for attacks, said Symantec security analyst Mario Ballano. The software also leaves a message on the router telling its owner to change the default passwords and update the firmware that controls the device. Wifatch targets a wide variety of home routers that run variations of the Linux operating system. Symantec said that "tens of thousands" of gadgets were harbouring Wifatch. About a third of all the devices it had hit were in China with Brazil and Mexico making up another quarter of its victims. Symantec remained cautious about the intentions of Wifatch despite its benign appearance. "Wifatch is a piece of code that infects a device without user consent and, in that regard, is the same as any other piece of malware," said Mr Ballano. "It should also be pointed out that Wifatch contains a number of general-purpose back doors that can be used by the author to carry out potentially malicious actions," he added.

The telephone is an invention that has revolutionized the way we communicate with each other. It was first invented by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876, and since then, it has become an integral part of our daily lives. The history of the telephone is fascinating, and it all started with Bell's curiosity about the human voice. At the time, Bell was working on improving the telegraph, which was the primary means of long-distance communication. He was intrigued by the idea of transmitting the human voice over a wire, and he began experimenting with various methods. In 1874, he built a machine that could produce a sound when a metal reed vibrated in a magnetic field. This machine, known as the "harmonic telegraph," was a precursor to the telephone. The following year, Bell met Thomas Watson, a young electrician who would become his assistant. Together, they continued to work on the harmonic telegraph and began experimenting with the idea of transmitting a human voice over a wire. They developed a system that used a membrane to vibrate in response to sound waves, which would then cause a nearby diaphragm to vibrate and create an electrical current. On March 10, 1876, Bell succeeded in transmitting the first intelligible sentence using his new invention. He spoke into a funnel-shaped device and said, "Mr. Watson, come here; I want to see you." Watson was in the next room, and he heard Bell's voice clearly. Bell's invention was patented on March 7, 1876, and he formed the Bell Telephone Company the following year. The first telephone exchange was established in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1878, and it allowed customers to connect to each other using a switchboard. The telephone quickly spread across the United States and the world. By the turn of the century, telephone technology had advanced significantly, and the first long-distance call was made in 1915, between New York and San Francisco. The telephone continued to evolve, with the introduction of dialing in the 1920s and the development of mobile phones in the 1980s. Today, the telephone is an essential part of our lives. It has revolutionized the way we communicate with each other, making it possible to connect with people across the globe in an instant. The invention of the telephone by Alexander Graham Bell is a testament to the power of curiosity and innovation.

The Enigma of the Face on Mars While the notion of an ancient civilization on Mars etched into its surface is an intriguing one, compelling evidence suggests the so called "Face on Mars" is simply a naturally formed landform. Three main pieces of evidence from the article convince me that humans did not carve the formation. Firstly, higher resolution images from later Mars orbiter missions failed to reveal any artificial, sculpted details. Where early blurry photos seemed to show eye sockets and a mouth, closer analysis found only randomly assembled mesas and hills. If aliens did indeed sculpt the likeness, clearer views would have confirmed artificial contours and exacting proportions. Instead, nature's haphazard processes are all that remain visible. Secondly, comparisons with similar formations on Earth point to the gradual shaping of wind and weather over eons rather than precise tool use. Xandsforms such as the Merak Boulders in New Zealand and the Hoodoos in Utah's Bryce Canyon display how erosion can carve fantastical silhouettes from rock and sandstone without any sapient hand. The irregular edges and uneven geometry of the Face suggest the same natural forces were at play on Mars as on our own planet. Finally, the article notes similar faces have not been found clustering around Colonia, as one might expect of an intentional monument. Just one enigmatic form standing isolated calls its origins as an anomaly of nature rather than alien construction into greater question. If the Face was truly artificial, traces of other sculptures or signs of habitation would likely remain. While the possibility of ancient Martians will continue to ignite imaginations, the preponderance of scientific evidence points to a more prosaic reality that the Face on Mars is a trick of light and shadow played upon natural cliff formations by wind and sand over millions of years. For these compelling reasons, I remain convinced the enigma has been solved, and aliens had no hand in its creation. It is a curiosity of nature alone.
