Polemics about humanism have sometimes assumed paradoxical twists and turns. Early 20th century critics such as Ezra Pound, T. E. Hulme, and T. S. Eliot considered humanism to be sentimental "slop" (Hulme) [citation needed] or "an old bitch gone in the teeth" (Pound) and wanted to go back to a more manly, authoritarian society such as (they believed) existed in the Middle Ages. Postmodern critics who are self-described anti-humanists, such as Jean-Francois Lyotard and Michel Foucault, have asserted that humanism posits an overarching and excessively abstract notion of humanity or universal human nature, which can then be used as a pretext for imperialism and domination of those deemed somehow less than human. "Humanism fabricates the human as much as it fabricates the nonhuman animal," suggests Timothy Laurie, turning the human into what he calls "a placeholder for a range of attributes that have been considered most virtuous among humans (e.g. rationality, altruism), rather than most commonplace (e.g. hunger, anger) ." Nevertheless, philosopher Kate Soper notes that by faulting humanism for falling short of its own benevolent ideals, anti-humanism thus frequently "secretes a humanist rhetoric."

Feature selection (FS) has become an indispensable task in dealing with today's highly complex pattern recognition problems with massive number of features. In this study, we propose a new wrapper approach for FS based on binary simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (BSPSA). This pseudo-gradient descent stochastic algorithm starts with an initial feature vector and moves toward the optimal feature vector via successive iterations. In each iteration, the current feature vector's individual components are perturbed simultaneously by random offsets from a qualified probability distribution. We present computational experiments on datasets with numbers of features ranging from a few dozens to thousands using three widely-used classifiers as wrappers: nearest neighbor, decision tree, and linear support vector machine. We compare our methodology against the full set of features as well as a binary genetic algorithm and sequential FS methods using cross-validated classification error rate and AUC as the performance criteria. Our results indicate that features selected by BSPSA compare favorably to alternative methods in general and BSPSA can yield superior feature sets for datasets with tens of thousands of features by examining an extremely small fraction of the solution space. We are not aware of any other wrapper FS methods that are computationally feasible with good convergence properties for such large datasets. Keywords: Classification; feature selection; stochastic approximation; genetic algorithm

All of the value - the ' worth ' - produced by a country in a year is their GDP ( gross domestic product ) . This is value that is actually * created * out of nothing . A tree has some value , a house has more . If you turn a tree into a house , the difference between their values adds to the GDP . The country needs a way to represent all of this value in a simple and measurable way that everyone can agree on - money . The government can guarantee that currency ( coins and bills ) has a set value by making sure the banks all treat it the same , but they ca n't just give it any value they want . The total value of all the currency in a country ca n't be higher than the total wealth of the country ( which comes from GDP ) since that is what the currency represents in an abstract way . So the government can * print * more money no problem , but it 's the * total * value of * all * the money that is anchored to something in reality , not the individual value of each dollar . If they simply print more money without GDP going up , then the value of each individual dollar goes down by a bit to keep things equal . That 's basically what inflation is , the devaluing of currency over time .

Between Bingen and Bonn, the Middle Rhine flows through the Rhine Gorge, a formation which was created by erosion. The rate of erosion equaled the uplift in the region, such that over the last million years, a valley between 300 and 400 meters deep and 15 kilometers wide was created. The numerous castles and ruins along the Rhine, the vineyards and steep vineyards and the famous Loreley, the legendary rock on the western shore, are all part of the Rhine Gorge. The first fortification on the site of the Lorelei rock was a Roman signal tower, built in 1300. In 1726, the "Loreley" was built, a massive sandstone structure 37 meters high. In 1814, the tower was demolished, leaving behind only a 2.5 meter high wall. As a result of erosion, the rocky cliff was almost entirely destroyed in 1837 and 1842, then stabilized in 1843 with a wall. In 1862, a new castle was built, and the cliff was stabilized by means of steel rails. The new construction was demolished in 1923, and the Loreley was replaced by a wall. This, too, was demolished in 1924, leaving only a staircase and a parapet. The sandstone staircase, which provides access to the Loreley, was erected in 1994. In 1992, the United Nations recognized the Rhine Gorge, the surrounding Rhine Valley and the vineyards as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

I'm not aware that any US bank has any way to access your credit rating in France (especially as you basically don't have one!). In the US, banks are not the only way to get finance for a home. In many regions, there are plenty of "owner financed" or "Owner will carry" homes. For these, the previous owner will provide a private mortgage for the balance if you have a large (25%+) downpayment. No strict lending rules, no fancy credit scoring systems, just a large enough downpayment so they know they'll get their money back if they have to foreclose. For the seller, it's a way to shift a house that is hard to sell plus get a regular income. Often this mortgage is for only 3-10 years, but that gives you the time to establish more credit and then refinance. Maybe the interest rate is a little higher also, but again it's just until you can refinance to something better (or sell other assets then pay the loan off quick). For new homes, the builders/developers may offer similar finance. For both owner-will-carry and developer finance, a large deposit will trump any credit rating concerns. There is usually a simplified foreclosure process, so they're not really taking much of a risk, so can afford to be flexible. Make sure the owner mortgage is via a title company, trust company, or escrow company, so that there's a third party involved to ensure each party lives up to their obligations.

Traffic jams in big cities can start for a variety of reasons. Here are a few common causes: 1. Sudden stops: If a car in front of you suddenly slows down or stops, it can cause a traffic jam as other cars also slow down or stop to avoid a collision. 5. Congestion at intersections: If there are a lot of cars trying to turn at the same time, it can cause a traffic jam as cars have to wait their turn. Traffic jams can happen at the same time every day because many people have predictable schedules, such as commuting to and from work at the same times every day. movies When you go see a 3D movie in the theater, you are wearing special glasses that help your eyes see the images in three dimensions. The glasses have one red lens and one blue lens, and each eye sees a slightly different image. The brain combines these two images into a single three-dimensional image. To create a 3D movie, the filmmakers start with a regular 2D movie. They then use special software to add a second image that is slightly offset from the first one. This second image is called the "left eye" image, and it is meant to be seen by your left eye only. They also create a third image, called the "right eye" image, which is meant to be seen only by your right eye. When these three images are combined and shown on the big screen, your brain does the work of combining them into a single 3D image.

When faced with an important decision, it can be wise to seek advice from more than one person. Getting different perspectives allows you to view the decision from new angles and consider aspects you may not have thought of on your own. Multiple opinions help provide a more well-rounded understanding of the situation before committing to a choice. One benefit of seeking advice from multiple people is that each person likely has unique experiences that shape their point of view. By talking to individuals with diverse backgrounds, you can learn from their particular knowledge and past lessons. One friend may offer practical solutions based on what worked for them in a similar situation, while another can provide emotional support or point out new factors. No single person knows everything, so talking to more sources helps uncover well-informed insights you wouldn't get from just one discussion. Another advantage is that multiple opinions help balance each other out. Any one adviser may miss some important considerations or have unintentional biases that affect their advice. But consulting a variety of people reduces this risk, as their combined perspectives help identify flaws or blind spots in any particular recommendation. They can also challenge overly simplistic solutions and prompt deeper thought about pros and cons. If different advisors reach similar conclusions, it suggests their advice may be well-rounded and objective. Finally, multiple perspectives prevent "tunnel vision" that can occur when fixating on just one viewpoint. Looking at a decision from additional angles prevents being locked into the first idea presented. It opens your mind to creative alternatives and compromises you may not have thought of on your own. Considering nuanced input from trusted sources helps weigh all factors carefully before committing to a choice, reducing chances of future regret. In conclusion, seeking advice from multiple knowledgeable people provides a more well-informed starting point for any important decision. Their combined experiences and unbiased perspectives help create a fuller picture to consider before determining the best choice.

In this paper we study the dynamics of Klein bottle integrable systems on quasi-one dimensional manifolds. A special case of the L2 manifold and its submanifold are considered: the space of (1-2) -dimensional particle trajectories in conformally invariant metric spaces and their differential operators acting via the complex tensor product. Their dynamics can be described using the ordinary differential equation. By means of variational methods it is shown that the dynamics is reentrant if the structure operator acts as an identity operator on the metric space. An average European worker tends to produce more value in a given hour of work than the average worker in an Asian country. A seamstress in Bangladesh will produce less value than a line operator at a Volkswagen plant. Europeans have far more capital (embodied both in physical stuff like the plant in my example as well as non-physical things like education) that allow them to be more productive, on average.','In a modern service economy most jobs don't generate a lot of wealth. Wealth generating activities, such as manufacturing, research, agriculture and mining, only employ a minority of workers. The bulk of workers is employed in wealth redistributing activities, such as sales, marketing, finance, administration, tax, regulatory affairs, etc. Those activities are zero-sum. Think of the economy as a collection of row boats. Pairs of "workers" sitting in each row boat are rowing in opposite directions and the boats stay more or less stationary. Each worker is fighting for his employer's share of wealth. Those opposing sides might be two competitors but could also be a government bureaucrat vs. a corporate bureaucrat. Now, if one side rows harder the other side also has to row harder in order to win back their slice of the pie. But the end result is that both sides are rowing harder but the boat still hasn't shifted position. In Europe, the government is more interventionist than in Asia (there are stricter labor laws) and mandates that both sides should row a little less hard. Since both sides are forced to oblige, it doesn't make much of a difference to their individual incomes, neither to the aggregate wealth of the economy.', "Culture - Europeans believe that life is worth living and that having to work every waking hour is basically slavery. We're not going to put up with it and neither should you.

In marketing, facial action coding system can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of different marketing strategies and to make data-driven decisions about advertising campaigns. For example, a company can use the system to analyze customer reactions to different advertisements and adjust their approach accordingly to increase engagement and conversion rates. However, the system is not without its limitations. One of the main challenges with facial action coding is that it can be difficult to accurately classify certain emotions, particularly in complex or ambiguous situations. Many industrial machine learning (ML) systems require frequent retraining to keep up-to-date with constantly changing data. This retraining exacerbates a large challenge facing ML systems today: model training is unstable, i.e., small changes in training data can cause significant changes in the model's predictions. In this paper, we work on developing a deeper understanding of this instability, with a focus on how a core building block of modern natural language processing (NLP) pipelines - pre-trained word embeddings - affects the instability of downstream NLP models. We first empirically reveal a tradeoff between stability and memory: increasing the embedding memory 2 x can reduce the disagreement in predictions due to small changes in training data by 5 to 37 (relative). To theoretically explain this tradeoff, we introduce a new measure of embedding instability - the eigenspace instability measure - which we prove bounds the disagreement in downstream predictions introduced by the change in word embeddings. Practically, we show that the eigenspace instability measure can be a cost-effective way to choose embedding parameters to minimize instability without training downstream models, outperforming other embedding distance measures and performing competitively with a nearest neighbor-based measure. Finally, we demonstrate that the observed stability-memory tradeoffs extend to other types of embeddings as well, including knowledge graph and contextual word embeddings.

Acquiring High Resolution (HR) Magnetic Resonance (MR) images requires the patient to remain still for long periods of time, which causes patient discomfort and increases the probability of motion induced image artifacts. A possible solution is to acquire low resolution (LR) images and to process them with the Super Resolution Generative Adversarial Network (SRGAN) to create a super-resolved version. This work applies SRGAN to MR images of the prostate and performs three experiments. The first experiment explores improving the in-plane MR image resolution by factors of 4 and 8, and shows that, while the PSNR and SSIM (Structural SIMilarity) metrics are lower than the isotropic bicubic interpolation baseline, the SRGAN is able to create images that have high edge fidelity. The second experiment explores anisotropic super-resolution via synthetic images, in that the input images to the network are anisotropically downsampled versions of HR images. This experiment demonstrates the ability of the modified SRGAN to perform anisotropic super-resolution, with quantitative image metrics that are comparable to those of the anisotropic bicubic interpolation baseline. Finally, the third experiment applies a modified version of the SRGAN to super-resolve anisotropic images obtained from the through-plane slices of the volumetric MR data. The output super-resolved images contain a significant amount of high frequency information that make them visually close to their HR counterparts. Overall, the promising results from each experiment show that super-resolution for MR images is a successful technique and that producing isotropic MR image volumes from anisotropic slices is an achievable goal.

The use of Facial Action Coding System (FACS) technology to read students' emotional expressions in the classroom could provide both benefits and risks that require careful consideration. One potential benefit is that teachers may gain valuable insights into how their lessons are being received on an individual level. By understanding when students appear engaged, confused, bored or frustrated, educators could tailor their instruction strategies to better meet student needs and maximize learning. This technology may help identify students struggling with material who may not speak up, allowing teachers to provide additional support. However, there are also privacy and developmental risks to consider. Continually monitoring students' facial reactions may create an uncomfortable or restrictive environment where natural emotional responses are discouraged. Additionally, facial expressions do not always directly correlate to what students are thinking or feeling on the inside. Younger students, in particular, are still developing self-awareness and the ability to articulate their emotions. Relying too heavily on surface-level readings from FACS data could result in misinterpretations that negatively impact students. Overall, the use of emotional detection technology in classrooms requires careful oversight and limits. If implemented transparently and with student consent, FACS could offer insights to enhance teaching and learning experiences. However, reading too much into facial cues or violating student privacy would outweigh any benefits. A balanced approach that supplements, rather than replaces, teachers' observations and relationships with students seems most suitable if this technology is to be utilized at all. While promising as a tool, FACS alone cannot replace the human element that is most important to education.

In reinforcement learning (RL), agents often operate in partially observed and uncertain environments. Model-based RL suggests that this is best achieved by learning and exploiting a probabilistic model of the world. The conventional approach to learning such a model is to use maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to learn the transition and reward functions, which are assumed to be drawn from a known class of functions. This assumes that the agent knows exactly how its actions affect the environment, which is rarely true in practice. To address this, in this work we propose a method for learning a probabilistic model of the world in settings where the agent has only partial knowledge of the effect its actions have on the environment. This is achieved by using the ideas of confounded prediction and causal inference to learn a model of the world that is invariant to the effect of confounding variables. Our approach is implemented in a novel way as a model-based RL agent. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method in two different settings. First, we show that it improves exploration by evaluating it in a tabular exploration task. Second, we present results from an implementation of our method as a model-based RL agent that is competitive with several other model-based approaches. Healthcare is a fundamental human right, and the model of healthcare a nation chooses can have a significant impact on the health and well-being of its citizens. There are four main models of healthcare systems: single-payer, multi-payer, privatized, and national health insurance. Each model has its advantages and disadvantages, and their effectiveness varies depending on the specific context in which they are implemented. In this essay, we will evaluate these models and discuss their effectiveness in providing quality healthcare to citizens. Single-payer healthcare, also known as a single-tier or national healthcare system, is a model in which a single public agency collects taxes and pays for all healthcare expenses. This model is often associated with countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, and Taiwan. In this system, private healthcare providers can exist, but they must operate within the framework set by the public agency, and patients are not responsible for paying out-of-pocket expenses. One of the primary advantages of a single-payer system is its equity. Since healthcare is funded through general taxation, everyone contributes to the system and has access to care regardless of their ability to pay. This eliminates the financial barriers that can prevent people from seeking necessary medical treatment. Additionally, single-payer systems tend to have lower administrative costs due to the centralization of payment processing. This allows for more resources to be allocated directly to patient care. However, single-payer systems can also have some drawbacks. Because the public agency has control over healthcare spending, there may be instances where certain treatments or services are deemed too expensive and are not covered. This can lead to rationing of care, which can be controversial and difficult for patients and providers. Furthermore, single-payer systems can be less responsive to local needs, as decisions about healthcare provision are made at a national level.

We all have our own philosophies on life, and how we should live it. Thomas Jefferson seemed to suggest that being idle was not ideal, famously saying, “Determine never to be idle.” While this can be excellent advice, it is also important to balance it by embracing the value of doing nothing once in a while. Doing something productive all the time can lead to overwhelming stress and exhaustion that can set us back further as opposed to moving us forward. This inactivity can produce a welcome relief that can give us the mental break needed to come back feeling relaxed and ready to grab the reins of life again. It is important to not fall into the trap of a lazy routine; doing something productive sometimes can be incredibly beneficial. Taking time to work on our passions, helping out a friend, investing in our own learning these are all examples of meaningful and useful activities that can help us develop. However, it is also important to recognize that doing nothing can provide the same benefits. Taking a break from the hustle and bustle of our busy lives can allow us to unwind, race stock of what's important, cultivate creativity, and more. It is clear that both doing something and nothing have their own important merits. While Jefferson's advice to “determine never to be idle” can be sound, it is essential that we remember to factor in the importance of taking a break, in both an active and inactive form. In doing so, we can enjoy a balanced lifestyle, and find a healthy equilibrium between our activities and inactivity.

Counter-argument: While it may seem logical that people who want to do y would try to avoid any undesirable outcome x, it is not always the case. Sometimes, people may prioritize their immediate desires over long-term consequences, and choose to ignore or downplay the potential negative effects of their actions. Furthermore, even if individuals are aware of the potential negative outcomes, there may be external factors that prevent them from finding alternative solutions. For example, some individuals may not have the resources or knowledge to find alternative methods to achieve y without causing x. Lastly, some individuals may simply not care about the negative outcome x, either because they do not view it as a problem or because they believe the benefits of y outweigh any negative consequences. Thus, it is not always guaranteed that individuals will try to find alternative solutions to achieve y without causing x.

Fair Value Use for Companies’ Non-Financial Assets Essay The convergence to the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) is linked with diverse issues related to accounting. The need to choose between historical cost and fair value (FV) accounting when it comes to non-financial assets is among the highly debated issues. Based on current studies, FV measurement’s insufficient standardization and partial reliance on institutional facts could reduce its helpfulness for accounting for non-financial assets. In relation to real estate, equipment, or intellectual property, FV is often unknowable, unstable, and disengaged from institutional reality. In their case study of pharmaceutical, telecommunications, and industrial companies that use FV accounting for non-financial assets, Barker and Schulte (2017) highlight FV measurement’s contributions to producing misleading information. From their analysis, FV accounting offers two possibilities: reporting well-established institutional facts (IFs) or creating new data not constituting valuable IFs. Based on the empirical evidence that Barker and Schulte (2017) retrieved, the second option is dominant in most cases. These challenges’ potential implications for accounting are tremendous, including substantial overall value deviations in companies’ financial statements. Another disadvantage of using FV for businesses’ non-financial assets is the absence of the universally accepted FV measurement approach that would facilitate international comparison practices. Despite the commonly discussed promise of FV in terms of accuracy, influential non-financial companies in Tanzania and India rarely practice FV accounting (Kaaya & Noorbasha, 2017). Resistance to FV accounting for non-financial assets stems from insufficient standardization. During low market liquidity periods, FV accounting practices can encourage the manipulation of FV estimates (Kaaya & Noorbasha, 2017). This results in the inconsistent application of the IFRS, which reduces the ability to analyze diverse companies’ data comparatively (Kaaya & Noorbasha, 2017). Taking that into account, the massive use of FV with non-financial assets could hinder the collection of objective data pointing to specific companies’ positions relative to other businesses. Venus, the second planet from the sun, has always been a subject of fascination to scientists, space enthusiasts and the general public. It is often referred to as the Earth's "sister planet" due to its similarities in size, composition and atmosphere. However, despite its closeness to Earth, much about Venus remains a mystery. In recent years, space agencies and private companies have launched several missions to explore the planet and gather data. One of the most significant discoveries about Venus was made by the Magellan spacecraft in the 1990s. The spacecraft mapped 100% of the planet's surface and discovered that it was covered in thick, swirling clouds. These clouds are made up of sulfuric acid and water droplets, and they obscure most of the planet's surface, making it extremely difficult to study. More recent missions, such as the Venus Atmosphere and Volatile Environment (VAVENE) mission, have focused on studying the planet's atmosphere. The mission's data has shown that Venus's atmosphere is extremely dense and traps heat, causing surface temperatures to reach up to 460 degrees Celsius. This has made it virtually impossible for any life forms to survive on Venus's surface. However, there is still hope that we may one day find signs of life on the planet. Some scientists believe that Venus may have had liquid water on its surface in the past, and that it may still harbor some form of life in its subsurface reservoirs. To search for these potential life forms, future missions to Venus will need to focus on drilling into the planet's crust to reach these subsurface regions. In conclusion, Venus remains one of the most mysterious planets in our solar system. Despite its proximity to Earth, we still have much to learn about its composition, atmosphere, and possible habitability. With new spacecraft and missions planned for the future, we may soon unlock the secrets of this fascinating planet.

The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is a method for analyzing and categorizing facial expressions. It was developed by Dr. Paul Ekman and Dr. Wallace Friesen in the late 1970s. This innovative approach helps people better understand the subtle movements and muscle contractions that occur on our faces when we experience different emotions or react to situations. FACS uses a set of specific codes to describe the actions that occur in our faces when we smile, frown, raise eyebrows, or show surprise. These codes are divided into Action Units (AU), which represent the basic components of facial expressions. For instance, AU10 refers to the raising of the eyebrows, AU4 refers to the lowering of the eyebrows, and AU11 refers to the tightening of the lips in a smile. Each action unit is further categorized into muscle movements, which are called Manipulators. The system also considers Action Description Entries (ADE), which are the combinations of action units used to create more complex facial expressions. The FACS has been widely used in various fields, including psychology, neuroscience, and computer science. It helps researchers better study human emotions, understand how we communicate non-verbally, and create more realistic facial animations in computer graphics and video games. One example of how FACS is being used today is in the development of virtual reality (VR) technology. VR headsets and software can now analyze facial expressions in real-time using algorithms based on the FACS system, enabling more lifelike interactions between humans and computer-generated characters. In conclusion, the FACS is an important tool for understanding the complexities of human facial expressions and their role in non-verbal communication. Its applications in various fields continue to expand, helping us better comprehend our emotions and create more realistic representations of them in digital media.

Cells are programmed to divide and make new cells only when the body needs them. When the body has enough cells, the cells stop dividing. This is called cell cycle regulation.

Cell cycle regulation is controlled by special proteins inside the cell called cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs). Cyclins and CDKs work together to control when the cell should divide.

There are also other proteins that help regulate the cell cycle. For example, there are proteins called tumor suppressors that help keep cells from dividing too much and becoming cancerous.

So, even though cells can divide and make new cells, there are systems in place to make sure that cells do not divide too much and cause problems for the body.

But they still need to be able to find any of the campers if asked , so they need the campers to each keep track of some of the other campers . Linked List : each camper keeps track of one other camper . So if they need to find a certain camper they ask the one camper they pay attention to to tell them where the guy he keeps track of is . They go down the chain until they find the guy they 're looking for . Folk medicine and traditional healing practices have been used for centuries in various cultures around the world. These practices are based on the belief that the body has an innate ability to heal itself, and that traditional remedies can help to restore balance and promote health. While modern medicine has made significant advancements in the treatment of illness and disease, many people still turn to folk medicine and traditional healing practices for a variety of reasons. One of the main reasons people turn to folk medicine and traditional healing practices is that they are often more affordable and accessible than modern medical treatments. In many parts of the world, traditional healers are readily available and can be consulted for a fraction of the cost of a visit to a modern medical clinic. Additionally, many traditional remedies can be made from natural ingredients that are readily available, such as herbs and spices. Another reason people turn to folk medicine and traditional healing practices is that they often provide a more holistic approach to health and healing. In contrast to modern medicine, which often focuses on treating specific symptoms or conditions, traditional healing practices take a more holistic approach that considers the whole person and their environment. This can include practices such as dietary changes, exercise, and spiritual or emotional healing. Folk medicine and traditional healing practices are also often rooted in cultural traditions and beliefs, which can be important to many people. For some, the use of traditional remedies and healing practices provides a sense of connection to their cultural heritage and can help to preserve important cultural traditions. However, there are also some concerns about the use of folk medicine and traditional healing practices. In some cases, traditional remedies can be ineffective or even dangerous. Additionally, there is a risk that people may delay seeking modern medical care for serious conditions in favor of traditional treatments that may not be effective. In conclusion, folk medicine and traditional healing practices have played an important role in the healing and health of people for centuries. While modern medicine has made significant advancements, there are still many people who turn to traditional remedies and healing practices for a variety of reasons. It is important for people to be informed about the benefits and risks of these practices and to consult with a healthcare professional before using any traditional remedies.

Instead of mandates, the principal could encourage participation by promoting the variety of extracurricular options available and their benefits. Highlighting how activities can help students develop skills, make new friends and strengthen college applications may inspire more voluntary involvement. The school could also ensure all interested students have a fair chance to get involved by addressing any barriers like fees, schedules or transportation issues that may currently limit participation. Rather than require extracurriculars, the principal would be better served supporting student choice and wellbeing. Students who participate of their own accord will likely gain more from the experience. For those with additional responsibilities or time constraints outside of school, mandatory extracurriculars could negatively impact their performance, health or family relationships. Overall school spirit and community engagement are best served when participation stems from personal motivation rather than compulsion. For these reasons, I do not think the principal should require all students to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. Student choice and priorities should be respected.

The civil rights movement in the United States was a long and difficult struggle for equality. It began in the 19th century with the abolition of slavery and continued into the 20th century with the fight for desegregation, voting rights, and equal opportunity. Her arrest sparked a year-long boycott of the Montgomery bus system by the black community. The boycott was a success, and it helped to bring national attention to the issue of segregation. Another important event in the civil rights movement was the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. In 1963, over 200,000 people marched on Washington, D.C., to demand equal rights for black Americans. The march was a peaceful and orderly event, and it helped to show the world that the civil rights movement was a powerful force for change. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was a landmark piece of legislation that outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The act was a major victory for the civil rights movement, and it helped to bring about a more just and equal society. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 was another important piece of legislation that outlawed discrimination in voting. The act helped to ensure that black Americans had the right to vote, and it played a major role in increasing the number of black elected officials. The civil rights movement achieved many important victories, but there is still work to be done. Discrimination and racism continue to exist in the United States, and the fight for equality is not over. However, the civil rights movement has made great progress, and it has helped to create a more just and equal society. The civil rights movement is a testament to the power of nonviolent protest. The movement showed that people can achieve great things when they come together peacefully to demand change. The civil rights movement is an inspiration to people all over the world who are fighting for justice and equality.

First impressions are an important aspect of our lives. They are the initial judgments we make about someone or something, based on our first encounter with them. First impressions can have a significant impact on our relationships with others, as they often shape our perceptions and attitudes towards people. In this essay, I will analyze the importance of first impressions and share my experiences and opinions to support my conclusions. First impressions are often based on physical appearance, body language, and tone of voice. These initial judgments can be influenced by factors such as age, gender, race, and socioeconomic status. Similarly, someone who speaks confidently and clearly may be perceived as more intelligent and competent than someone who speaks hesitantly or with a heavy accent. Once we have formed our initial impressions of someone, these judgments can influence our behavior and interactions with them. If we have a positive first impression, we may be more likely to approach and engage with the person. On the other hand, if we have a negative first impression, we may avoid the person or dismiss them as unimportant. This can lead to missed opportunities for forming meaningful relationships and can also lead to misunderstandings and conflicts. Personally, I have experienced the impact of first impressions on my relationships with others. In high school, I once had a classmate who I initially found intimidating due to their confident and outgoing demeanor. However, as I got to know them better, I realized that they were actually very kind and caring. If I had not initially judged them based on their first impression, I may have approached them sooner and formed a stronger friendship. In conclusion, first impressions are an important aspect of our lives and can have a significant impact on our relationships with others. While physical appearance, body language, and tone of voice can influence our initial judgments, it is important to remember that these impressions are not always accurate. By being open to forming relationships with people based on more than just their first impression, we can miss out on valuable opportunities for connection and understanding. It is important to remember that people are complex and multifaceted, and that our judgments should be based on more than just superficial characteristics.

It is an ill-posed problem to recover the true scene colors from a color biased image by discounting the effects of scene illuminant and camera spectral sensitivity (CSS) at the same time. Although several methods have been proposed to address this problem, they are either based on the color constancy assumption or require a complicated reconstruction algorithm, making them not suitable for large-scale applications. In this paper, we present a simple but effective framework for robust color bias removal based on the assumption that scene illuminant and CSS are mutually independent and spatially invariant in the scene. The problem is reformulated as an optimization problem to estimate the CSS and scene illuminant from the input image. To solve the optimization problem, we propose a novel algorithm that is based on the principle of least square and can be efficiently implemented. Extensive experiments on several challenging color bias removal datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Facial action coding system (FACS) is a method used to track and analyze facial movements and expressions. Developed by Paul Ekman in the 1970s, FACS has been widely used in various fields such as psychology, neuroscience, and marketing. The FACS method involves coding and categorizing specific facial movements and expressions into a standardized system. This system allows researchers to systematically observe and analyze facial expressions over time. Some of the key aspects of the FACS method include: 1. Action units: The basic unit of facial movement is the action unit. FACS identifies seven basic action units, which include eyebrow raises, eye wrinkles, mouthopenings, and head movements. 2. Facial expression coding: FACS uses a specific coding system to describe facial expressions. Each expression is described as a combination of action units, which are measured on a scale of intensity. 3. Microexpressions: In addition to expressions such as happiness, anger, and sadness, FACS also includes coding for microexpressions, which are brief, involuntary facial movements that may indicate specific emotions or intentions. 4. Fusion rules: FACS includes fusion rules, which specify how different action units are combined to create a specific expression. For example, the fusion rule for a smile involves raising the eyebrows, opening the mouth, and wrinkling the skin around the eyes. FACS has been used in a variety of applications. For example, it has been used to study the development and expression of emotions in infants and young children. It has also been used to analyze facial expressions in advertising and marketing to improve sales and brand recognition. However, there are potential limitations to the FACS method. For example, some studies have suggested that facial expressions may be influenced by culture and individual differences, which could affect the reliability of the method. Additionally, the method may not be accurate in detecting complex emotions and intentions. Overall, the FACS method provides a useful framework for studying and analyzing facial expressions. While there are potential limitations, FACS continues to be a valuable tool in various fields and has the potential for further research and development.

It deals with various science fiction elements such as spontaneous generation, futurology, the end of the world and doomsday, resurrection, and the afterlife. Rather than giving supernatural or mythological explanations for these events, Ibn al-Nafis attempted to explain these plot elements using the scientific knowledge of biology, astronomy, cosmology and geology known in his time. Ibn al-Nafis' fiction explained Islamic religious teachings via science and Islamic philosophy.

Claims are a fundamental unit of scientific discourse. The exponential growth in the number of scientific publications makes automatic claim extraction an important problem for researchers who are overwhelmed by this information overload. Such an automated claim extraction system is useful for both manual and programmatic exploration of scientific knowledge. In this paper, we introduce a new dataset of 1,500 scientific abstracts from the biomedical domain with expert annotations for each sentence indicating whether the sentence presents a scientific claim. We introduce a new model for claim extraction and compare it to several baseline models including rule-based and deep learning techniques. Moreover, we show that using a transfer learning approach with a fine-tuning step allows us to improve performance from a large discourse-annotated dataset. Our final model increases F1-score by over 14 percent points compared to a baseline model without transfer learning. We release a publicly accessible tool for discourse and claims prediction along with an annotation tool. We discuss further applications beyond biomedical literature.

Car-free cities have been becoming increasingly popular in recent years as people become more conscious of the impact of vehicles on the environment. These cities have been designed to encourage walking, cycling, and public transportation usage, and they have been proven to be more livable and sustainable than traditional cities that rely heavily on cars. One of the main advantages of car-free cities is the reduced air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Cars are one of the biggest contributors to air pollution and climate change, and a significant reduction in their usage can have a positive impact on the environment. Car-free cities have seen a significant decrease in accidents as well, as they require drivers to be more careful and attentive when navigating through the city. Another benefit of car-free cities is the increased safety and security. With fewer cars on the road, there is less opportunity for theft and vandalism, and people can walk around with peace of mind knowing that they are in a safer environment. Additionally, cities that are built around pedestrian and cycling infrastructure have been proven to be safer for pedestrians and cyclists, as they are less likely to be hit by a car. Car-free cities are also more livable and sustainable. They prioritize the needs of people over the convenience of cars, with more green spaces, public parks, and bike lanes. This creates a more vibrant and community-friendly environment, where people can interact with one another and enjoy their surroundings. Additionally, the reduction in cars allows for more efficient use of public space, as roads can be reallocated for other purposes, such as public events and festivals. In conclusion, car-free cities have a wide range of benefits that go beyond just environmental sustainability. They create safer and more livable environments, encourage healthy habits, and promote social engagement. As the world continues to change and become more conscious of the impact of human activity on the environment, it is likely that car-free cities will become more common and widely adopted.

While it is true that having only one chamber in the United States Congress may seem like an efficient idea, in reality, it would be a grave mistake. The two-chamber system of Congress provides a necessary check and balance on legislative power. The House of Representatives and the Senate represent different constituencies and have different powers, which ensure that both larger and smaller states have a say in the lawmaking process. The Senate represents states equally, giving smaller states a voice in the lawmaking process, while the House of Representatives represents population, ensuring that larger states have a say. Without these two chambers, the larger states would ultimately have greater power than smaller states, eroding the importance of the founding principle of federalism. A one-chamber system would also lead to hasty decisions and the potential for one group or political party to dominate the legislative process. With a two-chamber system, lawmakers are forced to compromise and seek the input of their colleagues, which often results in more thoughtful and fair legislation. The two-chamber system has been in place in the United States for over two centuries and has been fundamental in ensuring that all voices are heard, and the legislative process is fair, thoughtful, and inclusive. A one-chamber system would undermine the important principles upon which our country was founded, and could have serious consequences for the future of our democracy.

Gerrymandering is a way of drawing the boundaries of electoral districts in a way that gives an unfair advantage to a particular political party or group. It's called gerrymandering because it was first done by a man named Elbridge Gerry in the early 1800s. Imagine you have a group of people who all want to vote for the same candidate in an election. If you draw the boundaries of the voting districts in a way that puts all of those people in the same district, then that candidate is very likely to win that district. But if you draw the boundaries differently, so that those people are spread out across several different districts, then it's less likely that the candidate will win any of those districts. Gerrymandering is bad because it means that some people's votes count more than others. It can also make it harder for certain candidates to win elections, even if they have a lot of support, because they are "packed" into a few districts where they are sure to win, rather than being spread out where they might be able to win a few more districts. This can make it harder for a minority group or political party to have their voices heard and to have a fair chance of winning elections.

A plus-minus sign (±) is a mathematical symbol that is used to indicate that a value is subject to change. It is often used in mathematics, statistics, and science to denote a range of values or uncertainties in measurements.

For example, if a measurement is given as "10 ± 2," this means that the true value of the measurement could be anywhere from 8 to 12. The plus-minus sign indicates that the value is uncertain or subject to change, and the number following the sign (in this case, 2) indicates the range of possible values.

In general, the plus-minus sign is used to indicate that a value is approximate or uncertain, and that it may vary within a certain range. It is a useful way to convey information about the precision of a measurement or calculation, and it is often used in scientific and technical contexts to help convey the level of uncertainty associated with a given value.

In computer science, a tree is a widely used abstract data type that represents a hierarchical tree structure with a set of connected nodes. Each node in the tree can be connected to many children (depending on the type of tree), but must be connected to exactly one parent, except for the root node, which has no parent. These constraints mean there are no cycles or "loops" (no node can be its own ancestor), and also that each child can be treated like the root node of its own subtree, making recursion a useful technique for tree traversal. In contrast to linear data structures, many trees cannot be represented by relationships between neighboring nodes in a single straight line. Binary trees are a commonly used type, which constrain the number of children for each parent to exactly two. When the order of the children is specified, this data structure corresponds to an ordered tree in graph theory. A value or pointer to other data may be associated with every node in the tree, or sometimes only with the leaf nodes, which have no children. The abstract data type can be represented in a number of ways, including a list of parents with pointers to children, a list of children with pointers to parents, or a list of nodes and a separate list of parent-child relations (a specific type of adjacency list). Representations might also be more complicated, for example using indexes or ancestor lists for performance. Trees as used in computing are similar to but can be different from mathematical constructs of trees in graph theory, trees in set theory, and trees in descriptive set theory.

It shows that the most important factors in understanding the cross-border legal order are the rules of private international law and the specific features of the different areas of law. The Shang dynasty oracle bone script and the Zhou dynasty scripts found on Chinese bronze inscriptions are no longer used; the oldest script that is still in use today is the Seal Script ( , zhuanshu). It evolved organically out of the Spring and Autumn period Zhou script, and was adopted in a standardized form under the first Emperor of China, Qin Shi Huang. The seal script, as the name suggests, is now used only in artistic seals. Few people are still able to read it effortlessly today, although the art of carving a traditional seal in the script remains alive; some calligraphers also work in this style.

The challenges of interplanetary colonization are numerous and daunting, yet they remain a tantalizing prospect for humanity's future. The idea of establishing permanent settlements beyond Earth has captivated the imagination of scientists, engineers, and dreamers for centuries. From the harsh realities of radiation, extreme temperatures, and microgravity to the logistical nightmares of supply chains, communication, and sustainability, there are many obstacles to overcome before human beings can truly call another planet home. First and foremost among these challenges is the issue of survival itself. The harsh environments of other planets and moons pose significant threats to human life. From the bone-chilling cold of Mars to the blistering heat of Venus, living conditions on these hostile worlds would require extensive modifications to our bodies and technology. Additionally, the lack of a protective atmosphere on many celestial bodies means that exposure to radiation could be fatal without adequate shielding. Another major challenge is the physical isolation of interplanetary colonies. Traveling to and from Earth would be time-consuming and expensive, limiting the frequency and quantity of supplies that could be delivered. This would require colonists to rely heavily on local resources, potentially including agriculture and mining, to sustain themselves. The development of advanced robotics and artificial intelligence could help mitigate this issue by enabling remote operations and autonomous exploration. The psychological effects of living in isolation for extended periods of time are also a significant concern. The physical and social challenges of living in close quarters with a small group of people for years or even decades would be immense. Maintaining mental health and preventing conflict within the colony would be crucial to its success. Finally, the financial burden of interplanetary colonization is staggering. The cost of developing the technology, building habitats, and sustaining colonies would require substantial investment from governments and private organizations. This raises questions about the feasibility of such an endeavor, especially in light of the many competing priorities here on Earth. Despite these immense challenges, the potential rewards of interplanetary colonization are equally great. From the scientific discoveries that could be made to the sense of adventure and accomplishment that would come from expanding humanity's reach beyond Earth, there are compelling reasons to pursue this ambitious endeavor. With continued research, development, and collaboration, the dream of interplanetary colonization may one day become a reality.

The FACS system is based on the idea that facial expressions are relatively uniform across individuals, and that these expressions can be accurately coded and analyzed through the use of specific actions and movements of the facial muscles. By analyzing these movements, the FACS system can generate a detailed and precise facial expression code that can be used to track and measure facial expressions in real-time. One of the key advantages of the FACS system is its ability to record and analyze facial expressions in real-time. This allows for the precise measurement of emotional responses and reactions, which can provide valuable insights into consumer behavior, market trends, and brand sentiment. For example, the FACS system has been used to analyze consumer responses to various marketing campaigns, allowing businesses to track the effectiveness of their messaging and advertising strategies. In addition to its practical applications, the FACS system has also been used for research purposes in fields such as psychology and neuroscience. By studying facial expressions using the FACS system, researchers have been able to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying neural mechanisms that govern emotional processing and expression. This information can be used to develop new treatment strategies for psychological disorders such as depression and anxiety. Overall, the Facial Action Coding System is a powerful tool that has the potential to revolutionize the way we understand and analyze facial expressions. With its ability to accurately track and measure facial expressions in real-time, it has the potential to provide valuable insights into consumer behavior, market trends, and brand sentiment, as well as to advance our understanding of the underlying neural mechanisms that govern emotional processing and expression.

Skew polynomials, which have a noncommutative multiplication rule between coefficients and an indeterminate, are the most general polynomial concept that admits the degree function with desirable properties. This paper presents the first algorithms to compute the maximum degree of the Dieudonne determinant of a x k k submatrix in a matrix A whose entries are skew polynomials over a skew field F. Our algorithms make use of the discrete Legendre conjugacy between the sequences of the maximum degrees and the ranks of block matrices over F obtained from coefficient matrices of A. Three applications of our algorithms are provided: (i) computing the dimension of the solution spaces of linear differential and difference equations, (ii) determining the Smith-McMillan form of transfer function matrices of linear time-varying systems and (iii) solving the "weighted" version of noncommutative Edmonds' problem with polynomial bit complexity. We also show that the deg-det computation for matrices over sparse polynomials is at least as hard as solving commutative Edmonds' problem. Keywords: skew polynomials, Dieudonne determinant, matrix expansion, discrete Legendre conjugacy, differential equations, difference equations, Smith-McMillan form, Edmonds' problem

When you're watching a scene and the camera moves, say left to right for example; The stuff that's closer to the camera will move faster than the stuff that's further away. This is called Focusing Speed. Focusing speed can be controlled by two different parameters: 1) Focus Lock (the framing lock usually) 2) Motion Blur Reduction (MBR) Focus Lock - enable focus locking if you want it. MBR - reduce motion blur in case of slow shutter speeds or long focal lengths. In general when MBR is enabled, it's good practice to disable focus lock as well. A: You should not use either one at all without knowing exactly what purpose they're intended for. It's like using goggles instead of glasses because they look cool. Not only are there some situations where this makes sense but also there's no reason to do so. (And actually with my own eyes I don't notice any significant difference between them.) However many filmmakers seem to have fallen into the habit which may have been instilled from their education that something looks better on paper than reality. This might apply particularly to people who make movies primarily for home video. In these cases the picture quality isn't important enough to spend much time maintaining an optical performance beyond "it works most of the time." But generally speaking both methods were invented precisely because sometimes pictures aren't perfect whether due to poor light conditions, bad lens design, improper handling etc. So even though we expect material produced today to require less effort on top of the best available technology the opposite seems to be true in other areas - namely over exaggeration of its imperfections. For instance, we're used to having a computer monitor display perfectly sharp images. If you find yourself looking directly at an LCD screen you'll probably see more artifacts than you'd get from viewing a projector running backlit slideshow films. But it's still impossible to predict how patients would react to your particular combination of lensesprojectorlens clotheslenses run through airflow etc., so in those circumstances you're just going to assume everything's fine until proven otherwise..

Among the many ways of quantifying uncertainty in a regression setting, specifying the full quantile function is attractive, as quantiles are amenable to interpretation and evaluation. A model that predicts the true conditional quantiles for each input, at all quantile levels, presents a correct and efficient representation of the underlying uncertainty. To achieve this, many current quantile-based methods focus on optimizing the so-called pinball loss . However, this loss restricts the scope of applicable regression models, limits the ability to target many desirable properties (e.g. calibration, sharpness, centered intervals), and may produce poor conditional quantiles. In this work, we develop new quantile methods that address these shortcomings. In particular, we propose methods that can apply to any class of regression model, allow for selecting a Pareto-optimal trade-off between calibration and sharpness, optimize for calibration of centered intervals, and produce more accurate conditional quantiles. We provide a thorough experimental evaluation of our methods, which includes a high dimensional uncertainty quantification task in nuclear fusion.

Existing tools for Question Answering (QA) have challenges that limit their use in practice. They can be complex to set up or integrate with existing infrastructure, do not offer configurable answer generation, or do not provide a robust confidence score. To address these challenges, we present DeepQA, a tool for QA that integrates deep learning with knowledge bases and text corpora to produce an answer prediction, as well as a confidence score, which can be used to reject low-confidence answers. We perform an extensive evaluation of DeepQA across different use cases, including customer service, human resources, and technical support, where we show that DeepQA outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches. We also show that DeepQA can be used to identify and reject low-confidence answers, reducing human effort in a semi-automated QA setting by up to 90 while maintaining an acceptable accuracy rate. We present a case study of DeepQA used in a large enterprise, which shows how DeepQA reduces human effort and improves system reliability. Finally, we conduct a human study to evaluate the trustworthiness of DeepQA's confidence score, and show that people correctly judge the answer's reliability from the confidence score in most cases.

It has allowed nations to expand their markets, increase their revenue, and provide more opportunities for businesses and individuals. However, global trade also presents significant challenges that must be addressed. In this essay, we will explore both the benefits and challenges of global trade and commerce. The benefits of global trade and commerce are numerous. First, it enables countries to access resources that are not available domestically. For instance, a country with limited natural resources can import the necessary materials to manufacture goods, boosting its economy. Second, global trade promotes competition, which can lead to innovation and improved product quality. Companies are forced to adapt to the international market, creating new products and services to stay competitive. Lastly, international trade stimulates economic growth as countries can specialize in producing goods and services in which they have a comparative advantage. This specialization leads to increased efficiency and productivity, ultimately benefiting consumers who enjoy a wider variety of goods at lower prices. However, global trade and commerce also present several challenges. One significant challenge is the potential for unfair trade practices, such as dumping, where companies sell products at artificially low prices to gain a larger market share. This can harm domestic industries and lead to job losses. Additionally, global trade can contribute to income inequality within and between nations. While some countries may benefit from increased exports, others may struggle to compete, leading to a widening gap in wealth distribution. Another challenge is the impact of global trade on the environment. The increase in international trade has led to an increase in the volume of goods transported, which contributes to greenhouse gas emissions and pollution. This can have detrimental effects on the environment and public health if not properly regulated. In conclusion, global trade and commerce have both benefits and challenges. While it presents opportunities for economic growth, increased competition, and specialization, it also comes with potential risks such as unfair trade practices, income inequality, and environmental degradation. It is crucial that nations and international organizations work together to address these challenges and ensure that global trade and commerce remain a force for good. Through collaboration and responsible practices, global trade can continue to be a vital engine of economic growth and development.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable accuracy in many artificial intelligence applications, e.g. computer vision, at the cost of a large number of parameters and high computational complexity. Weight pruning has emerged as a promising technique to reduce the number of parameters and the computational complexity of deep neural networks without sacrificing their accuracy. Weight pruning involves removing or sparsifying the weights (i.e. connections) between neurons in a neural network that contribute the least to the overall input-output mapping. This is typically done by setting these weights to zero, thereby reducing the number of parameters in the network. There are various algorithms that can be used for weight pruning, ranging from simple thresholding to more sophisticated methods such as iterative pruning and magnitude pruning. These algorithms differ in their complexity, effectiveness, and implementation details. Overall, weight pruning is a powerful technique for reducing the size and computational cost of deep neural networks while maintaining their accuracy. This makes it an important tool for building practical and efficient AI systems.

While the Facial Action Coding System technology described in the article has potential benefits, using it to read students' emotional expressions in the classroom raises significant privacy and ethical concerns that outweigh its value. On one hand, this technology could help teachers gain insights into how students are feeling about lessons and catch signs of distress or disengagement that a teacher may otherwise miss. Identifying struggling students earlier could help improve learning outcomes. However, constantly monitoring students' facial expressions also amounts to continual surveillance of them without consent. It intrudes into students' personal lives and emotions in a way that could undermine trust in the learning environment. Students should feel comfortable freely expressing a range of natural human emotions like confusion, frustration or boredom in class without having each micro-expression tracked and analyzed. Constant monitoring could put pressure on students to mask their true feelings and feel like they are never fully able to relax or process thoughts privately. It may discourage creative or independent thinking if students feel an artificial need to always appear positively engaged. While the intent is to help teachers, this technology could end up having a chilling effect on the classroom atmosphere and students' psychological well-being. Education requires an environment where open inquiry and grappling with new ideas is not stifled by fear of surveillance. Students' privacy and ability to internally experience lessons should be respected over any marginal benefits this type of tracking may provide. On balance, the risks of implementing facial expression tracking technology in the classroom seem to outweigh its value, given the strong importance of maintaining student privacy, trust and comfort in the learning process.

The first nuclear power plant was built in the Soviet Union in 1954, and the first commercial nuclear power plant was built in the United States in 1957. Nuclear power grew rapidly in the 1960s and 1970s, as countries around the world sought to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels. However, the growth of nuclear power slowed down in the 1980s and 1990s, due to concerns about safety and the high cost of building and operating nuclear power plants. Overall, nuclear power is a complex and controversial issue. There are both pros and cons to consider, and it is up to each individual to decide whether or not they support nuclear power.

The permutahedron is the convex polytope with vertex set consisting of the vectors ( (1), ... , (n for all permutations (bijections) over {1 , ... , n } . We study a bandit game in which, at each step t , an adversary chooses a hidden weight weight vector s t , a player chooses a vertex t of the permutahedron and suffers an observed instantaneous loss of i 1 n t (i) s t (i). We study the problem in two regimes. In the first regime, s t is a point in the polytope dual to the permutahedron. Algorithm CombBand of Cesa-Bianchi et al (2009) guarantees a regret of O ( n T log n) after T steps. Unfortunately, CombBand requires at each step an n -by- n matrix permanent computation, a P -hard problem. Approximating the permanent is possible in the impractical running time of O (n 10), with an additional heavy inverse-polynomial dependence on the sought accuracy. We provide an algorithm of slightly worse regret O ( n 3 2 T) but with more realistic time complexity O (n 3) per step. The technical contribution is a bound on the variance of the Plackett-Luce noisy sorting process's 'pseudo loss', obtained by establishing positive semi-definiteness of a family of 3-by-3 matrices of rational functions in exponents of 3 parameters. In the second regime, s t is in the hypercube. For this case we present and analyze an algorithm based on Bubeck et al.'s (2012) OSMD approach with a novel projection and decomposition technique for the permutahedron. The algorithm is efficient and achieves a regret of O ( n T), but for a more restricted space of possible loss vectors.

Homework, a word that can bring stress and anxiety to many students. However, there is an ongoing debate on whether homework is essential for learning or if it puts unnecessary stress on students. For example, if a student learns about a new mathematical concept, homework can help them understand how to apply it to real-life problems. Secondly, homework teaches students valuable time management and organization skills. In order to complete their homework, students must plan their time effectively, prioritize their tasks and meet deadlines. These skills are essential for success in all areas of life, not just academics. Additionally, homework encourages students to take ownership of their learning. When students are given homework, they are expected to complete it on their own. This encourages them to take responsibility for their own learning and to seek help only when necessary. This sense of ownership also motivates students to learn more and to explore topics beyond what is covered in class. However, it is important to note that homework should be used effectively. Homework should be challenging enough to engage students, but not so difficult that it leads to frustration. Teachers should also provide students with the necessary resources and support to complete their homework successfully. In conclusion, homework is a valuable tool for learning, as it reinforces classroom learning, teaches students time management and organization skills, and encourages them to take ownership of their learning. But it must be used effectively, to avoid causing unnecessary stress and anxiety to students. As a student myself, I believe that homework is essential for my learning process and it has helped me to become a better learner.

The Electoral College has been a long-standing institution in the United States that has served a crucial role in the democratic process. However, its validity in modern times continues to be a debated topic. While there are valid arguments favoring change or elimination of the Electoral College, I believe that retaining it is crucial to ensure stability, fairness, and the integrity of our democratic values. First of all, retaining the Electoral College would provide a clear and decisive winner in presidential elections with less likelihood of controversy and recounts. This would ensure certainty of result and a sense of closure that can be achieved without the need for run-off elections which are common in parliamentary or multi-party system elections where there are no clear majorities. Furthermore, the Electoral College encourages candidates to have broad-based support across different regions of the country, instead of only focusing their message and resources on a few large cities with a high number of voters. This means that candidates need to have a wider perspective on various issues facing different regions and populations of the United States instead of only catering to specific groups or states that could swing the popular vote. The Electoral College system ensures that all states have a voice in the election of the president and that smaller, less densely-populated states are not ignored by politicians who may focus primarily on large, population-dense states if the popular vote system was used. By balancing the influence of small and populous states, the Electoral College provides a balance of power and representation in the election of Americas commander-in-chief. Moreover, the winner-takes-all nature of almost all states in the Electoral College encourages voter turnout in states that otherwise may have little impact. This increases participation and engagement of voters, even in states where one candidate or another is predicted to win, making every citizens vote count and feel important, which in-turn increases democracy. In summary, retaining the Electoral College is crucial to ensure the stability, fairness, integrity, and democratic values of our representative democracy while providing every state with a voice in electing our president.

A special memorandum account (SMA) is a type of account used by brokerage firms to track the buying and selling activity of a particular security by a client. Neural conversation models such as encoder-decoder models are easy to generate bland and generic responses. Some researchers propose to use the conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) which maximizes the lower bound on the conditional log-likelihood on a continuous latent variable. With different sampled latent variables, the model is expected to generate diverse responses. Although the CVAE-based models have shown tremendous potential, their improvement of generating high-quality responses is still unsatisfactory. In this paper, we introduce a discrete latent variable with an explicit semantic meaning to improve the CVAE on short-text conversation. A major advantage of our model is that we can exploit the semantic distance between the latent variables to maintain good diversity between the sampled latent variables. Accordingly, we propose a two-stage sampling approach to enable efficient diverse variable selection from a large latent space assumed in the short-text conversation task. Experimental results indicate that our model outperforms various kinds of generation models under both automatic and human evaluations and generates more diverse and informative responses.

This has led to a greater understanding of different cultures and a more tolerant and cosmopolitan world. Additionally, globalization has helped to promote the spread of democracy and human rights around the world. Overall, globalization has had a significant impact on national cultures and identities. Kernel regression is a nonparametric method for estimating the conditional expectation of a random variable. It is a type of smoothing method that allows us to make predictions about the value of a variable based on the values of other variables in the dataset. The basic idea behind kernel regression is to estimate the value of the target variable at a given point by taking a weighted average of the target variable's values at nearby points. The weights are determined by a kernel function, which is a mathematical function that assigns a weight to each point based on its distance from the target point. One of the key benefits of kernel regression is that it is flexible and can adapt to nonlinear relationships between the variables. It does not require any assumptions about the underlying distribution of the data, and can be used with any type of data, including continuous, categorical, and ordinal variables. Kernel regression is often used in machine learning and statistical modeling, and has a wide range of applications in fields such as economics, finance, and engineering. It is particularly useful for analyzing time series data, and can be used to make predictions about future values of the target variable based on past observations.

The ability to switch from looking at one object to another and always hit accurately is called saccadic suppression. In modern cryptography, the secret sharing scheme is an important cryptographic primitive and it is used in various situations. In this paper, a timed-release secret sharing scheme (TR-SS) with information-theoretic security is first studied. TR-SS is a secret sharing scheme with the property that participants more than a threshold number can reconstruct a secret by using their shares only when the time specified by a dealer has come. Specifically, in this paper we first introduce a model and formalization of security for TR-SS based on the traditional secret sharing scheme and information-theoretic timed-release security. We also derive tight lower bounds on the sizes of shares, time-signals, and entities' secret-keys required for TR-SS. In addition, we propose a direct construction for TR-SS. Our direct construction is optimal in the sense that the construction meets equality in each of our bounds. As a result, it is shown that the timed-release security can be realized without any additional redundancy on the share-size.
