Me ( Aaron ) and my brother Bob are dating two sisters , Alice and Betty . We are all strange people , so me and Bob are each writing 100 - page novels for our girlfriends . Each page that we write takes 2 days , and each page takes 2 days for Alice and Betty to read . We want to send the novels to them in the most efficient way possible , but because this is all fictional the post office can only mail a single one - page letter per day from our house to the girls ' home . What options do we have ? I could wait 200 days for Bob to write and send his whole novel , then I can send mine . But that makes Alice have to wait a really long time to receive her novel , and during the time that she 's reading it Betty will just be sitting around idle , having finished her novel already . The whole thing takes 400 days . A better system might be for me and Bob to alternate mailing pages . As long as Alice and Betty are aware of the system , or we mark our pages with which one of us wrote them , this method still gets all the information where it needs to go but nobody is idling for nearly as long . It takes me 200 days to write my novel , and also 200 days to send it , and it takes Alice 200 days to read it . Bob and Betty also just need 200 days to write , send and read their novel . Instead of 400 total days , we just need ( about ) 200 total days . & nbsp ; Often when sending data over a network , there are multiple senders and multiple receivers . The network can only transfer a limited amount of data per second . Since it takes time for the senders to generate messages and time for the receivers to process them , it 's often most efficient to * multiplex * the messages by interleaving them into a single continuous stream , then * demultiplex * them at the receiving end .

The Impact of Driverless Cars Driverless cars hold promise for both improved convenience and societal risks. While autonomous vehicles could increase mobility and reduce accidents, developing this new technology also raises privacy, ethical and economic concerns that must be addressed. Ln balance, driverless cars may ultimately benefit society if certain safeguards are established. According to the article, driverless cars could offer substantial benefits. By taking human error out of driving, they may decrease collisions and increase roadway capacity. This safety feature could be lifesaving, as over 90% of crashes are currently caused by human mistake. Automated vehicles could also help the elderly and disabled gain independent transportation. By detecting traffic and road conditions, they may improve fuel efficiency through optimized braking and acceleration patterns. However, the article also notes several challenges. Autonomous cars will need to make ethical decisions in emergency situations, deciding whether to protect passengers or pedestrians for instance. How to program vehicles to prioritize different lives will be complex. Additionally, large scale adoption of driverless technology could significantly impact transportation jobs like long haul trucking. Replacing human drivers with software and sensors risks disrupting livelihoods unless complementary social programs support career transitions. Cybersecurity is another concern, as hackers targeting autonomous systems could endanger road users. Scars are a natural part of the healing process after your skin has been injured. When your skin is injured, your body starts to repair the damage by creating new collagen fibers. These collagen fibers help to rebuild the damaged tissue, but they don't always align in the same direction as the surrounding tissue. This can cause the scar to look different from the surrounding skin. Scars also don't go away because the skin cells at the bottom of the scar (called the dermis) are different from the skin cells at the top (called the epidermis). The dermis is made up of thicker, stronger cells that are more difficult to replace. The epidermis is made up of thinner, more delicate cells that are constantly being replaced as they die off. When you have a scar, the dermis remains unchanged, while the epidermis cells continue to regenerate on top of it. This is why scars don't disappear, even though the top layer of skin cells is constantly being replaced.

There are, in fact, two balances kept for your account by most banks that have to comply with common convenience banking laws. The first is your actual balance; it is simply the sum total of all deposits and withdrawals that have cleared the account; that is, both your bank and the bank from which the deposit came or to which the payment will go have exchanged necessary proof of authorization from the payor, and have confirmed with each other that the money has actually been debited from the account of the payor, transferred between the banks and credited to the account of the payee. The second balance is the "available balance". This is the actual balance, plus any amount that the bank is "floating" you while a deposit clears, minus any amount that the bank has received notice of that you may have just authorized, but for which either full proof of authorization or the definite amount (or both) have not been confirmed. This is what's happening here. Your bank received notice that you intended to pay the train company $X. They put an "authorization hold" on that $X, deducting it from your available balance but not your actual balance. The bank then, for whatever reason, declined to process the actual transaction (insufficient funds, suspicion of theft/fraud), but kept the hold in place in case the transaction was re-attempted. Holds for debit purchases usually expire between 1 and 5 days after being placed if the hold is not subsequently "settled" by the merchant providing definite proof of amount and authorization before that time. I believe that schools should implement policies that allow parents to monitor their children's grades and attendance online. This practice can have numerous benefits for both parents and students. Firstly, it helps parents stay involved in their child's education. By being able to access their child's grades and attendance records online, parents can easily track their child's progress and identify areas where they may need extra help or support. This can lead to more effective communication between parents and teachers, which can ultimately lead to better academic outcomes for the student. Secondly, it promotes accountability and responsibility among students. Knowing that their parents are able to monitor their grades and attendance online may motivate students to work harder and attend school more regularly. This can lead to improved academic performance and better attendance rates overall. On the other hand, some may argue that this practice can create unnecessary pressure and stress for students. Additionally, some students may feel embarrassed or ashamed if their grades or attendance records are not up to par, which can negatively impact their self-esteem and overall well-being. Despite these potential drawbacks, I still believe that the benefits of allowing parents to monitor their child's grades and attendance online outweigh the risks. By promoting parental involvement and accountability among students, this practice can help improve academic outcomes and foster a stronger sense of community within the school.

Competition and cooperation are both essential components of a successful society, but it is cooperation that better prepares young people for leadership. Competition is a natural instinct that can be used to foster individual achievement and drive progress, but it is cooperation that fosters a sense of community and encourages collective action. Cooperation is essential to promote collaboration and a sense of collective responsibility, both of which are key qualities of successful leadership. There are many reasons why cooperation should be prioritized when preparing young people for leadership. First, cooperation teaches young people to work together towards common goals. In order to achieve any type of success, teamwork is essential, and cooperation encourages young people to collaborate on projects, assignments, and tasks. This provides the opportunity to develop skills such as problem-solving, communication, and empathy, all of which are invaluable when it comes to leading a team. Furthermore, cooperative activities encourage young people to take initiative and make decisions, while giving them the tools to build trust and understanding within a group. Cooperation also promotes a sense of social responsibility. Working in a cooperative setting encourages young people to think critically about the impact of their decisions and actions on the world around them. This teaches them to be conscious of the consequences of their decisions and consider how their actions can benefit the greater good. This type of mindset is vital for effective leadership, as it encourages a sense of collective responsibility. Finally, cooperative activities provide a platform for young people to develop their interpersonal skills. Cooperation requires listening, understanding, and trust, which are essential for successful leadership. Working in a cooperative setting allows young people to hone their skills in negotiation, communication, and problem-solving, as well as how to manage a team. This gives them the ability to lead with integrity and respect. In conclusion, cooperation should be emphasized when preparing young people for leadership, as it provides the necessary skills and tools to be successful. Lesion segmentation is an important problem in computer-assisted diagnosis that remains challenging due to the prevalence of low contrast, irregular boundaries that are unamenable to shape priors. We introduce Deep Active Lesion Segmentation (DALS), a fully automated segmentation framework that leverages the powerful nonlinear feature extraction abilities of fully Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and the precise boundary delineation abilities of Active Contour Models (ACMs). Our DALS framework benefits from an improved level-set ACM formulation with a per-pixel-parameterized energy functional and a novel multiscale encoder-decoder CNN that learns an initialization probability map along with parameter maps for the ACM. We evaluate our lesion segmentation model on a new Multiorgan Lesion Segmentation (MLS) dataset that contains images of various organs, including brain, liver, and lung, across different imaging modalities - MR and CT. Our results demonstrate favorable performance compared to competing methods, especially for small training datasets.

It can be caused by various underlying conditions, such as liver disease, hepatitis, or an obstruction in the bile ducts. While jaundice itself is not contagious, the underlying cause of jaundice may be contagious and it is important to follow proper hygiene measures to prevent the spread of infection. It is important to listen to the recommendations of your doctor and follow their guidance on your diet and treatment plan. They will be able to advise you on the best course of action based on your specific circumstances and the underlying cause of your jaundice.

Many industrial machine learning (ML) systems require frequent retraining to keep up-to-date with constantly changing data. This retraining exacerbates a large challenge facing ML systems today: model training is unstable, which is the main reason for poor generalization and poor training stability. For example, while training a deep neural network (DNN) for image classification, the DNN is prone to overfitting the training data, which causes poor generalization. This problem can be further exacerbated by instability in training a DNN. For example, if a data point is removed from the training data set, the network will retrain the weights of the DNN to better generalize on the training data, and as a result, will not generalize well on unseen data. However, the network will not be able to generalize well on data that was never included in the training data set, and the network will not generalize well on new data that was added to the training data set. The cause of this instability is not well understood. In the past, these issues were addressed by limiting the number of data points used in the training of the network, or by forcing the network to train to a fixed point. However, this solution limits the range of the problem that the network can be trained on.

In addition to the environmental benefits, limiting car use can also have economic benefits. For example, limiting car use can lead to a reduction in traffic congestion, which can lead to increased productivity and lower costs for businesses. Additionally, reducing car use can lead to a decrease in air pollution, which can lead to improved public health and lower healthcare costs. Overall, the advantages of limiting car use are clear. By reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving public health, and increasing productivity, limiting car use can help to create a more sustainable and equitable society. For example, 400 BC is 400 years before the birth of Jesus Christ. There is a difference between BC and BCE. BCE stands for "Before the Common Era." It is used in place of BC as a way to label years that come before the birth of Jesus Christ in a way that is not tied to Christianity. For example, 400 BCE is 400 years before the birth of Jesus Christ, but it is not tied to Christianity. So, in summary: AD stands for "Anno Domini," which means "in the year of our Lord." The history of the internet is a fascinating journey that encompasses the evolution of technology, the innovation of brilliant minds, and the collaboration of individuals across the globe. From its humble beginnings as a military experiment to its current status as a global network, the internet has revolutionized the way we communicate, access information, and conduct business. The story of the internet begins in the 1960s during the height of the Cold War. The United States Department of Defense, concerned about the potential vulnerability of its communication systems, initiated a research project called ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network). The goal of ARPANET was to create a decentralized network that could withstand a nuclear attack and continue functioning. This project laid the foundation for what would eventually become the internet. In 1969, the first successful connection was made between two computers at different locations. This significant achievement marked the birth of the internet. Over the next few years, more computers were added to the network, allowing for greater communication and information sharing. By 1971, the term "internet" was coined to describe this interconnected network of computers. Throughout the 1970s, the internet continued to grow, with more universities, research institutions, and government agencies joining the network. The development of email in 1971 further fueled the expansion of the internet, as it provided a fast and efficient means of communication. The introduction of the TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) in the late 1970s standardized the way data was transmitted across the network, making it easier for different types of computers to communicate with one another. The 1980s marked a significant turning point in the history of the internet. In 1983, the National Science Foundation (NSF) established NSFNET, a high-speed network that connected five supercomputer centers across the United States. This network served as the backbone of the internet and facilitated the exchange of data and information between research institutions and universities. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, the internet experienced a tremendous growth spurt. The introduction of the World Wide Web in 1991 by Tim Berners-Lee revolutionized the way we navigate and access information on the internet. The web made it possible to organize and link documents, creating a user-friendly interface that allowed people to browse the internet with ease. This breakthrough led to the commercialization of the internet and the rapid expansion of online services

This can cause artifacts like flash - lighting , where you can see glows around where the LEDs are located at the edge of the screen ( typically only visible in dark scenes or in the black bands when viewing letterbox content ) . LED is more a marketing term when it comes to TVs , and full array back - lighting is going to cost you . I wish I had one .

The two symbols most commonly associated with pharmacy in English-speaking countries are the mortar and pestle and the (recipere) character, which is often written as "Rx" in typed text. The mortar and pestle has several possible origins.[1] These include its use for crushing or grinding spices to release their flavors,[2] the fact that it resembles a chef's hat, and similarity of shape to an hourglass;[34] they may also represent opposite poles of matter and spirit: earthmatter on one side, airspirit on another, just like the Greek philosophy universe consisting of heavenly bodies and human souls respectively. In alchemy, these were symbolized by vitriol and saltpeter, while gold represented spirit in apothecary circles - see Golden Dawn and philosopher's stone. Some believe them to be related to ancient Egyptian glyphs used during mummification practice.[5] A more recent theory proposes that both items derive from early medieval Christian practices where icons representing God could be found at every stage of production within the craft business cycle.[6] Others point out that the characters have been adopted into modern culture via the drug trade and skateboarding subcultures who appropriated elements of pharmaceutical imagery such as pill bottles and brand names.[7]

In the contemporary global environment, corporations have a significant impact on the world around them. As such, they must acknowledge their role in society and strive to create positive change, which is where the concept of corporate social responsibility (CSR) comes into play. This essay will discuss the importance of CSR in today's world, how shareholder activism and responsible investment play a crucial role in promoting it, and the benefits of implementing CSR practices in businesses. In the modern world, it is evident that businesses have an extensive reach and influence. They can significantly affect the environment, society, and economy. Therefore, it is essential for corporations to recognize their role in society and make efforts to improve it. CSR refers to the voluntary actions taken by businesses to address social, environmental, and economic issues that impact their stakeholders. By embracing CSR, corporations can foster a positive relationship with their stakeholders, enhance their brand image, and contribute to the betterment of society. Moreover, shareholder activism and responsible investment can be powerful tools in promoting CSR. Shareholder activism involves investors using their rights as owners to influence the company's policies and decisions in the interest of long-term sustainability. By doing so, they can push companies to adopt more responsible practices, such as reducing carbon emissions, promoting gender equality, and ensuring fair labor practices. On the other hand, responsible investment refers to the integration of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment decision-making process. As a result, investors can support companies that align with their values and encourage them to adopt better CSR practices. By promoting CSR, shareholder activism, and responsible investment, businesses can benefit from improved stakeholder relationships, enhanced brand image, and better long-term sustainability. This can lead to increased customer loyalty, reduced risk exposure, and higher returns for investors. Furthermore, corporations can foster a positive impact on society, environment, and economy, which is essential for the overall well-being of the global community. In conclusion, it is crucial for businesses to acknowledge their role in society and adopt CSR practices to address the issues faced by stakeholders. Shareholder activism and responsible investment can be powerful tools in promoting CSR and ensuring the long-term sustainability of businesses. By embracing CSR, companies can contribute to the betterment of society, environment, and economy, creating a world that is more sustainable and equitable for all.

Presumably you need a car to get to work, so let's start with the assumption that you need to buy something to replace the car you just lost. The biggest difficulty to overcome in buying a car is the concept of the monthly payment. Dealers will play games with all of the numbers to massage a monthly payment that the buyer can swallow, but this usually doesn't end up giving the customer the best deal. The 18 month term is not normal for a lease, typically you'll see 24 or 36 months. You are focusing on another goal of paying your student loans by then which would free up much more money for other wants (like a car) but at what cost? The big difficulty of personal finance is the mental mind game of delaying gratification for greater long-term benefit. You are focusing on paying your student loans now so that you can be free of that debt and have more flexibility for the future. Good. You're tempted to spend another $5400 (assuming no down-payment or other surprise fees) to drive a car for 18 months. That doesn't sound any wiser than $5,000 for an unreliable used car that gave you more problems than you bargained for. Presumably you got some percentage of that money back from the insurance company when the car was totaled, but even if not, the real lesson should be finding a car that you can afford up-front, but also one that you can still use when the loan is paid off (like your education--that investment will keep giving even when the loans are a distant memory). My advice would be to look for a car that has about 30k miles on it and pay for it as quickly as possible, then drive it at least for 70-120k more miles before replacing it. You may wish for a newer car, especially in 3 or 4 more years when it starts to show its age, but you'll also thank yourself when you can buy a newer better car with cash and break out of the monthly payment game that dealers try to push on you. You might even enjoy negotiating with car salesmen when you see through their manipulations and simply work for the best cash price you can get.

The Electoral College has been a controversial and long-standing aspect of the United States' presidential election process. The system was established by the founding fathers in the Constitution as a means to balance the power between states with varying populations. The Electoral College is composed of 538 electors, with each state receiving a number of electors equal to their total number of members in the United States House of Representatives (based on population) and Senate. The District of Columbia receives three electors, making a total of 538 electors. In order to win the presidency, a candidate needs to secure a majority of electoral votes. The candidate who receives the most votes becomes the winner, even if they don't have a majority of the popular vote. The Electoral College was designed to give smaller states more power in the election process, as well as provide some safeguards against the potential of a tyrannical leader being chosen by the people. Critics of the Electoral College argue that it undermines the democratic process and can lead to unrepresentative outcomes, as it disproportionately favors certain states with smaller populations. Additionally, it allows for a candidate to win the presidency without winning the majority of the popular vote. Supporters of the Electoral College contend that it preserves state power and ensures a more balanced representation in the federal government. They also argue that the Founding Fathers intentionally designed the system to avoid direct democracy, which could potentially lead to mob rule. In conclusion, the Electoral College is not without its flaws and controversies. However, it continues to serve as the system for electing the President and Vice President of the United States. Whether it works or not remains debatable, as it can lead to unpopular or undemocratic outcomes, yet it also preserves the interests and power of smaller states in the political process.

Diagnosis of infectious disease sometimes involves identifying an infectious agent either directly or indirectly. In practice most minor infectious diseases such as warts, cutaneous abscesses, respiratory system infections and diarrheal diseases are diagnosed by their clinical presentation and treated without knowledge of the specific causative agent. Conclusions about the cause of the disease are based upon the likelihood that a patient came in contact with a particular agent, the presence of a microbe in a community, and other epidemiological considerations. Given sufficient effort, all known infectious agents can be specifically identified. The benefits of identification, however, are often greatly outweighed by the cost, as often there is no specific treatment, the cause is obvious, or the outcome of an infection is benign.

To this end, we propose QED, a linguistically informed, extensible framework for explanations in question answering. We describe and publicly release an expert-annotated dataset of QED explanations built upon a subset of the Google Natural Questions dataset, and report baseline models on two tasks - post-hoc explanation generation given an answer, and joint question answering and explanation generation. One way to measure the size of an object is to use something called "angular size." Angular size is the size of an object as it appears from Earth, measured in degrees. For example, the angular size of the Moon as seen from Earth is about 0.5 degrees, which is about the same as the angular size of your little finger held at arm's length. By measuring the angular size of an object and knowing its distance from us, we can calculate the actual size of the object. Another way to measure distance is to use something called "parallax." Parallax is the apparent shift in the position of an object due to a change in the observer's position. For example, if you hold your finger in front of your face and close one eye, then open that eye and close the other eye, your finger will appear to shift relative to the background. Astronomers use this same principle to measure the distances to nearby stars. By measuring the amount of shift in a star's position over the course of a year, we can calculate its distance from Earth. There are many other techniques that astronomers use to measure the sizes and distances of celestial objects, such as using the brightness of stars to determine their distance, or using the redshift of galaxies to measure their speed and distance. These techniques can be a bit more complex, but they all rely on basic principles of physics and mathematics to help us understand the vastness of the universe.

Model-based strategies for control are critical to obtain sample efficient learning. Dyna is a planning paradigm that naturally interleaves learning and planning, by simulating one-step experience to update the action-value function. This elegant planning strategy has been mostly explored in the tabular setting. The aim of this paper is to revisit sample-based planning, in stochastic and continuous domains with learned models. We first highlight the flexibility afforded by a model over Experience Replay (ER). Replay-based methods can be seen as stochastic planning methods that repeatedly sample from a buffer of recent agent-environment interactions and perform updates to improve data efficiency. We show that a model, as opposed to a replay buffer, is particularly useful for specifying which states to sample from during planning, such as predecessor states that propagate information in reverse from a state more quickly. We introduce a semi-parametric model learning approach, called Reweighted Experience Models (REMs), that makes it simple to sample next states or predecessors. We demonstrate that REM-Dyna exhibits similar advantages over replay-based methods in learning in continuous state problems, and that the performance gap grows when moving to stochastic domains, of increasing size.

The rapid growth of multimedia consumption has triggered technical, economic, and business innovations that improve the quality and accessibility of content. It has also opened new markets, promising large revenues for telecommunications companies, media firms, or both. In fact, it is believed by many analysts to be one cause behind today's intense competition among telecom operators worldwide (e.g., ATT vs Verizon Wireless). In order to survive in such a competitive environment, networks must handle ever increasing traffic while supporting multiple applications with different Quality-of-Service requirements - all at an acceptable cost level per subscribercustomer. Recent research into this problem indicates great interest in network slicing as well as more general approaches aimed to support different QoS classes independently from each other on the same physical infrastructure [1]. Network slices are logical partitions within the underlying transport network which can provide distinct services to data flows belonging to individual subscribers, henceforth referred to as users. Examples of such functionalities include: 1) Guaranteed bandwidth service; 2) Service differentiation based upon user profile information; 3) Shared resource allocation between several users depending upon their current demands; 4) User-independent admission control mechanism; 5) Allocation of resources according to specific policies tailored towards certain groups of subscribers. Network slice management offers opportunities not only to offer differentiated quality to customers but also to reduce operating expenses due to simplified architecture and reduced number of hardware nodes required compared to traditional solutions. Some recent studies have shown how these capabilities could potentially result in significant savings whilst helping carriers cope better with peak loads during heavy usage periods. For example, if four independent virtualised transport domains were available over a single core router, they might allow provisioning 16 times the overall capacity without any additional equipment investment when compared to today's broadband access networks where two separate routers would need to be deployed. Additional benefits may arise through improved network efficiency since some functions typically performed locally inside each node, like IP address allocation and TCP stack configuration, will now take place centrally rather than being distributed across all devices in the system. Furthermore, flexible SLA-based charging mechanisms should make possible fair billing schemes resulting in even higher customer satisfaction levels.

The location on the banks of the river Rhine allowed Utrecht to become an important trade centre in the Northern Netherlands. The growing town Utrecht was granted city rights by Henry V in 1122. When the main flow of the Rhine moved south, the old bed, which still flowed through the heart of the town became evermore canalized; and the wharf system was built as an inner city harbour system. On the wharfs storage facilities (werfkelders) were built, on top of which the main street, including houses was constructed. The wharfs and the cellars are accessible from a platform at water level with stairs descending from the street level to form a unique structure.[nb 2] The relations between the bishop, who controlled many lands outside of the city, and the citizens of Utrecht was not always easy. The bishop, for example dammed the Kromme Rijn at Wijk bij Duurstede to protect his estates from flooding. This threatened shipping for the city and led the city of Utrecht to commission a canal to ensure access to the town for shipping trade: the Vaartse Rijn, connecting Utrecht to the Hollandse IJssel at IJsselstein.

This can provide the potential for long-term growth, but also carries the risk of volatility.Bonds: You could invest in a diversified portfolio of bonds, which tend to be less volatile than stocks and can provide a steady stream of income. However, bonds also carry some level of risk, such as interest rate risk and credit risk.Real estate: You could consider investing in real estate through a real estate investment trust (REIT) or by purchasing rental properties. Real estate investing can provide a potential for long-term growth and a steady stream of income from rental payments. However, it also involves significant upfront costs, ongoing maintenance expenses, and the risk of vacancy.Savings accounts and certificates of deposit (CDs): If you have a short time horizon or are risk-averse, you may want to consider keeping your money in a high-yield savings account or a CD. These options offer relatively low risk, but also tend to have lower potential returns compared to other investments.It's important to remember that investing involves risk and you should carefully consider your investment goals and risk tolerance before making any investment decisions. Medical conditions: Certain medical conditions, such as retrograde ejaculation or varicoceles, can also cause watery sperm. It's important to note that the appearance of semen can vary from person to person and can also change over time. These bonds can be categorized into three main types: covalent, ionic, and hydrogen bonds. 1. Covalent bonds: These occur when two atoms share electrons in order to achieve a full outer electron shell. This type of bond is very strong and stable, and can be found in many different types of molecules. 2. Ionic bonds: These occur when one atom donates an electron to another atom, resulting in positively and negatively charged ions that attract each other. Ionic bonds can be quite strong and are often found in common salts like table salt. 3. Hydrogen bonds: These occur when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to an electronegative atom like oxygen or nitrogen, and then interacts with another electronegative atom nearby. This creates a partial positive charge on the hydrogen and a partial negative charge on the other atom, allowing them to be attracted to each other. Hydrogen bonds are weaker than covalent and ionic bonds, but are still important in many biological processes like DNA replication and protein folding. Understanding the different types of bonds is important in many fields, ranging from chemistry and biology to engineering and material science.

The electoral college system is one of the most significant aspects of the American political system. It is a mechanism that determines who will become the next President of the United States. The system was created by the Constitution in order to address the concerns of the framers, but it has also been subject to criticism and debate over the years. In this essay, we will discuss whether or not the electoral college works. On the one hand, defenders of the electoral college argue that it is necessary for a fair and democratic election. The electoral college is composed of 538 electors divided among the states based on their populations. This system gives each state a proportional role in the election, regardless of its size or population. This ensures that everyone's voice is heard, even in smaller states. Proponents also argue that the electoral college prevents candidates from focusing solely on urban or heavily populated areas and instead motivates candidates to appeal to a broader range of voters. On the other hand, opponents of the electoral college argue that it is undemocratic and that the system can lead to unintended consequences. One major concern is that candidates may ignore states with lower populations in favor of swing states, which could lead to them being elected even if they do not have the support of most voters. Additionally, the winner of the majority of the popular vote can still lose the presidency if they do not win enough states, which is known as a "faithless elector." This system can also perpetuate political polarization and create an "us versus them" mentality between the two major parties. In terms of its effects on democracy, the electoral college can be seen as both a positive and negative force. While it addresses concerns of fairness and prevents candidates from ignoring certain states, it can also lead to unintended consequences such as ignoring certain voter groups and perpetuating political polarization. Overall, it is clear that the electoral college system will remain a subject of debate for many years to come. Once upon a time, there was a small Italian restaurant in downtown that had the best spaghetti in town. The restaurant was always full of people, from families celebrating birthdays to friends hanging out on Friday nights. However, no one dared to ask for a second serving of soda, as the restaurant had a policy of "No free refills." Maggie, a regular customer who loved the spaghetti, was always curious about the policy. She finally mustered the courage to ask the owner one day. "Why don't you offer free refills?" Maggie asked. The owner, Mr. Russo, replied with a laugh, "It's because we don't want people to stay here forever!" Maggie was a bit confused. "I don't understand. Don't you want customers to enjoy their meal and have a good time?" "We do, but we also have to run a business," Mr. Russo explained. "If we allow free refills, people might just order one drink and stay here for hours, taking up our valuable table space, and we would lose potential customers." Maggie thought about it for a moment and realized that it was indeed true. She had seen people staying for hours with just one drink, while others waited outside for a table. "But don't you think it's a bit strict?" she asked. Mr. Russo shook his head. "It might seem strict, but we need to keep our business profitable. We try to offer the best food and service possible, but we can't afford to let people stay here all day for just one drink." Maggie nodded in agreement and continued to enjoy her spaghetti. From that day on, she respected the policy and never asked for a refill again. Although some customers were disappointed, they soon realized that the restaurant's policy was just part of their business model to ensure the best possible experience for customers. In the end, the restaurant continued to thrive, and Maggie continued to be a loyal customer, always enjoying her delicious spaghetti and agreeing that "No free refills" was just a part of the experience.

While the Commission has a monopoly on initiating legislation, the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union have powers of amendment and veto during the legislative process. According to the EU's legislative procedures, the Commission proposes legislative initiatives and drafts laws, which are then debated and amended by the Parliament and the Council. The Parliament has the power to amend or reject the proposal, and the Council can also suggest changes or reject the proposal. If agreement cannot be reached, a conciliation process between the Parliament and Council is triggered, and the final draft must be approved by both institutions before becoming law. Therefore, although the Commission has the initial monopoly on initiating legislation, the Parliament and Council have significant powers of review and amendment throughout the legislative process.

In connectionless mode each packet includes complete addressing information. The packets are routed individually, sometimes resulting in different paths and out-of-order delivery. Each packet is labeled with a destination address, source address, and port numbers. It may also be labeled with the sequence number of the packet. This precludes the need for a dedicated path to help the packet find its way to its destination, but means that much more information is needed in the packet header, which is therefore larger, and this information needs to be looked up in power-hungry content-addressable memory. Each packet is dispatched and may go via different routes; potentially, the system has to do as much work for every packet as the connection-oriented system has to do in connection set-up, but with less information as to the application's requirements. At the destination, the original messagedata is reassembled in the correct order, based on the packet sequence number. Thus a virtual connection, also known as a virtual circuit or byte stream is provided to the end-user by a transport layer protocol, although intermediate network nodes only provides a connectionless network layer service.

"I think that some popes gave out the wrong message.... and some archbishops too," local media reported Bishop Robinson telling the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse. Bishop Robinson said Pope John Paul II did not immediately condemn the abuse claims when they emerged in the 1990s. "We still haven't had that kind of leadership, not even from (Pope) Francis," he said, explaining that bishops followed the Vatican's line by remaining silent on the issues. Bishop Robinson said that while he was drafting a national response for the Australian Catholic Church to abuse victims in 1990s, the then Archbishop of Melbourne, Cardinal Pell, released his own protocol for Melbourne. Unlike the national strategy, it required alleged sex abuse victims to speak to church lawyers first. Recommender systems can influence human behavior in significant ways, in some cases making people more machine-like. In this sense, recommender systems may be deleterious to notions of human autonomy. Many ethical systems point to respect for human autonomy as a key principle arising from human rights considerations, and several emerging frameworks for AI include this principle. Yet, no specific formalization has been defined. Separately, self-determination theory shows that autonomy is an innate psychological need for people, and moreover has a significant body of experimental work that formalizes and measures level of human autonomy. In this position paper, we argue that there is a need to specifically operationalize respect for human autonomy in the context of recommender systems. Moreover, that such an operational definition can be developed based on well-established approaches from experimental psychology, which can then be used to design future recommender systems that respect human autonomy.

The influence of parenting styles on child development is a topic that has been studied extensively in the field of psychology. Many different parenting styles have been identified, and each has been found to have a unique impact on a child's development. One of the most influential parenting styles is authoritarian parenting. Authoritarian parents are characterized by their high expectations and strict rules. They may be quick to punish their children and may not be very responsive to their children's needs. Children of authoritarian parents may be more likely to be obedient and respectful, but they may also be more likely to experience anxiety and depression. Another common parenting style is authoritative parenting. Authoritative parents are characterized by their high expectations and responsiveness to their children's needs. They set limits for their children, but they also explain the reasons for those limits and are willing to listen to their children's opinions. Children of authoritative parents tend to be more confident and self-reliant, and they are less likely to engage in risky behaviors. A third common parenting style is permissive parenting. Permissive parents are characterized by their low expectations and lack of rules. They may be very responsive to their children's needs, but they may not provide much guidance or structure. Children of permissive parents may be more likely to be independent and creative, but they may also be more likely to engage in risky behaviors. Finally, there is uninvolved parenting. Uninvolved parents are characterized by their lack of involvement in their children's lives. They may be physically present, but they are not emotionally engaged with their children. Children of uninvolved parents may be more likely to experience problems with social development and academic achievement. The parenting style that is best for a particular child will depend on the child's individual needs. However, research suggests that authoritative parenting is the most effective parenting style overall. Authoritative parents are able to provide their children with the structure and guidance they need to thrive, while also allowing them the freedom to explore and develop their own interests. In conclusion, parenting style has a significant impact on child development. Parents who are authoritative, responsive, and involved in their children's lives are more likely to raise children who are healthy, happy, and successful.

Change-point detection (CPD) aims at detecting the abrupt property changes lying behind time series data. The property changes in a multivariate time series often result from highly entangled reasons, ranging from the interaction of system moments with other indicators to systematic errors due to accumulation effects and uncertainty due to repeated measurement while observing over periods which are too short for statistically significant trends to emerge as fast moving variables. The principle aim of this work is to explore CPD by applying new techniques to an existing database of two hundred and twenty two (212) optically active molecules derived from optical spectroscopy, atomistic simulations, quantum mechanical modelling and linearized random walk models. We address three main problems: 1) CPD based on the reliability of properties such as the minimum intensity or maximum temperature required by each change point; 2) identification of a set of possible Kullback-Leibler equations, that is a way of identifying a change point if we know all other properties of the first few points. 3) Fixing the transition between these properties so that it does not represent only a small but important change point in the current state of affairs. In order to do this, one has to model the entire behaviour of the molecule; all interactions, including those with external fields, must be taken into account; and we want to distinguish between slow changes and fast ones where there is a strong dependence on time scale. These complexities require further investigation using more sophisticated methods, such as phase space analysis and machine learning algorithms. Maintenance of high quality statistics using frequent measurements and accurate statistical functions requires careful control, hence our choice of a hierarchical statistical framework. This allows us to maintain a high level of consistency across large number of samples without introducing additional noise, thus ensuring high accuracy when processing real data sets of multiple measurement intervals. Furthermore, this approach can be used to identify the most interesting points in the history of formation of complex structures through inference of their probability distribution function.

Montana's motto, Oro y Plata, Spanish for "Gold and Silver," recognizing the significant role of mining, was first adopted in 1865, when Montana was still a territory. A state seal with a miner's pick and shovel above the motto, surrounded by the mountains and the Great Falls of the Missouri River, was adopted during the first meeting of the territorial legislature in 1864-65. The design was only slightly modified after Montana became a state and adopted it as the Great Seal of the State of Montana, enacted by the legislature in 1893. The state flower, the bitterroot, was adopted in 1895 with the support of a group called the Floral Emblem Association, which formed after Montana's Women's Christian Temperance Union adopted the bitterroot as the organization's state flower. All other symbols were adopted throughout the 20th century, save for Montana's newest symbol, the state butterfly, the mourning cloak, adopted in 2001, and the state lullaby, "Montana Lullaby," adopted in 2007.

It also shows up in things like music and art. Some people even use it to try to predict stock prices! Overall, the Fibonacci sequence is an interesting and important idea in math and science because it shows up in so many different places, and because it has so many interesting properties.

A discrete-time Quantum Walk (QW) is essentially an operator driving the evolution of a single particle on the lattice, through local unitaries. Some QWs admit a continuum limit, leading to infinite walk times and low energy. Other QWs derive from quantum mechanics with monotone operators subject to classical time reversal invariance. They are modeled in the classical limit by a slow but finite time evolution process that results in trajectories moving away from equilibrium toward stabilization. This talk will review recent progress in both the study of short walks and the development of algorithms for their numerical simulation. While many different methods have been used so far for this purpose, we will present new approaches based on a unified formulation which include a time-dependent nonlinear Schrodinger equation as well as linearized integrals over timesteps. This framework allows us to deal with synchronization issues more effectively than currently possible. We will illustrate our ideas using examples from the domain of high Q constants, including perturbation theory, critical phenomena for dilute crystals and superconductors, and the behavior of sparse systems.

Muslims also believe in the angels, the Day of Judgment, and predestination. The Five Pillars of Islam are the core beliefs and practices that form the foundation of Muslim life. They are: belief in God (tawhid), prayer (salah), giving charity (zakah), fasting during Ramadan (sawm), and making the pilgrimage to Mecca (hajj). Islam is the second largest religion in the world with over 1.6 billion followers. The majority of Muslims are Sunni (80-90), while the Shia make up 10-20 of the Muslim population.

As a student in grade ten, I am increasingly becoming aware of the impact my choices have on the environment. One such choice is my diet, and more specifically, my consumption of meat. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that livestock production is responsible for 14.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions. This is more than the entire transport sector combined. By reducing our meat consumption or eliminating it entirely, we can significantly reduce our carbon footprint and mitigate the effects of climate change. Furthermore, the production of meat also requires a significant amount of land, water, and other resources. Livestock farming is responsible for around 80% of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest, which is not only devastating for the environment but also for the indigenous communities that call it home. By reducing our meat consumption, we can also reduce the demand for land and resources, which in turn will help to preserve our planet. In addition to environmental concerns, there are also numerous health benefits to adopting a vegetarian or vegan diet. Studies have shown that plant-based diets can help to reduce the risk of chronic diseases such as heart disease, diabetes, and certain types of cancer. This is because plant-based diets are typically lower in saturated fat and cholesterol and higher in fiber, vitamins, and minerals. Finally, adopting a vegetarian or vegan diet is also more ethical. The conditions in which livestock are often raised are inhumane and cruel. By reducing or eliminating our meat consumption, we can help to reduce the demand for meat and ultimately, reduce the number of animals raised in such conditions. In conclusion, adopting a vegetarian or vegan diet is a responsible choice for the environment, our health, and animal welfare. While it may seem daunting at first, there are numerous resources available to help individuals make the transition. By reducing or eliminating our meat consumption, we can make a positive impact on the planet and live a healthier and more ethical lifestyle.

The first note of Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings is a solitary B flat, in a minor key. As the fragile note softly tip-toes across the air, the rest of the strings follow slowly behind, settling into the listener's heart with an unspeakable, almost unbearable sadness. The first time I heard this piece, I did not even listen to more than a minute. I wanted to listen to something uplifting, something more pleasurable to listen to. However, although I had listened to no more than a few notes, they dwelled heavily on my mind. I could not get the melancholy melody out of my mind, and thus returned to it the day after. Eight minutes later, I was left slumped in my chair, awestruck and emotionally drained. The uneasy, step-like melody was almost physically tangible, and had left me close to tears. Although the background context of the piece was unknown to me at the time, the piece itself left no doubts what it was about. Representing a nation struggling to recover from the wake of the Great Depression, as well as the tension of a world on the brink of World War II, Barber's simplistic masterpiece had the emotional impact of a battering ram, striking me unprepared every time I listened to it. Adagio for Strings embodied every sorrow I had experienced, yet the beauty of the piece is an unforgettable experience I cherish.

Title: The Benefits of Car-Free Cities Introduction Imagine a city where people move around on bikes, scooters, or even just by walking, instead of using cars. This might sound like a far-fetched concept, but car-free cities are becoming more popular as they provide numerous benefits to their residents, the environment, and overall urban planning. 1. Reduced traffic congestion One of the primary advantages of car-free cities is that they experience significantly reduced traffic congestion. Without cars, roads are not clogged with vehicles, allowing for smoother and faster transportation. This not only improves commuting times but also reduces air pollution and noise pollution, making the city a more pleasant environment. 2. Improved public health As people rely on more active modes of transportation, they tend to get more exercise. In car-free cities, residents are more likely to walk or cycle, which helps improve their physical fitness. This can lead to better overall health and reduced obesity rates among city dwellers. 3. Enhanced urban design and planning With less space dedicated to cars, urban designers and planners can focus on creating more pedestrian-friendly areas with wider sidewalks, bike lanes, and green spaces. This results in a safer and more pleasant living environment, encouraging residents to spend more time outdoors and fostering a stronger sense of community. Additionally, car-free cities often have more accessible public transportation, which further enhances urban planning and design. 4. Reduced environmental impact Car-free cities significantly reduce carbon emissions and pollution levels. Fewer cars on the road mean less pollution from vehicle exhaust and less need for energy-intensive infrastructure. This, in turn, contributes to a cleaner, healthier environment, benefiting both the residents and the planet. 5. Enhancement of public safety With fewer vehicles on the road, car-free cities typically have lower rates of accidents and traffic-related incidents. This leads to a safer living environment, especially for pedestrians and cyclists, who are more vulnerable in a car-dominated setting. Conclusion In conclusion, car-free cities offer numerous benefits for both their residents and the environment, such as reduced traffic congestion, improved public health, enhanced urban design and planning, reduced environmental impact, and enhanced public safety. As the world strives for more sustainable and liveable cities, car-free initiatives are likely to continue gaining traction and may become the norm in the future.

The ethics of space tourism and the commercialization of spaceflight raise important questions about equity, accessibility, and the responsible use of resources. While space exploration has the potential to inspire and benefit humanity, it is crucial to consider the ethical implications associated with these endeavors. One primary concern is the issue of equity. Space tourism, as it currently stands, is largely accessible only to a privileged few who can afford the exorbitant costs of space travel. It is essential to develop sustainable practices and regulations to minimize the environmental footprint of space activities and protect the long-term viability of space exploration. Furthermore, the commercialization of space raises concerns about the potential for exploitation and commodification of celestial bodies. Space tourism companies may prioritize profit over scientific research or environmental stewardship, leading to a degradation of the space environment and a loss of focus on the broader societal benefits of space exploration. Ethical considerations should also encompass the rights and well-being of any potential extraterrestrial life forms that may be encountered in the course of space exploration. In conclusion, the ethics of space tourism and the commercialization of spaceflight require careful consideration and ongoing dialogue. By addressing issues of equity, environmental impact, responsible commercial practices, and the well-being of space workers and potential extraterrestrial life, we can ensure that space exploration proceeds in a manner that benefits humanity as a whole and aligns with our shared values and responsibilities.

The rise and fall of Weimar Germany after World War I was a tumultuous period marked by political, economic, and social upheaval. The Treaty of Versailles, which ended the war, placed harsh sanctions on Germany, causing widespread discontent and resentment among the population. This discontent would eventually lead to the rise of Nazism and the downfall of the Weimar Republic. After World War I, Germany was in ruins. The Treaty of Versailles imposed punitive measures on the country, including heavy reparations, the loss of territory, and restrictions on its military. This led to economic instability and hyperinflation, with the value of the German mark plummeting. The government was unable to maintain order, and political parties were divided along ideological lines. The rise of communism and fascism reflected the deepening social and political divisions in the country. One of the key factors in the rise of Nazism was the failure of the Weimar Republic to maintain order and stability. The government was weak and ineffective, and the political system was plagued by corruption and political infighting. The Great Depression, which began in the United States in 1929 and spread to Europe in the early 1930s, further exacerbated these problems. Unemployment skyrocketed, and the already-struggling economy collapsed. The rise of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party was a direct result of the social and political turmoil in Germany during this time. Hitler capitalized on the discontent among the German people, promising to restore order and bring prosperity to the country. His charismatic personality, combined with his anti-Semitic and nationalist rhetoric, appealed to many who were struggling in the post-war economy. In 1933, Hitler was appointed Chancellor of Germany, and within months, he had consolidated power and established a dictatorship. He began implementing his policies of rearmament, expansionism, and anti-Semitism, which led to the persecution and murder of millions of Jews, Romani, and other minorities. The Nazi regime also pursued a policy of aggressive expansion, annexing Austria, the Sudetenland, and Czechoslovakia, eventually leading to the outbreak of World War II. The fall of Weimar Germany was a tragic event in world history. The failure of the government to address the economic and social problems facing the country paved the way for the rise of Nazism and the Holocaust. The lessons learned from this period remain relevant today, as the world continues to grapple with the challenges of nationalism, extremism, and economic inequality.

Title: A Cowboy Who Rode the Waves Have you ever heard a story about a cowboy who traded his spurs for a surfboard and rode the waves instead of the range? Well, that's the story of Tom Blake, a remarkable figure in surfing history who combined his cowboy roots with his passion for water sports. Tom Blake was born in 1902 near Santa Ana in Southern California. His parents were farmers and he grew up in an area known as Orange County, where the land was fertile and agriculture thrived. Blake was an adventurous boy, always looking for new ways to have fun. He loved to ride horses and work with cattle on his family's farm. As Blake matured, he became fascinated by the ocean, which was just a few miles away from his childhood home. He began exploring the nearby beaches, learning to swim, and discovering the thrill of bodysurfing. He quickly realized that the ocean offered an endless source of excitement and challenges. As Blake continued to spend time near the ocean, he noticed the local Hawaiians riding the waves on their boards. This sparked his interest in surfing, and he decided that he wanted to learn how to do it too. However, he didn't have a traditional surfboard, as they were not commonly available in those days. Instead, Blake took inspiration from his cowboy background. He crafted his first surfboard using a wooden plank, some leather straps, and a pair of saddlebags from his family's horse. This makeshift surfboard allowed him to ride the waves like a cowboy, sitting on the board and using the leather straps to maintain balance. As Blake's skills improved, he began modifying his homemade surfboard. He added a fin to improve stability and a rope to aid in steering. This innovative design eventually led him to create the first commercially successful hollow surfboard, which was lighter and more buoyant than traditional solid surfboards. Blake's innovations in surfboard design revolutionized the sport. His hollow surfboards allowed surfers to ride larger waves and perform more advanced maneuvers, paving the way for modern surfing. Tom Blake's unique combination of cowboy roots and love for water sports made him an influential figure in surfing history. Today, surfers continue to benefit from his innovative designs and pioneering spirit, while his story serves as inspiration for those who dare to think outside the box and pursue their passions.

Correlation filter (CF) based tracking algorithms have demonstrated favorable performance recently. Nevertheless, the top performance trackers always employ complicated optimization methods which constraint their real-time applications. How to accelerate the tracking speed while retaining the tracking accuracy is a significant issue. In this paper, we propose a multi-level CF-based tracking approach named MLCFT which further explores the potential capacity of CF with two-stage detection: primal detection and oriented re-detection. The cascaded detection scheme is simple but competent to prevent model drift and accelerate the speed. An effective fusion method based on relative entropy is introduced to combine the complementary features extracted from deep and shallow layers of convolutional neural networks (CNN). Moreover, a novel online model update strategy is utilized in our tracker, which enhances the tracking performance further. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms the most state-of-the-art trackers while tracking at speed of exceeded 16 frames per second on challenging benchmarks.

The impact of climate change on the Arctic tundra is an issue that cannot be overlooked. As the planet warms, Arctic temperatures are rising at twice the rate of other areas on Earth, leading to rapid changes in one of our planet's most fragile ecosystems. The effects of these temperature increases can already be seen in this delicate region as permafrost melts and species struggle to adapt to a quicker-than-expected shift in their environment. For starters, melting ice has caused sea levels around the world to rise while also impacting local wildlife such as polar bears and walruses who rely on stable ice shelves for hunting and migration routes. Additionally, the exposed soil due to melting permafrost is already showing signs of erosion which could further destabilize land surfaces in northern regions if left unchecked. Moreover, other nearby species such as caribou have been directly affected by more frequent forest fires driven by hotter summer temperatures; this event not only reduces food sources for animals but also contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions worldwide when forests burn up acreage. In addition, warmer winters increasingly expose vulnerable plants and animals living within arctic habitats including snow foxes or reindeer populations whose numbers are being depleted from overhunting combined with reduced access to food sources due to melting snow cover. With all this said, it is clear that steps must be taken now before we lose one of our planet's key resources: the Arctic Tundra ecosystem itself. Nations need to come together under international agreements such as the Paris Climate Accord or even through individual efforts like reducing carbon footprints at home – both will contribute towards curbing global warming so that this fragile ecosystem can continue providing invaluable services into future generations without disruption from human activity.

With the rapid growth of financial services, fraud detection has been a very important problem to guarantee a healthy environment for both users and providers. Conventional solutions for fraud detection mainly use some rule-based methods or distract some features manually to perform prediction. However, in financial services, users have rich interactions and they themselves always show multifaceted information. These data form a large multiview network, which is not fully exploited by conventional methods. Additionally, among the network, only very few of the users are labelled, which also poses a great challenge for only utilizing labeled data to achieve a satisfied performance on fraud detection. To address the problem, we expand the labeled data through their social relations to get the unlabeled data and propose a semi-supervised attentive graph neural network, named SemiGNN to utilize the multi-view labeled and unlabeled data for fraud detection. Moreover, we propose a hierarchical attention mechanism to better correlate different neighbors and different views. Simultaneously, the attention mechanism can make the model interpretable and tell what are the important factors for the fraud and why the users are predicted as fraud. Experimentally, we conduct the prediction task on the users of Alipay, one of the largest third-party online and offline cashless payment platform serving more than 4 hundreds of million users in China. By utilizing the social relations and the user attributes, our method can achieve a better accuracy compared with the state-of-the-art methods on two tasks. Moreover, the interpretable results also give interesting intuitions regarding the tasks.

Movies are typically shot at 24 frames per second (fps) because that is the frame rate that has traditionally been used in the film industry. One reason for this is that 24 fps is the minimum frame rate required to create the illusion of continuous motion. At lower frame rates, the motion in a film can appear jerky or choppy.

Another reason that 24 fps is used is because it is the frame rate that is most compatible with the way that film stock and movie projectors work. Film stock is a type of celluloid material that is used to record movies, and it is typically shot at 24 fps. Similarly, most movie projectors are designed to play film at 24 fps.

While it is true that higher frame rates, such as 60 fps, can provide a more smooth and realistic appearance, there are also some trade-offs to consider. For example, shooting at a higher frame rate can require more powerful and expensive equipment, and it can also result in larger file sizes. In addition, some people argue that the "look" of a movie shot at a higher frame rate can be less cinematic and more "video game-like," although this is a matter of personal preference.

Title: Exploring Venus Venus, the second planet from the Sun, is known as Earth's twin sister. However, there's more to it than just being our neighbor in space. Venus is a fascinating planet with unique features, making it an intriguing destination for exploration. Venus' Atmosphere Venus has an extremely thick atmosphere, composed mostly of carbon dioxide with clouds of sulfuric acid. This dense atmosphere creates extremely high surface pressures that can be compared to the pressure found 900 meters (3,000 feet) below the ocean's surface on Earth. Venus' Cloud Cover The planet's cloud cover is made up of droplets of sulfuric acid, which form a layer known as the clouds. The cloud cover on Venus is so thick that it completely obscures the planet's surface, making it impossible to see what lies beneath without the help of advanced technology. Venus' Surface Despite not being able to directly observe the surface of Venus, scientists have gathered valuable information about it through radar imaging. The liquidity of an asset refers to how easily it can be bought or sold without affecting the price. An asset with high liquidity will typically have a tight spread, which is the difference between the bid price and the ask price. It will also have low slippage, which is the difference between the expected price of a trade and the price at which the trade is actually executed.This is because there are many buyers and sellers willing to trade the asset, so it is easy to find a counterparty to take the other side of the trade. This means that the bid and ask prices are close together and there is little difference between the expected price and the actual execution price.On the other hand, an asset with low liquidity may have a wide spread and high slippage because there are fewer buyers and sellers, and it may be difficult to find a counterparty to take the other side of the trade. This means that the bid and ask prices are farther apart, and the actual execution price may be significantly different from the expected price.

I 'm not sure when the game industry started using motion capture , it is definitely something that adds realism to animation . The way it works is that actors have their bodies covered in small little balls . Each ball is a reference point for the location of part of the body ( e.g. elbows , hands , shoulders , etc ) . These balls are tracked in a 3 dimensional space using multiple camera 's . The more balls on the actor , the more detail you can get . The data ( movement of the reference points ) is than " attached " to certain parts of a model . By running the motion capture , the model starts to do the same movements . This way they can make humans look natural in their movements , almost any game uses it these days if they need detail in animations . And yes , before motion capture this was all done by hand and is still done to this day if an object ca n't be represented by a motion capture actor .

Historical memory is the remembrance and recognition of past events that have shaped the present. It is a crucial aspect of contemporary politics because it influences the way people understand and interpret the world around them, and it shapes their attitudes and beliefs. Historical memory is a powerful tool that can be used to construct and maintain identities, and it can be used to justify or challenge existing power structures. One of the ways in which historical memory is used in contemporary politics is through the construction of national identities. Nations are often defined by their history, and the way in which they remember and commemorate their past can be used to create a sense of unity and belonging amongst their citizens. For example, in many countries, the commemoration of independence or the struggle against colonialism is used to create a sense of national pride and identity. Historical memory can also be used to justify or challenge existing power structures. For example, in many countries, the memory of past injustices or oppression can be used to challenge existing power structures and demand change. In South Africa, for example, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission was established to investigate and document the human rights abuses committed during the apartheid era. The commission's findings were used to promote reconciliation and to hold those responsible for the abuses accountable. However, historical memory can also be used to justify existing power structures and to perpetuate injustice. For example, in many countries, the memory of past glories or victories can be used to justify existing power imbalances and to maintain the status quo. In some cases, this can lead to the erasure or distortion of history, and the perpetuation of false narratives that serve to legitimize existing power structures. In conclusion, historical memory is a powerful tool that can be used to construct and maintain identities, to promote reconciliation and change, or to perpetuate injustice and maintain the status quo. It is therefore important that we approach the study of history with a critical and questioning mindset, and that we use historical memory in a responsible and nuanced way.

Beyond the Pleasure Principle Essay Introduction The pleasure principle is a drive to behavior and thoughts which seek pleasure and avoid negative emotions. While Freud recognizes this, he suggests that the principal does not solely dominate mental processes since that would be impossible. Therefore, psychological analysis implies that there is a continuous opposition between the pleasure principle ( eros ) and the aspects that go beyond ( Thanatos ) which are death and repetition. This demonstrated a major turning point in Freud’s perspective that all human action is based on libido but rather a complex interaction of life and death. Freud offers specific examples of beyond the pleasure principle which as children’s games, recurring dreams, self-harming, and repetition compulsion. Main body It was particularly interesting to read about the repetition compulsion that Freud observed in his grandson. Re-enacting an inherently traumatic event, even as a game, as a manner of feeling control over a situation we experience is traumatic is at the same time self-destructive but therapeutic. Freud could not categorize repetition compulsion as a premise of the pleasure principle and deduced it to be a separate aspect. Freud’s observation in the beyond the pleasure principle served as early research into therapies and psychological state for conditions such as PTSD that are well-known in the modern-day. Conclusion Ultimately, all these elements of the beyond the pleasure principle beginning with a child’s game to self-harm and recurring dreams are examples of repetition compulsion. It is a psychological technique that relieves the pressure of the trauma, no matter its extent, from a mother leaving her child for a few hours to veterans of a horrific war. However, it may also be an opening to self-destructive forces which lead to masochism. Overall, the principle represents a dual nature of man which strives for pleasure and to an extent good and love, but also a side that is seeking to die and destroy.

Genetically modified foods (GMFs) have been a topic of intense debate for decades, with proponents extolling their potential benefits and opponents raising concerns about their safety and long-term effects. While the scientific community has largely deemed GMFs to be safe for human consumption, the ethical, environmental, and economic implications of their widespread adoption warrant careful consideration. One of the primary advantages of GMFs lies in their potential to enhance food production and address global hunger. By modifying crops to be more resistant to pests, diseases, and harsh environmental conditions, GMFs can significantly increase yields, reducing the need for pesticides and herbicides and mitigating the impact of climate change on agriculture. This, in turn, can contribute to food security and ensure a stable food supply for a growing global population. Moreover, GMFs offer the opportunity to improve the nutritional value of crops. By introducing genes that encode essential vitamins, minerals, and other nutrients, GMFs can address nutrient deficiencies and malnutrition, particularly in regions where access to a diverse diet is limited. This holds immense potential for improving public health and reducing the burden of diet-related diseases. However, concerns surrounding the safety of GMFs cannot be dismissed lightly. The long-term effects of consuming genetically modified organisms (GMOs) on human health remain largely unknown, and there is a need for comprehensive and independent research to assess any potential risks. The potential for GMOs to transfer their modified genes to non-target organisms, such as wild plants, also raises ecological concerns, as it could disrupt natural ecosystems and biodiversity. Furthermore, the issue of corporate control and intellectual property rights associated with GMFs has sparked ethical and economic debates. The dominance of a few multinational corporations in the development and distribution of GMFs raises concerns about monopolization, control over the food system, and the accessibility of these technologies to small-scale farmers. In conclusion, while GMFs hold promise for addressing global food security and malnutrition, their widespread adoption must be approached with caution. Rigorous scientific research, transparent regulation, and careful consideration of the ethical, environmental, and economic implications are essential to ensure that the potential benefits of GMFs are realized without compromising human health and ecological integrity.

Capitalism is based on private ownership of the means of production, with the goal of making profits in a free market system. Socialism, on the other hand, is based on public ownership of the means of production, with the goal of redistributing wealth and providing social services to everyone. While both systems have their advantages and disadvantages, they differ significantly in the way they view resources and how they function.
