Venus, our neighbor in our solar system, has long captivated our curiosity due to its many unique and fascinating features. In this essay, I aim to discuss what makes Venus so intriguing, as well as some of the ongoing and future missions to better understand this mysterious planet. Venus, the second planet from the sun, has often been dubbed the "Earth's sister planet." While it's not too dissimilar in size, Venus has a thick atmosphere composed mostly of dense carbon dioxide, which gives it its unique appearance and extreme surface conditions. With surface temperatures reaching up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit, Venus has one of the hottest climates in our solar system. Its atmospheric pressure at the surface is 90 times that of Earth's, making it difficult for spacecraft to withstand and study the planet's surface. In spite of these harsh conditions, Venus still holds many secrets waiting to be discovered. Scientists believe there could be a vast ocean beneath the planet's surface, which could potentially harbor extraterrestrial life. The search for evidence of this ocean, as well as understanding the origins and evolution of the planet's atmosphere, are some key objectives for future missions to Venus. Currently, there are no active missions on Venus, though there has been significant interest in returning to the planet. NASA's VERITAS and DAVINCI+, part of their Discovery-class mission, are both planned for the 2020s. VERITAS (Venus Emissivity, Radio Science, Infrared, and Topography) will map the planet's surface to study its geology, while DAVINCI+ (Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble Gases, Chemistry, and Imaging) will study the planet's atmosphere, measuring its composition and temperature distribution. In conclusion, Venus remains a mysterious planet with many fascinating aspects that are yet to be uncovered. With ongoing and future missions like VERITAS and DAVINCI+, we are one step closer to understanding the secrets of this intriguing world in our solar system.

Orthogonal time frequency and space (OTFS) modulation is a promising technology that satisfies high Doppler requirements for future mobile systems. OTFS modulation encodes information symbols and pilot symbols into the two-dimensional (2D) delay-Doppler (DD) domain. The received symbols suffer from inter-Doppler interference (IDI) in the fading channels with fractional Doppler shifts that are sampled at noninteger indices in the DD domain. IDI has been treated as an unavoidable effect because the fractional Doppler shifts cannot be obtained directly from the received pilot symbols. In this paper, we provide a solution to channel estimation for fractional Doppler channels. The proposed estimation provides new insight into the OTFS input-output relation in the DD domain as a 2D circular convolution with a small approximation. According to the input-output relation, we also provide a low-complexity channel equalization method using the estimated channel information. We demonstrate the error performance of the proposed channel estimation and equalization in several channels by simulations. The simulation results show that in high-mobility environments, the total system utilizing the proposed methods outperforms orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) with ideal channel estimation and a conventional channel estimation method using a pseudo sequence.

An RSS feed is simply a file which lists articles on a website in a machine - readable way . When you open your RSS reader , it downloads these files from the websites you subscribe to , and reads them . The file specifies article titles , dates , authors , and usually contains the text content of the article itself or a short summary and a link to the article . tl;dr : RSS lets you check for updates and read articles from your favorite websites all in one place , and it does it using RSS feeds , which are special files that list available articles along with useful information about the articles . As you may know, the Electoral College is a system in which each state is assigned a number of electors equal to its total number of seats in Congress. The candidate who wins the popular vote in a state receives all of that state's electoral votes, except Maine and Nebraska, which award their electoral votes proportionally. The Electoral College has been in place since the United States was founded, and there are a number of reasons why it should be abolished. First, it is undemocratic. The candidate who wins the popular vote does not always win the election. In fact, this has happened five times in American history, most recently in 2016. This means that the majority of voters can be overruled by the Electoral College. Second, the Electoral College gives more power to small states than they deserve. Each state, regardless of its population, gets three electoral votes for its two senators and one for each of its representatives in the House of Representatives. This means that a voter in Wyoming has more power than a voter in California because Wyoming has fewer people but the same number of electoral votes. Third, the Electoral College encourages candidates to focus their campaigns on a few swing states, rather than campaigning in all 50 states. This is because the Electoral College system gives all of a state's electoral votes to the winner of the popular vote in that state. This means that a candidate can win the presidency by winning just a few key states, even if they lose the popular vote overall. There are a number of ways to abolish the Electoral College. One way would be to pass a constitutional amendment. Another way would be to enact legislation that would award electoral votes proportionally to the popular vote in each state. I urge you to support abolishing the Electoral College. It is an undemocratic system that gives more power to small states and encourages candidates to ignore the majority of voters. Living cells like to be encased in membranes. These membranes are made mostly of lipids. Just as oil and water repel each other, a lipid membrane in water holds together without much to connect it. The repellent and attractive forces of water also determine the folded shape of proteins, which determines their function. Lipids, however, are soluble in less-polar compounds than water, like ethanol. Immersing micro-organisms in alcohol dissolves their membranes, bursting them apart. Proteins don't take on the right shape in alcohol, which stops them from functioning.

In a sponsored search auction, decisions about how to rank ads impose tradeoffs between objectives such as revenue and welfare. In this paper, we examine how these tradeoffs should be approached in short-run auctions that consider the effect of advertisers on market prices for short periods on impressions. We mainly focus on bidding mechanisms where some buyers have more information than others but do not know whether they are being bidded against or bid by an advertiser. We analyze two kinds of short-run auctions: 1) Bidirectional auctions, which animate or model bids from both sellers (i.e., buyers) and buyers (Sellers), respectively; 2) Oblique auctions, which treat all buyers equally. We find that oblique auctions generally offer larger discounts than bidirectional auctions because of their opaque nature. The effects of advertising discounting on impression prices can thus vary over time depending on different parameters. In particular, we examine two well-known methods of bidding optimization: 1) "bid auction," the weighting method proposed by MacLeod et al. (1999); 2) "donation auction', the weighted average method proposed by Carlsen et al. (2009).

We explore application of multi-armed bandit algorithms to statistical model checking (SMC) of Markov chains initialized to a set of states. We observe that model checking problems requiring maximization of probabilities of sets of execution over all choices of the initial states, can be formulated as a multi-armed bandit problem, for appropriate costs and rewards. Therefore, the problem can be solved using multi-fidelity hierarchical optimistic optimization (MFHOO). Bandit algorithms, and MFHOO in particular, give (regret) bounds on the sample efficiency which rely on the smoothness and the near-optimality dimension of the objective function, and are a new addition to the existing types of bounds in the SMC literature. We present a new SMC tool - HooVer - built on these principles and our experiments suggest that: Compared with exact probabilistic model checking tools like Storm, HooVer scales better; compared with the statistical model checking tool PlasmaLab, HooVer can require much less data to achieve comparable results.

The use of animals in cosmetic testing raises serious ethical concerns. While some argue that it is necessary to ensure product safety, others argue that it is cruel and inhumane to subject animals to painful testing procedures, especially for the purpose of developing cosmetic products. There are also concerns about the applicability of animal test results to humans. Cosmetic testing on animals often involves subjecting animals to painful procedures that cause significant distress and suffering. Rabbits, mice, rats, and guinea pigs are commonly used for cosmetic testing. Procedures can include rubbing chemicals into the animals' skin or eyes, and then observing the results. These tests are often repeated many times on the same animals. The chemicals used are intended for human use and application, so they are not guaranteed to be safe for animals. The suffering inflicted on animals for the purpose of developing new cosmetic products raises moral concerns, especially considering that cosmetics are not essential products. While ensuring cosmetic safety is important, the suffering of sentient creatures is hard to justify for a non-essential purpose. There are also questions about how applicable animal test results are to humans. Animals and humans have significant biological differences, so results from animal tests may not accurately predict the effects that a chemical may have on humans. This means that cosmetics deemed "safe" based on animal tests could still be harmful or irritating to humans. Due to these differences, cosmetic testing on animals may not achieve its stated purpose of ensuring cosmetic safety for humans. If the applicability of results is limited, it further strengthens the argument that subjecting animals to painful tests for this purpose is unethical. Some argue that animal testing is necessary to establish the safety of new cosmetic ingredients and that strict regulations prevent undue harm. However, the ethical concerns with subjecting animals to distress and suffering for a non-essential purpose like cosmetics still stand. Alternative testing methods like cell cultures, computer models, and human clinical trials could help phase out or minimize live animal testing. A total ban on animal testing for cosmetics may not be practical, but higher standards of care, more stringent regulations, alternative testing methods, and minimizing live testing where possible could help address ethical concerns. The debate around cosmetic testing on animals involves complex issues, but preventing cruelty and suffering of sentient creatures should be an important consideration.

The fridge and freezer doors stood open, their contents melted or spilled onto the countertops below them. Tim turned his attention to the sideboard and its drawers. Some shelves contained ruined jars containing food, some still intact but stained red. There were also half-empty containers littering the top shelf. Our groceries sat scattered around the table like paper debris or toys left abandoned after playtime is over. What did we think about now? This wasn't a place you wanted to spend your time. I couldn't help thinking: why are these things happening to us? Why do we have to live here? Yet despite my apprehension, despite the fact that every fibre of my being screamed for something to be done, even before I knew what needed to be done, I felt no fear. Airseas' Seawing is a parafoil kite designed to attach to ships to reduce emissions on shipping trips by up to 20. It can be mounted onto the deck of any ship, making it ideal for use in harbours and coastal areas where there are low wind speeds. The Seawing was created as part of an EU Horizon 2020 project named CHIMIRAD (Controlling Harmful Industrial Marine Emissions with Remote Controlled Devices). The design process began when engineering student Craig Morrison visited Shipskaar, Norway in May 2009. He filmed and photographed what he saw from the air while flying his paraglider. After completing this experience, he worked out how to make something similar using only materials available at school: polystyrene foam sheets, rope and a rubber band. Three months later, after talking about his ideas with other students at York University they suggested that he should form into a company. Within six weeks of working full-time on the idea, Morrison founded Airseas Aviation Ltd in October 2010 which included five members who had all been involved with the original concept. By January 2011, the first prototype "Seawing" was ready for testing. As well as being used aboard commercial passenger ferries, Royal Mail vessels have also been fitted with them. In the early days they were made privately but now many seacraft firms buy a batch of 25 or more. They cost 1,000 each plus VAT depending upon size. One airline has bought 250 for its fleet, one ferry firm ordered five dozen for their craft and another four hundred series 1s are currently under construction with orders coming through already. The company's power continued to grow and by the early nineteenth century it controlled much of India. British imperialism reached its peak in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. During this period Britain acquired a number of overseas territories, including Egypt, South Africa, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. At its height the British Empire was the largest empire in history and it was said that the sun never set on it. However, the British Empire began to decline after World War One. A number of factors contributed to this, including the cost of maintaining such a large empire, growing nationalism in the colonies and the rise of the United States as a world power. By the mid-twentieth century the British Empire had all but disappeared.

In conclusion, the Face on Mars continues to be a subject of fascination and debate. We outline a detection method for adversarial inputs to deep neural networks. By viewing neural network computations as graphs upon which information flows from input space to output distribution, we can identify regions of input space which cause unexpected flow through the model. This is done by computing the gradients of the output probability vector with respect to the input and sorting them by magnitude. The resulting distribution of gradients can then be used to identify parts of the input which have an unexpectedly large effect on the output of the network. We refer to this as the gradient-based saliency map and show that it can be used to detect adversarial inputs. In the context of neural network classifiers, the gradient-based saliency map is the Shapley value, a well-known concept in cooperative game theory.

As these ecosystems come under threat due to increasing CO2 concentrations or other environmental factors such as warmer temperatures or lower oxygen levels, many other organisms will also be affected including fish larvae which need healthy reefs for shelter and food sources; seagrasses which act as nurseries for juvenile fish; mollusks like oysters and clams which form beds along coasts that provide habitats for small animals; filter feeders like mussels who take up nutrients by filtering water through their gills; algae bloom bacteria that help support keystone predators like whales etc., all suffer from slow death when exposed to rising sea temperatures or low oxygen levels brought about by anthropogenic activities . . The Role of Transnational Advocacy Networks in Global Policy Making Transnational advocacy networks (TANs) play an increasingly important role in shaping global policies. These networks are characterized by their ability to collectively lobby, advocate, and influence decision-makers across national borders and policy arenas. TANs are largely composed of civil society organizations (CSOs), academics, activists, and individuals who share a common cause or interest. Through their collaborative efforts, they are able to generate awareness, mobilize resources, and exert pressure on governments and international institutions to adopt policies that align with their objectives. One of the key features of TANs is their ability to bridge geographical and cultural divides. By bringing together individuals and organizations from different parts of the world, they are able to promote shared values and build global solidarity around specific issues. This is particularly important in an era of globalization, where policies and decisions made in one part of the world can have significant impacts in other parts. Through their transnational reach, TANs are able to ensure that the voices of those who are affected by these policies are heard and considered in decision-making processes. Another important aspect of TANs is their ability to shape the global policy agenda. By focusing attention on specific issues, they can influence the direction of policy debates and shape the priorities of policymakers. For example, TANs have been instrumental in promoting human rights, environmental sustainability, and social justice at the global level. They do this by raising awareness about these issues, generating research and data, and developing policy recommendations that are then disseminated to policymakers. TANs also play a critical role in holding governments and international institutions accountable for their actions. By monitoring policy implementation and advocating for compliance with international norms and standards, they can ensure that commitments made by policymakers are upheld. This helps to build trust and credibility in the global policy-making process, which is essential for achieving sustainable and equitable outcomes. In conclusion, transnational advocacy networks are a powerful force in global policy making. They bridge geographical and cultural divides, shape the global policy agenda, and hold governments and international institutions accountable for their actions. As the world becomes increasingly interconnected, the role of TANs will only become more important in shaping the policies that affect us all.

The Literary and Philosophical Society of Newcastle upon Tyne (popularly known as the'Lit Phil is the largest independent library outside London, housing more than 150,000 books. History Founded in 1793 as the Newcastle upon Tyne Literary and Philosophical Society, it was initially based on the reading clubs of London and Edinburgh. The first members were drawn from the ranks of the city's rapidly expanding middle class, although some wealthy individuals were also members. The society's membership continued to grow throughout the 19th century, reaching 1,200 by 1850. In 1825, the society moved to its current premises on Westgate Road, which were designed by John Dobson. The building was extended in 1854 and 1892. The society's library began with a donation of 300 books from Dr William Turner, the society's first president. It soon began to purchase books on a wide range of topics, and by 1850 it held around 10,000 volumes. Today, the library contains more than 150,000 books, as well as a music library with over 30,000 items. The Lit Phil has been a Grade I listed building since 24 December 1999. In 2012, the society launched a successful 1 million appeal to fund the restoration of its historic building.

An option is a contract that allows ( but does not obligate ) you to make a transaction at a fixed price at a future time . There are two kinds , call options ( which let you buy something ) and put options ( which let you sell something ) . That 's pretty much all there is to it . If you buy an August 19 , 2016 $ 160 call option for IBM , that means that you have the ability to purchase a share of IBM stock for $ 160 at any point between now and August 19 , 2016 ( when the option expires ) , though you 're not required to go through with it . Currently , such an option costs about $ 1.30 , so if you exercise the option when the stock is at least $ 161.30 , you 'll make a profit , and if you do n't , you 'll lose $ 1.30 . Options can be bought and sold on exchanges just like shares of stock . They can be used in a lot of ways , but the most common are as insurance against a significant drop in price ( by buying put options ) or as a way to speculate that a stock will go up ( by buying call options ) .

However, teacher-designed projects maintain consistency in curriculum objectives and standards across grade levels. When assignments are designed by educators, they can ensure projects reinforce key concepts and contents from the previous academic year in an review. This consolidates prior learning and helps prevent summer learning loss or forgetting. Teacher guidance also provides scaffolding to challenge students appropriately for their grade level. Social networking has become an integral part of how we communicate and stay connected with friends and family. However, this increased connectivity does come with some downsides regarding privacy and how we develop and maintain close relationships. Social media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter have given us new ways to share details about our lives, interests, hobbies, relationships, and more with wider audiences. While this can help us stay in touch with more distant friends and acquaintances, it also means we are sharing a lot more personal information in a public or semi-public forum. This constant stream of personal life updates and photos shared on social media has led to concerns over privacy and data security. Our information and images on these platforms can potentially be seen and used by the companies themselves as well as hackers and others. Social media also impacts how we form and engage in close relationships. While social networks open up more opportunities to connect with others and stay in touch with friends, they are not a substitute for in-person interactions and bonding. Messaging, commenting, and liking posts on social media do not provide the same depth of emotional connection as seeing someone face to face. There is a risk of superficiality in relationships that exist primarily through the lens of carefully curated social media profiles and updates. Social networking platforms have become deeply embedded in how we live and interact. But with this increased connectivity we need to be mindful of how we can protect our privacy and nurture meaningful relationships that extend beyond likes, hearts, and temporary digital interactions. We must find a balance of using social media to enhance our lives rather than replace real human connection. Overall, social media has provided both opportunities as well as challenges regarding how we relate to one another in an increasingly digitally-mediated world. The impact on privacy and relationships will depend on how we choose to engage with these powerful tools.

Algorithmic statistics has two different (and almost orthogonal) motivations. From the philosophical point of view, it tries to formalize how the statistics works and why some statistical models are better than others. From the point of view of data analysis, it aims at using statistical theory to design new algorithms for unsupervised learning. We will start by discussing the first motivation. Then we will show that understanding some theoretical statistical properties of some of the most common unsupervised learning algorithms is a necessary step for devising new algorithms for different problems. We will consider three basic problems in statistics. The first one is supervised classification. The second one is unsupervised classification. The third one is principal component analysis. In supervised classification, the goal is to predict the class label of an unseen observation given a training set of labeled examples. In unsupervised classification, the goal is to partition the examples in the training set into two groups. In principal component analysis, the goal is to describe the correlations between the components of the data. The talk will focus on the algorithmic side of the problems. We will show how to design algorithms that use theory of statistical models to achieve their goal. Finally, we will consider an example of how to design algorithms for unsupervised classification using a similar approach. Joint work with P. Diaconis, D. Koller, C. McDiarmid, and J. Pitassi.

Venus, the second planet from the sun, has long fascinated scientists and explorers alike due to its unique characteristics. Known as Earth's "Sister Planet," Venus is similar in size to Earth but with a few key differences that make it an intriguing subject for exploration. One of the primary reasons for studying Venus is its atmosphere, which is made up of a dense layer of carbon dioxide. The pressure on the surface of the planet is around 90 times that of Earth, making it extremely difficult to explore the surface. In fact, probes that have landed on Venus have only survived for a short period due to the extreme conditions. Despite the challenges posed by the atmosphere, scientists have made significant progress in understanding Venus' geological history and its potential for supporting life. The planet's surface is covered with volcanoes, mountains, and canyons. It is also believed to have had a watery past, which may have supported life in the distant past. Another area of interest in Venus' exploration lies in its atmosphere, which has a complex composition of clouds. These clouds are composed of sulfuric acid, which makes them highly reflective, causing the planet to appear as a bright white object in the night sky. This unique characteristic of Venus' atmosphere has been studied extensively by astronomers and atmospheric scientists. In addition to these scientific pursuits, there have been numerous proposals to explore Venus in a more direct manner, such as through human exploration or colonization. While these plans are currently speculative, it is important to understand the challenges and opportunities presented by our closest planetary neighbor. In summary, the exploration of Venus offers a wealth of knowledge about our solar system and the possibility of understanding Earth's history and potential for supporting life in the universe. As technology advances, we may be able to overcome the challenges posed by the planet's atmosphere, allowing us to delve deeper into the secrets of Earth's sister planet.

Torrenting is a way to download and share files over the internet. When you download a file using a torrent client, you are downloading small pieces of the file from many different sources, rather than downloading the entire file from a single source. This makes it possible to download large files more quickly. When you download a torrent file, you are also uploading the pieces of the file that you have already downloaded to other people who are downloading the same file. This is called "seeding." When you seed a file, your IP address is visible to other people who are downloading the file. Copyright holders and law enforcement agencies can monitor torrent swarms and collect the IP addresses of people who are seeding or downloading copyrighted material. They can then send a notice to the internet service provider (ISP) associated with that IP address, asking them to identify the owner of the IP address. If the owner of the IP address is found to be downloading or sharing copyrighted material without permission, they may be fined or sued. So, to answer your question, people can get caught torrenting games, movies, or music by uploading (seeding) the torrent file, and having their IP address identified by copyright holders or law enforcement agencies.

Ok, so the way refrigeration works is by manipulating the energy carrying capacity of a liquidgas. It does this by moving it between the two states and pressure areas. When a liquid evaporates, it absorbs heat from its environment. In refrigerators, you have a reservoir of liquid refrigerant that's passed through something called the metering device. The reservoir is on the high pressure side and when it passes through the metering device to the low pressure side, it evaporates and absorbs heat. This takes place in the A coil, which is the cold part in the system. Here's where things get different from regular refrigeration. In your ac at home, the gas travels through the A coil to the compressor, which squeezes the gas back into a liquid and blows air on it to carry the heat away. In an absorption refrigerator, the gas isn't condensed, it's absorbed by another liquid. This allows the refrigerant gas to return to a liquid state without the energy cost of running a compressor motor. Now you have a liquid saturated in the refrigerant and you need to separate them again. Because the refrigerant has a lower boiling point than the other liquid, this is done by applying heat, whether it be geothermal, solar, or fossil fuels. Now you have heated refrigerant gas coming out of the liquid and you need to get rid of the heat and get it back to the liquid reservoir. This is done by sucking the gas outside and passing it through a bunch of metal fins, which causes the gas to condense and flow back to the reservoir. So, the absorption liquid serves to separate the high and low pressure sides of the system, while avoiding the high energy demand of a compressor motor.

The old warehouse loomed over the pier, casting an ominous shadow in the pale moonlight. Jake walked toward the rusted metal door, a chill running down his spine. His friend Mark had dared him to spend the night in the abandoned building, claiming that it was haunted. Jake didn't believe in ghosts, but the place gave him the creeps. He opened the door with a loud creak and stepped inside. Moonlight filtered in through grimy windows, revealing a vast, empty space. As Jake's eyes adjusted to the darkness, he noticed a rickety staircase leading to an upper level. "Anyone here?" Jake's voice echoed through the emptiness. No response. He walked through a maze of cobwebs, his footsteps echoing on the concrete floor. An old sign hung crookedly from the ceiling, swaying slightly. Jake strained his eyes to read it in the dim light. "Warning: Authorized Personnel Only. Trespassers Will Be Prosecuted." Jake chuckled, his nerves easing a bit. As he explored the main floor, his imagination ran wild. He pictured the warehouse bustling with workers decades ago, filled with voices and the sounds of machinery. Now only silence remained. After a while, Jake's initial fear faded into boredom. He sat down, leaning against a wall, and closed his eyes. The building seemed completely ordinary. Mark's dare had been silly. Jake was about to nod off when he heard a loud CRASH from above. His eyes flew open and his heart pounded. It came from the upper level. Jake froze in terror, listening. There it was again, the sound of something heavy falling over upstairs. His mind raced. Rats? Birds? Or something else...? Summoning his courage, Jake crept up the rickety steps toward the source of the sounds. The stairway groaned under his weight, each step threatening to collapse. At the top, Jake peered into the gloom. A shadowy figure stood by a window, pushing over old crates. Jake blinked in disbelief. It was Mark, laughing at his own trickery. "You should've seen your face, man!" Mark guffawed. Jake shook his head, torn between annoyance and relief that his friend's prank was the only 'haunting' he would encounter tonight. His fright melted into laughter, echoing off the walls of the old warehouse under the pale moonlight.

Yes , lossless formats are completely lossless . The simplest lossless compression is run - length encoding , where long runs of the same value are replaced with a number representing the length of the run . So instead of storing " 00000000000000000000 " longhand , they 'd store something like " 0 * 20 " instead . In something like an image file with big areas of the same colour , this can save a whole lot of space . Lossy formats , on the other hand , * approximate * the data fed into them - the one you 're likely most familiar with is the .jpg image format . Using some mathematical trickery , it 's possible to roughly replicate any 8 * 8 block of pixels with only a handful of bytes - stitch enough blocks together , and you have an entire image stored in far fewer bytes than you 'd otherwise need , saving vast amounts of disk space . The rougher the approximation you 're willing to put up with , the more space you save . Of course , this comes at a price in terms of image quality ; overly - compressed jpgs can [ look awful ] ( URL_0 ) . Similar techniques can be used with audio and video files - most lossy formats tend to exploit the limits of human perception , and throw away the details we 're least able to notice . The human eye , for instance , is very sensitive to the brightness of each pixel in an image , and will instantly notice blurring or glitching from lost brightness detail . On the other hand , it 's almost comically insensitive to smeary detail in the * colour * of each pixel - so the .jpg format faithfully stores as much brightness detail as it can , but throws away most of the fiddly colour detail , and you do n't even notice . Similarly , it 's almost impossible to notice fiddly high - frequency sounds when there are low - frequency sounds masking them , so the .mp3 format exploits this in a similar way . Most formats are tunable with regard to how much information they throw away , storing more or less detail according to how much space you need to save .

Schools should allow for both teacher designed and student designed summer projects. While teacher designed projects ensure students cover important academic topics, student designed projects encourage creativity and independence. A balanced approach combining these two options would be most effective. Teacher designed summer projects are important because they help students retain knowledge from the previous school year and prepare for upcoming grades. Teachers are experts in their subject areas and know the skills and concepts students need to learn. They can craft assignments that reinforce literacy, math, science and other core topics in an engaging way. This is especially useful for subjects that build year after year like math and foreign language. Students may be more motivated to complete assignments designed by their teachers compared to completely open ended projects. However, student designed projects are also valuable for learning. They allow students autonomy to explore topics they find interesting through creative means like building models, writing stories or conducting experiments. When students have ownership over their work, they are more invested in the learning process. Student designed projects foster skills like time management, problem-solving and independent research that are useful for academics and beyond. Creativity is equally important as core subjects and helps engaged students as lifelong learners. The best approach would combine these strengths. Teachers could provide a list of approved topics or general guidelines for projects related to the grade level curriculum. Then students work independently or in small groups to conceive novel ways to study and present their chosen topics. Teachers are still ensuring learning standards are met while students have freedom to customize projects to their individual interests and learning styles. This balanced model keeps students engaged in meaningful learning over summer breaks in a way that feels more like play than schoolwork. It helps them retain knowledge in a dynamic way and come back to school in the fall ready to build on new skills and concepts.

The most basic answer is that for a CPU the motherboard IS the card. A discrete video graphics card contains everything the graphics unit needs to operate. The motherboard I the board that connects all of the computer components required to make the computer 1 whole. It connects the ram, processor and various input and outputs. Some motherboards come with the graphics processing unit chip built into them. That chip uses the motherboard pathways and circuits to access the system ram and inputs and outputs. This is called "integrated" graphics. It's generally much slower than having a separate graphics card because the components are more general use and are not optimized for graphics.

The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is a system developed by Paul Ekman and Wallace V. Friesen in the 1970s that describes the movements and expressions of the face. The system categorizes facial expressions into six basic categories: happiness, sadness, surprise, anger, fear, and disgust. The system also includes hundreds of specific expressions and microexpressions that can be used to further analyze a person's emotional state. FACS is widely used in fields such as psychology, neuroscience, and even in industries like marketing and advertising. In psychology, it is used to study emotions and their expression in humans. In neuroscience, it is used to understand how different emotions are processed in the brain. In marketing and advertising, it is used to create more effective campaigns and to persuade people to buy products or services. One of the main advantages of FACS is that it is a standardized system that can be used consistently across different contexts and cultures. This makes it a valuable tool for researchers who want to compare results across different studies or to study human emotions in different cultures. However, one of the challenges of using FACS is that it can be difficult to interpret microexpressions, which are very brief and subtle facial expressions that can be difficult to detect. Additionally, some people may be aware of their expressions and may try to hide their true feelings, which can also make it difficult to accurately interpret their expressions. Overall, the Facial Action Coding System is a valuable tool for understanding human emotions and their expression. While it has some limitations, it provides a standardized and consistent framework for studying this important aspect of human psychology.

The Face on Mars: A Natural Landform For decades, the unusual pattern seen on the surface of Mars known as the "Face on Mars" has fueled speculation that it was sculpted by ancient aliens. However, scientific evidence tells a different story and shows that this landform is a result of natural geological processes rather than artificial construction. The main claim that the Face is a natural landform is based on analyses of higher resolution images taken by NASA's Viking orbiter in the late 1970s. These images revealed that the alleged "Face" is simply a pattern of light and dark patches formed by differences in rock composition and erosion. There are groups of mesas and hills in the area that are bisected by valley networks, creating the overall facial appearance from certain angles. However, up close it is clear that there are no definitive facial features like eyes or a mouth, just irregular rocky outcrops. Additional evidence comes from experiments done by NASA scientists to simulate the effects of natural weathering over long periods of time. When they exposed landscape models resembling the Cydonia region to conditions similar to Mars, patterns reminiscent of the "Face" began to emerge after hundreds or thousands of simulated years. The wind erosion gradually hollowed out darker rock and left lighter colored, harder rock behind - naturally forming strange patterns that resemble recognizable shapes from a distance, like faces or animals. In conclusion, while initial low-resolution images of the "Face on Mars" led some to imagine it was sculpted intentionally, higher quality evidence shows that it is clearly a natural rock formation shaped by normal geological processes like erosion. Claims of an artificial construct require extraordinary evidence, which has not been found. The "Face" is more reasonably explained as a trick of light and shadow perceived by our pattern-seeking minds rather than visitation by an ancient alien civilization. For these reasons, the scientific consensus is that Mars still retains no evidence of past or present life, artificial or otherwise.

Dear Senator, I am writing to you today to express my support for abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President of the United States by popular vote. I believe that this is the best way to ensure that the president is elected by the will of the people. There are several reasons why I believe that the Electoral College is no longer a necessary or desirable part of our electoral system. First, it is undemocratic. The Electoral College gives more power to voters in small states than voters in large states. This is because each state is allocated a number of electoral votes equal to the number of its representatives in Congress plus its two senators. This means that a voter in Wyoming has more than three times the voting power of a voter in California. Second, the Electoral College can lead to the election of a president who did not win the popular vote. This has happened five times in American history, most recently in 2000. In that election, George d. Bush won the presidency even though Al Gore won the popular vote by more than 500,000 votes. This is a clear example of how the Electoral College can undermine the will of the people. Third, the Electoral College is unwieldy and inefficient. The process of electing the president through the Electoral College is long and complicated. It can take weeks or even months for the results of the election to be known. This is because the electoral votes are not cast until December, and the electors are not required to vote for the candidate who won the popular vote in their state. Fourth, the Electoral College encourages candidates to focus their campaigns on a few "swing" states. This is because the candidate who wins the most electoral votes wins the presidency, regardless of the popular vote. This means that candidates have no incentive to campaign in states that are already guaranteed to go to one candidate or the other. I believe that the Electoral College should be abolished and replaced with a system of electing the president by popular vote. This would be the fairest and most democratic way to elect the president. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, [Your Name]

The Great Plains come to an abrupt end at the Rocky Mountains. The Rocky Mountains form a large portion of the Western U.S., entering from Canada and stretching nearly to Mexico. The Rocky Mountain region is the highest region of the United States by average elevation. The Rocky Mountains generally contain fairly mild slopes and wider peaks compared to some of the other great mountain ranges, with a few exceptions (such as the Teton Mountains in Wyoming and the Sawatch Range in Colorado). The highest peaks of the Rockies are found in Colorado, the tallest peak being Mount Elbert at 14,440 ft (4,400 m). The Rocky Mountains contain some of the most spectacular, and well known scenery in the world. In addition, instead of being one generally continuous and solid mountain range, it is broken up into a number of smaller, intermittent mountain ranges, forming a large series of basins and valleys.

To maximize practicality and applicability, we adopt four important point-to-point link models based on outage probability in our analysis: single-input single-output (SISO), single-input multiple-output (SIMO), multiple-input single-output (MISO), and multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO). Furthermore, we derive diversity and power scaling laws that dictate how boundary effects can be mitigated (to leading order) in confined dense networks for each of these models. Finally, in order to demonstrate the versatility of our theory, we analyze boundary effects for dense networks comprising MIMO point-to-point links confined within a right prism, a polyhedron that accurately models many geometries that can be found in practice. We provide numerical results for this example, which verify our analytical results.

The plague repeatedly returned to haunt Europe and the Mediterranean throughout the 14th to 17th centuries. According to Biraben, the plague was present somewhere in Europe in every year between (a study of human remains analyzed by Meryman et al. [1] attributed this period as a possible "plague-free" interval) except for 9 years from , with the exception of an anomaly during the Second World War when it reappeared primarily in Italy. A large number of cases were documented in France and other European countries through the late 19th and early 20th century. The appearance and spread of Ebola virus disease in central Africa in 1976 revealed that ancient strains of Yersinia pestis are still capable of infecting humans and causing significant morbidity and mortality in epidemic form. Yersinia is also known to cause plague epidemics among domestic dogs, cats, rats, mice, hares and rabbits in many parts of temperate Asia; however, there have been no recent outbreaks reported in these species in North America or Europe. Thus far, Y. pestis has not caused serious illness in humans outside of Asia. Importantly, although Y. pestis can be transmitted directly from animals to humans via consumption of rat meat infected with the organism, as well as indirectly via flea bites from pets or rodents, it usually does so only after prolonged contact between the host animal (s) and its fleas, which harbors Y. pestis on their bodies but may lack infection themselves.[3]. As such, Y. pestis commonly circulates undetected within communities until the flea stage becomes established[4],[5]. There have been several efforts over decades to develop vaccines against Y. pestis based upon classical vaccine design principles involving attenuated strains of the causative agent. Although some immunization technologies for successful control of polio,[6] smallpox[7], variola[8] and rabies[92],[11type viruses have been developed, none of them targeting Yersinia have resulted in particularly safe and effective treatments. In addition to the vaccine challenge study described earlier, several approaches aimed at expressing attenuated forms of Y. pestis antigens in insect cells intended for use in passive immunizations have failed in vivo trials due to the inability to induce protective antibody levels or high titer antibody production in animals. Accordingly, a need exists for new methods and compositions for treating Yersinia infections.

Originally alphabets were written entirely in majuscule letters, spaced between well-defined upper and lower bounds. When written quickly with a pen, these tended to turn into rounder and much simpler forms. It is from these that the first minuscule hands developed, the half-uncials and cursive minuscule, which no longer stayed bound between a pair of lines. These in turn formed the foundations for the Carolingian minuscule script, developed by Alcuin for use in the court of Charlemagne, which quickly spread across Europe. The advantage of the minuscule over majuscule was improved, faster readability.[citation needed]

A stop order is an order to buy or sell a security when its price moves beyond a certain point, specified by the investor as the "stop price." Once the stop price is reached, the stop order becomes a market order and is executed at the best available price.A stop limit order is similar to a stop order, but after the stop price is reached, the order becomes a limit order, which is an order to buy or sell at a specific price or better. The investor specifies the limit price at which they are willing to buy or sell the security.The main difference between a stop order and a stop limit order is that with a stop limit order, the investor has more control over the price at which their order is filled. With a stop order, the investor may get a price that is significantly different from the stop price, because the order becomes a market order and is filled at the best available price. With a stop limit order, the investor can specify the maximum or minimum price they are willing to pay or receive, so they have more control over the price they get for their trade.It's important to note that stop orders and stop limit orders are not guaranteed to be filled, as there may not be enough liquidity in the market to fill the order at the specified price.

Vicky Cherry, 44, had been missing for 15 months when police found her body wrapped in a duvet and plastic sheeting at a house in Toronto Street, Bolton, in January. This week, an inquest was opened and adjourned into the mum-of-four's sudden death. At the hearing at Bolton Coroner's Court, coroner Christopher Sumner said: "On January 15 this year police were called to a property in Toronto Street following reports of the discovery of a body. "Police have reported that Vicky Cherry, aged 44, was found wrapped in a duvet and plastic sheeting. "Vicky had been reported missing in October 2019 so you can imagine the shock when her body was found. "Further enquiries revealed she had died from strangulation." Mr Sumner said that it is unclear whether the mum-of-four was dead when she was wrapped in the plastic sheeting. He told the court how Vicky lived with her partner of almost two years and her four children, who are aged between 13 and 23. The inquest heard that Vicky had previously suffered with anxiety and had made previous attempts to take her own life. Mr Sumner said: "Before her disappearance she had fallen on hard times, living on benefits and had struggled to pay utility bills. "She had been unemployed for some time although she had previously worked as a care assistant. "She had also made previous attempts to commit suicide. "She had threatened to kill herself on several occasions and had taken multiple overdoses in the past." (Image: GMP) However, there was no evidence that she had made any similar threats before she went missing, Mr Sumner said. He added: "She did have a history of mental health problems but they had suddenly improved. "It may have been that she wanted to end her life but it is not known whether she did that or if someone else has killed her." A full inquest will be held on September 9, when Vicky's family and friends will hear more about the circumstances of her death.

Store brands, also known as private label brands, are products that are sold by a particular store or retailer under their own brand name rather than that of a name brand or other company. These products are often similar to name brand products and may be made by the same manufacturers or by other companies. To create a store brand product, a retailer may work with a manufacturer to develop a product that is similar to a popular name brand product. The retailer may provide the manufacturer with a list of ingredients and specifications for the product, such as flavor, texture, and packaging. The manufacturer will then create the product according to these specifications and sell it to the retailer, who will then sell it under their own brand name. In some cases, store brand products may be made using the same ingredients and formulas as name brand products, but they may also be made using different ingredients or formulas. The goal is often to create a product that is similar to the name brand product in terms of quality and performance, but at a lower price point. Synergistic interactions are ubiquitous in the real world. Recent studies have revealed that, for a single-layer network, synergy can enhance spreading and even induce an explosive contagion. There is at the present a growing interest in behavior spreading dynamics on multiplex networks. What is the role of synergistic interactions in behavior spreading in such networked systems? To address this question, we articulate a synergistic behavior spreading model on a double layer network, where the key manifestation of the synergistic interactions is that the adoption of one behavior by a node in one layer enhances its probability of adopting the behavior in the other layer. A general result is that synergistic interactions can greatly enhance the spreading of the behaviors in both layers. A remarkable phenomenon is that the interactions can alter the nature of the phase transition associated with behavior adoption or spreading dynamics. In particular, depending on the transmission rate of one behavior in a network layer, synergistic interactions can lead to a discontinuous (first-order) or a continuous (second-order) transition in the adoption scope of the other behavior with respect to its transmission rate. A surprising two-stage spreading process can arise: due to synergy, nodes having adopted one behavior in one layer adopt the other behavior in the other layer and then prompt the remaining nodes in this layer to quickly adopt the behavior. Analytically, we develop an edge-based compartmental theory and perform a bifurcation analysis to fully understand, in the weak synergistic interaction regime where the dynamical correlation between the network layers is negligible, the role of the interactions in promoting the social behavioral spreading dynamics in the whole system.

In the United States, churches and other religious organizations are generally exempt from paying taxes on their income. This tax-exempt status is granted to these organizations because of the principle of separation of church and state, which is an important part of the U.S. Constitution. The First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution guarantees the freedom of religion, which means that the government cannot tell people what to believe or how to practice their religion. This means that the government also cannot tax churches or other religious organizations, because doing so would be a way of indirectly controlling or influencing those organizations. In other words, the government gives tax-exempt status to churches and other religious organizations because it wants to respect the freedom of religion and keep a separation between the government and religious matters. This allows these organizations to operate without interference from the government and to focus on their religious and charitable work.

Sharding has emerged as one of the common techniques to address the scalability problems of blockchain systems. To this end, various sharding techniques for blockchain systems have been proposed in the literature. These techniques are broadly classified into two categories, namely, state sharding and transaction sharding. State sharding focuses on partitioning the blockchain ledger among multiple shards, while transaction sharding focuses on partitioning the incoming transactions among multiple shards. State sharding techniques can be further divided into two approaches: horizontal sharding and vertical sharding. In horizontal sharding, the ledger is split into multiple blocks, with each block representing a separate shard. The transactions in each shard are maintained in their own block. This allows for better scalability as each shard can process its own transactions independently of other shards. In vertical sharding, the ledger is split into multiple columns, with each column representing a different shard. The transactions belonging to each shard are stored in their respective columns. This approach allows for more efficient query execution since only the relevant columns need to be accessed. Transaction sharding techniques focus on partitioning the incoming transactions among multiple shards. These techniques include range-based sharding, random sharding, and hash-based sharding. Range-based sharding divides the transactions into intervals based on some attribute such as time or account ID, and assigns them to different shards. Random sharding assigns transactions to shards randomly. Hash-based sharding uses a cryptographic hash function to assign transactions to shards based on their hash value. Sharding techniques have been applied to various blockchain systems, such as Ethereum and Hyperledger Fabric, to improve their scalability. Sharding can also help to increase the throughput of blockchain systems by reducing the number of nodes that need to process a given transaction. However, there are still some challenges that need to be addressed before these techniques can be widely adopted, such as ensuring data integrity across shards and mitigating the impact of malicious nodes.

We propose the method to sanitize the privacy of the IFM (Input Feature Map) s that are fed into the layers of CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) s. The method introduces the degree of the sanitization that makes the application using a CNN be able to control the privacy loss represented as the ratio of the probabilistic accuracies for original IFM and sanitized IFM. For the sanitization of an IFM, the sample-and-hold based approximation scheme is devised to satisfy an application-specific degree of the sanitization. The scheme approximates an IFM by replacing all the samples in a window with the non-zero sample closest to the mean of the sampling window. It also removes the dependency on CNN configuration by unfolding multi-dimensional IFM tensors into one-dimensional streams to be approximated.

The Renaissance period was a time of immense cultural and intellectual change, and its influence can still be felt in the art and aesthetics of today. The Renaissance saw a renewed interest in classical learning and culture, and this led to a shift in artistic styles and techniques. Artists began to use more realistic and naturalistic depictions of the human form, and they also began to explore new ways of expressing emotion and movement. These innovations had a profound impact on the development of Western art, and they continue to influence artists today. One of the most significant contributions of the Renaissance to modern aesthetics is the development of perspective. Before the Renaissance, artists typically used a flat, two-dimensional style of painting. However, during the Renaissance, artists began to use linear perspective to create the illusion of depth in their paintings. This allowed them to create more realistic and immersive works of art. Another important contribution of the Renaissance to modern aesthetics is the development of chiaroscuro. Chiaroscuro is the use of light and shadow to create a sense of depth and realism in a painting. Renaissance artists used chiaroscuro to highlight the human form and to create a sense of drama and emotion. The Renaissance also saw the development of new techniques for sculpting. Artists began to use bronze and marble to create more durable and realistic sculptures. They also began to experiment with new poses and expressions, which allowed them to convey a wider range of emotions and ideas. The influence of Renaissance art can be seen in the work of many modern artists. For example, the paintings of Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque show the influence of Renaissance perspective and chiaroscuro. The sculptures of Auguste Rodin and Henry Moore show the influence of Renaissance techniques for sculpting. The Renaissance was a time of great artistic achievement, and its influence can still be felt in the art and aesthetics of today. The innovations of Renaissance artists laid the foundation for the development of modern art, and their work continues to inspire artists around the world.

I disagree with the principal's decision to require all students to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While extracurriculars provide benefits, mandatory participation should not be imposed on students. There are many valid reasons why a student may not have the time or desire to take on extracurricular commitments. Some students may need to prioritize academics and devote their limited free time to studying in order to maintain good grades. Others may have family responsibilities or jobs to help support their families financially. Forcing extracurricular participation fails to recognize these important obligations and could negatively impact students' school performance or home life. Furthermore, extracurricular activities will not be valuable for all personalities. Such mandatory activities could discourage introverted students who may feel stressed by required socializing outside of class. Not all students will find the particular clubs and sports offered engaging or worthwhile. Forcing participation removes students' autonomy to pursue activities that genuinely interest them. This one-size-fits-all approach disregards students' differing strengths, weaknesses and interests. Instead of making activities compulsory, the school should focus on promoting their value and increasing voluntary engagement. Providing descriptive information about each club could help students find ones aligned with their passions. Recognizing extracurriculars in college recommendations could incentivize participation without compulsion. The school should accommodate students' diverse needs and respects their freedom to set priorities. Overall responsibilities for school, work, family and interests will vary across students, so mandatory extracurricular policies risk doing more harm than good. In conclusion, while extracurricular activities offer benefits, requiring universal participation disregards students' varied circumstances and fails to respect their autonomy. A policy of mandated activities will not motivate genuine involvement and risks negatively impacting students' performance or life balance. The school should find ways to encourage voluntary participation through information and incentives rather than compulsion. Student interests, obligations and self-determination are best served through choice, not one-size-fits-all decrees.

It 's a fundamental truth of physics that all laws are time - reversible . If you film yourself throwing a ball into the air and then play the film back backwards , the laws of physics wo n't appear to be broken . They work the same backwards as they do frontwards . Many years ago , after black holes were known to exist but before they were understood , somebody wondered what they would look like if you viewed them backwards . The answer they came up with was a spherical mass that continually emits matter forever and ever . They called it a white hole . Some speculated that this might serve to explain how it is that black holes can swallow matter without limit : for every black hole there 's a corresponding white hole somewhere in the universe , so all the matter that falls into the black hole emerges from the white hole . But now we know that that 's nonsense . Black hole thermodynamics demonstrates , first , that black holes can not just keep swallowing matter forever , and second , that the matter that falls into a black hole gets emitted by * that same black hole * as thermal radiation . So white holes are not needed to explain anything , and now we know they do n't — in fact ca n't — exist .

It should be noted that although 6-month-olds can recall information over the short-term, they have difficulty recalling the temporal order of information. It is only by 9 months of age that infants can recall the actions of a two-step sequence in the correct temporal order - that is, recalling step 1 and then step 2. In other words, when asked to imitate a two-step action sequence (such as putting a toy car in the base and pushing in the plunger to make the toy roll to the other end), 9-month-olds tend to imitate the actions of the sequence in the correct order (step 1 and then step 2). Younger infants (6-month-olds) can only recall one step of a two-step sequence. Researchers have suggested that these age differences are probably due to the fact that the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus and the frontal components of the neural network are not fully developed at the age of 6-months.

F1 cars draw their cooling air directly from the front grille area - provided they've got front brakes - but that means as soon as you make contact with something at speed, all your mass goes towards making sure the driver doesn't die instead of extracting more performance from the machine. And that is almost always true in modern F1: every part of the chassis or bodywork has been designed for maximum efficiency, while the engines have become increasingly more complicated over time. We need a completely different approach if we want our engines to run on cleaner fuels without heating up so much they can no longer function properly. We already know how to do this through natural convection (the process by which warm air rises) within the machine itself; what's needed now is some ducting to feed fresh air into the radiators at high speeds so we don't need to rely just on the cowslip flap. Then, once we're cooled off again, we'll be able to let the dirty exhaust gases out again - all without having to disrupt the airflow around the car any further. This might sound like something only a handful of people could really understand or care about, but actually I think a lot of fans would love seeing a bit less fuss and fanfair surrounding the sport. After all, it's not exactly hard to imagine the sort of bloke who wants his grandkids to grow up playing video games watching a GP race rather than lying on the ground pretending he's driving one himself!

BitCoin is not considered a legitimate currency in the same way that the U.S. dollar is because it is not backed by a government or other institution that has the power to regulate its use. However, some people use BitCoin as a way to make financial transactions because it is fast, secure, and can be used anonymously.

We consider the problem of sparse atomic optimization, where the notion of "sparsity" is generalized to meaning some linear combination of few atoms. The definition of atomic set is very broad; popular examples include the standard basis, low-rank matrices, overcomplete dictionaries, permutation matrices, orthogonal matrices, etc. The model of sparse atomic optimization therefore includes problems coming from many fields, including statistics, signal processing, machine learning, computer vision and so on. Specifically, we consider the problem of maximizing a restricted strongly convex (or concave), smooth function restricted to a sparse linear combination of atoms. We extend recent work that establish linear convergence rates of greedy algorithms on restricted strongly concave, smooth functions on sparse vectors to the realm of general atomic sets, where the convergence rate involves a novel quantity: the "sparse atomic condition number." This leads to the strongest known multiplicative approximation guarantees for various flavors of greedy algorithms for sparse atomic optimization; in particular, we show that in many settings of interest the greedy algorithm can attain strong approximation guarantees while maintaining sparsity. Furthermore, we introduce a scheme for forward-backward algorithms that achieves the same approximation guarantees. Secondly, we define an alternate notion of weak submodularity, which we show is tightly related to the more familiar version that has been used to prove earlier linear convergence rates. We prove analogous multiplicative approximation guarantees using this alternate weak submodularity, and establish its distinct identity and applications.

Growth is a fundamental aspect of life, as it allows individuals to develop and evolve into their full potential. However, the pursuit of growth can sometimes be hindered by the desire for more. Being avaricious, or excessively desiring wealth and material possessions, can lead to a narrow focus on personal gain, rather than on personal growth. On one hand, the desire for more can drive individuals to push themselves to achieve their goals and reach their full potential. This drive can lead to innovation, progress, and success in various areas of life. For example, a person who is driven to succeed in their career may work hard to advance in their field, leading to recognition and success. On the other hand, the desire for more can also lead to a fixation on material possessions and personal gain, rather than on personal growth. When individuals become too focused on accumulating wealth and possessions, they may neglect other important aspects of their life, such as their relationships, health, and personal development. This can lead to a stagnation of growth and a lack of fulfillment in life. Moreover, the pursuit of more can also lead to a sense of discontentment and dissatisfaction. When individuals constantly strive for more, they may never feel satisfied with what they have, leading to a never ending cycle of desire and dissatisfaction. This can lead to a sense of emptiness and purposelessness, as individuals become disconnected from their true values and goals. In conclusion, the desire for more can have both positive and negative effects on growth. While it can drive individuals to achieve their goals and reach their full potential, it can also lead to a fixation on material possessions and personal gain, rather than on personal growth. It is important to strike a balance between the desire for more and the pursuit of personal growth, in order to lead a fulfilling and meaningful life.

What we know as sound is our response to pressure waves in the air around us . The frequency ( how close together ) and amplitude ( the size ) of these waves make different sounds . A speaker creates pressure waves by moving a cone back and forth . By moving at different speeds and over different distances , it creates waves of specific frequencies and amplitude . The cone of the speaker has a magnet attached to it . Near that magnet inside the speaker housing is a coil of wire . When electricity is run through the coil of wire the magnet gets pulled toward the coil . When the electricity in the coil stops , the magnet springs away from the coil due to the shape of the speaker cone . Running electricity through the coil at differing frequencies and for differing durations cause the speaker cone to move sound waves at various frequencies and amplitudes . Headphones usually have very small speaker cones and very small magnets . Because of this , they are usually not very good at creating low frequency sound waves .

Because of its abundance at these times, ctenophore fishing has been a major industry for many years, especially along Atlantic coastlines with shallow water depths. The most important commercially caught species are the blue mussel (Bryozoa mydas), which occurs in all parts of North America except Alaska. Because it is so valuable, however, extensive monitoring of the natural environment surrounding each fishery site is required before commercial harvest can begin. This is done by trail camera trapping and by using remote sensing techniques including satellite imagery and sonar imaging for mapping the sea floor. Although efforts have been made to increase awareness and understanding of this ecosystem resource, certain threats remain: invasive alien species like the Eurasian pond snail (Lepidoptera violacea) that colonize shell beds have been known to damage native ctenophore communities; overfishing continues to threaten the number and diversity of ctenophore populations; and climate change is expected to reduce connectivity between habitats, reducing habitat variation within fish stocks.

Dietary therapy emphasizes the importance of a balanced diet and the consumption of specific foods to promote health and healing. Finally, exercise plays a crucial role in TCM, as it helps to improve circulation, reduce stress, and promote overall well-being. One of the key benefits of TCM is its focus on treating the whole person, rather than just the symptoms of a disease. This holistic approach recognizes that physical, emotional, and spiritual health are all interconnected and that a imbalance in one area can lead to imbalances in others. By addressing the root cause of a condition, TCM can help to promote long-term health and well-being. Another advantage of TCM is that it is often less invasive than Western medicine, making it a popular choice for people who prefer a more natural approach to health care. Additionally, TCM has been shown to be effective in treating a wide range of conditions, including chronic pain, anxiety, and digestive issues. In conclusion, Traditional Chinese Medicine plays an important role in holistic health care by promoting overall well-being and addressing the root cause of health problems. In machine learning, feature learning or representation learning is a set of techniques that allows a system to automatically discover the representations needed for feature detection or classification from raw data. This replaces manual feature engineering and allows a machine to both learn the features and use them to perform a specific task. Feature learning is motivated by the fact that machine learning tasks such as classification often require input that is mathematically and computationally convenient to process. However, real-world data such as images, video, and sensor data has not yielded to attempts to algorithmically define specific features. An alternative is to discover such features or representations through examination, without relying on explicit algorithms. Feature learning can be either supervised, unsupervised or self-supervised.

Capybara, rabbits, hamsters and other related species do not have a complex digestive system as do, for example, ruminants. Instead they extract more nutrition from grass by giving their food a second pass through the gut. Soft faecal pellets of partially digested food are excreted and generally consumed immediately. The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is an analytical tool used to identify and analyze the subtle and unconscious facial expressions that reveal a person's true emotions. It was originally developed by Paul Ekman and Wallace V. Friesen in the late 1970s and has since become widely used in fields such as psychology, anthropology, and neuroscience. FACS is based on the idea that the face is a complex and dynamic system of muscles that work together to create a range of expressive movements. These movements can be categorized into seven fundamental categories: head movements, eye movements, eyebrows, corners of the eyes, nose, mouth, and chin movements. By combining and varying these movements in subtle and precise ways, the face can convey a vast range of emotions and feelings. The FACS coding system works by breaking down these facial expressive movements into smaller, more nuanced units called Action Units (AUs). There are now 46 AUs that have been identified and categorized, each representing a specific facial expression or muscle movement. Researchers use this system to code and analyze video recordings of facial expressions in order to study the neural and psychological mechanisms underlying emotion. One of the key advantages of using the FACS coding system is its ability to provide a standardized and objective measurement of facial expressions. This is particularly useful in research studies, where it can help researchers to compare and contrast different emotional states or to track changes in facial expressions over time. It can also be used to develop interventions aimed at improving emotional regulation and expression. Overall, the Facial Action Coding System is an important tool for studying and understanding the complex and dynamic nature of human emotion. Its ability to provide standardized and objective measurements of facial expressions makes it a valuable tool in a wide range of fields, including psychology, anthropology, and neuroscience.

The economic benefits of tourism are undeniable. In 2019, tourism generated $9.2 trillion in global GDP and supported 330 million jobs worldwide. In the United States alone, tourism contributed $1.9 trillion to GDP and supported 15.8 million jobs. These numbers are only expected to grow in the coming years, as tourism continues to be a major driver of economic growth. There are many direct economic benefits of tourism. When tourists visit a destination, they spend money on transportation, lodging, food, and attractions. This spending creates jobs and stimulates the local economy. For example, a study by the World Travel & Tourism Council found that in 2019, tourism spending in the United States supported 15.8 million jobs, including 7.7 million direct jobs and 8.1 million indirect jobs. In addition to direct spending, tourism also generates indirect economic benefits. For example, when tourists visit a destination, they often purchase souvenirs and other goods to take home with them. This spending benefits local businesses and helps to create jobs. In addition, tourism can lead to increased investment in infrastructure and other public goods, which can benefit both residents and visitors alike. There are also some potential challenges associated with tourism. One challenge is that tourism can lead to overcrowding and environmental degradation. For example, in some popular tourist destinations, the influx of tourists can put a strain on local resources, such as water and energy. Additionally, tourism can lead to increased pollution and traffic congestion. Another challenge associated with tourism is that it can be seasonal. In many tourist destinations, the number of visitors varies significantly throughout the year. This can make it difficult for businesses that rely on tourism to plan and budget effectively. Overall, the economic benefits of tourism outweigh the challenges. However, it is important to manage tourism in a sustainable way in order to minimize the negative impacts. By doing so, we can ensure that tourism continues to be a major driver of economic growth and development.
