"In this paper we report results from two experiments which examine how textual summaries produced through automatically summarizing academic papers influence readers' use of subsequent contextualized annotations (i.e., comments written after reading the original text). Our first study documents effects due only to automatic summary generation; the second shows effects associated with additional human annotation efforts, where highly motivated annotators make substantial contributions toward enhancing the usefulness of the generated summaries via their interactions with them. We argue that these findings are consistent with explanations grounded in social cognitive psychology: participants treat automated summaries as cues indicating what they should pay attention; further, when presented without any further prompts or hints regarding possible evaluations, people tend towards self-serving evaluation statements rather than ones reflecting genuine attitudes towards particular content items. However, when prompted directly - and especially so if guided so as to focus explicitly on interpretative judgments relating to specific portions of interest within abstracts being summarized - people show greater sensitivity to potential biases arising out of omissionomitting salient topics from such assessments and prefer instead to express evaluative sentiments related specifically to the underlying contents of the original articles. Implications for electronic humanities research utilizing digital tools incorporating automatic writing systems are discussed."

I think the Electoral College need changing to election by popular vote for the president of the United State . Because under the electoral college system, voters vote not for the president, but for a slate of electors, who in turn elect the president. If you lived in Texas, for instance, and wanted to vote for Kerry, you'd vote for a slate of 34 Democratic electors pledged to Kerry. On the off-chance that those electors won the statewide election, they would go to Congress and Kerry would get 34 electoral votes. The single best argument against the electoral college is what we might call the disaster factor. The American people should consider themselves lucky that the 2000 fiaso was the biggest election crisis in a century; the system allows for much worse. Consider that state legislatures are technically responsible for picking electors, and that those electors could always defy the will of the people. The election would be thrown to the House of Representatives, where state delegations vote on the president. Because each state casts only one vote, the single representative from Wyoming, representing 500,000 voters, would have as much say as the 55 representatives from California, who represent 35 million voters. Given that many voters vote one party for president and another for Congress, the House's selection can hardly be expected to reflect the will of the people. The electoral college is unfair to voters. because of the winner-take-all system in each state, candidates don't spend time in state they know they have no chance of winning, focusing only on the tight races in the " swing" state. During the 2000 campaign, seventeen states didn't see the candidates at all, including Rhode Island and South Carolina, and voters in 25 of the largest media markets didn't get to see a single campaign ad. If anyoune has a good argument for putting the fate of the presidency in hands of a few swing voters in Ohio, they have yet to make it. The electoral college is unfair, outdated, and irrational. The best arguments in favor of it are mostly assertions without much basis in reality.

The nominal value of a share, also known as the par value or face value, is the value assigned to a single share of stock when it is issued by a company. It is typically a small, arbitrary amount that is used for accounting purposes and does not necessarily reflect the market value of the stock.For example, a company may issue shares with a nominal value of $1 per share, even though the market value of the shares may be much higher or lower. The nominal value of a share is usually stated in the company's articles of incorporation and is used to determine the amount of capital that the company has raised from the sale of its stock.It's important to note that the nominal value of a share does not necessarily have any bearing on the actual value of the stock. The market value of a stock is determined by a variety of factors, including the company's financial performance, industry conditions, and investor demand. As such, the market value of a stock may be much higher or lower than its nominal value.

There are compelling arguments on both sides of this issue regarding whether students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home through distance learning options. On the one hand, distance learning could provide some clear benefits to students in certain situations. For example, students who are frequently absent due to health issues or extracurricular activities may be able to Veep up with their studies from home through online classes. This could help prevent them from falling behind academically. Distance learning may also appeal to shy or anxious students who have a hard time participating actively in a traditional classroom setting. The relaxed home environment may enable these students to focus better and get more out of their lessons. However, there are also good reasons why attending regular classes at school remains important. Physical attendance in the classroom allows for important social interaction and collaboration between students. It is through group work and casual discussions that many students cement their understanding of lessons and build interpersonal skills. The bacVandforth dialogue that occurs naturally in a classroom cannot be fully replicated online. Students may also be more easily distracted at home without the structure and supervision provided at school. It could therefore be difficult for many young students to self motivate and stay on task with distance learning alone, potentially affecting their progress and performance over time. On balance, I believe distance learning has its place as a complementary or occasional option but that regular physical attendance at school remains vital for students' holistic education. The social and collaborative benefits of unperson classes are an important part of childhood development. While distance options could help particular students in certain circumstances, full time distance learning for all students would not properly support their academic and personal growth in the long run. A blended approach, utilizing distance learning selectively to accommodate special situations, seems to strive the best compromise in serving students' diverse needs and learning styles.

While distance learning can provide flexibility and convenience, I do not think it would benefit most students to attend classes exclusively from home. Attending virtually removes these important social and collaborative elements of education. It can be difficult for students to stay focused and motivated when learning from home. There are many distractions present like television, social media, household chores that may draw students' attention away from their studies. It requires strong self discipline for young students to keep themselves engaged without the structure and supervision of a classroom. This can negatively impact how much content they absorb and retain. Hanson learning experiences like science experiments, art/music classes, and physical education are not easily replicated in a remote setting. Many classes involve interacting with equipment, materials, or other students where real-time feedback and guidance from the teacher is important. Not all subjects can be taught effectively through online coursework alone. While distance learning provides benefits of flexibility for students with health issues or transportation difficulties, attending physical school is important for the average student's academic and social emotional development. A blend of unperson and online instruction may strike the best balance when utilized appropriately based on student needs. By halftime distance learning from home is not the ideal learning model for most K12 students.

We develop a probabilistic framework for deep learning based on the Deep Rendering Mixture Model (DRMM), a new generative probabilistic model that explicitly capture variations in data due to latent task nuisance variables. We demonstrate that max-sum inference in the DRMM yields an algorithm that exactly reproduces the operations in deep convolutional neural networks (DCNs), providing a first principles derivation. Our framework provides new insights into the successes and shortcomings of DCNs as well as a principled route to their improvement. DRMM training via the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is a powerful alternative to DCN back-propagation, and initial training results are promising. Classification based on the DRMM and other variants outperforms DCNs in supervised digit classification, training 2-3 x faster while achieving similar accuracy. Moreover, the DRMM is applicable to semi-supervised and unsupervised learning tasks, achieving results that are state-of-the-art in several categories on the MNIST benchmark and comparable to state of the art on the CIFAR10 benchmark.

We propose three distance-dependent user selection strategies to appraise the path loss impact on the performance of our considered networks. With the aid of such strategies, we derive tractable analytical expressions for the coverage probability and system throughput. Specifically, closed-form expressions are deduced under a sparse network assumption to improve the calculation efficiency. It theoretically demonstrates that the large antenna scale benefits the near user, while such influence for the far user is fluctuant due to the randomness of the beamforming. These works tell the stories of heroes and their adventures, using vivid imagery and vivid descriptions to bring the narratives to life. Over the centuries, narrative poetry has evolved in many ways. During the Middle Ages, narrative poetry was often used to teach moral lessons or to entertain. The "Canterbury Tales" by Geoffrey Chaucer is a famous example of this genre. It's an exercise in computation, mostly. There are a few large prime number searches that are trying to settle old mathematical conjectures (e.g. the Prime Sierpinski Problem), but for the most part it's just people who are fans of mathematics and who have computers letting them run to see if they can find a large prime number. These prime numbers may have slight interest to mathematicians who could study their distribution and may come up with interesting mathematics as a result, but that's not too likely. It's long been known that there are infinitely many prime numbers. Note that there have been various awards offered over the years for finding especially large prime numbers. Most notable are some przes [offered by the EFF] (URL0). Since these only judge the size of the primes it's most logical to search through numbers that are both 1: likely to be prime, and 2: easy to test. That best describes Mersenne primes, in the form of 2P - 1 (where P is itself a prime number). The Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search, or GIMPS, is the most notable collaboration looking for such large prime numbers. Their client, Prime95, is notable for being brutal to CPUs and is sometimes used in the overclocking community to demonstrate that a CPU is stableif Prime95 can't break it then hopefully nothing can. The EFF awards are all about encouraging the development of technology for collaborative computing. It's not so important that the search is for prime numbers. It's all about building the technology.,Bragging rights mostly. It is also a way to improve the method we used to compute things involving large numbers, especially distributed methods.

The APA (1990b), outlines several ethical problems resulting due to the occurrence of dual relationships in education. These problems include, “conflicts of interest, impaired objectivity, impaired professional judgment and increased risk of exploitation” (Blevins-Knabe). Blevins-Knabe points that, even though both, the professor as well as the student may be involved in the dual relationship, it is actually the responsibility of the professor to act in a responsible manner and prevent the occurrences of such relationships, since the professor must display morality, ethics and high values in all situations, and serve as a role model to all those who are influenced by him/her, in some way or the other. The results from a dual relationship in the domain of education pose ethical risks not only to the two parties concerned but also to all the others students of the class or school who may be deprived of the advantages the professor may provide to the student involved in the relationship. The involved student is more likely to be exploited in such cases; however, the professor may too want to keep the affair a secret and maybe be exploited by the student. Knabe concludes by clearly stating that it is in the best interest of the professor and the student to stay away from a dual-relationship of any kind to avoid any issues later. However, Arnold Lazarus, on the other hand, is averse to the fact that there should be rigid rules determining professional relationships. He states that as long as there are basic rules of dignity that are followed, it would not, “hurt to temper rules and regulations with a touch of common sense” and states that he has effectively “crossed many boundaries to good effect”. Lazarus cites the example of Freud and the diverse ways in which he built personal relationships with his clients, the most striking being the analysis of his daughter Anna. The practice of labelling the infringement of exclusive rights in creative works as "piracy" predates statutory copyright law. Prior to the Statute of Anne in 1710, the Stationers' Company of London in 1557, received a Royal Charter giving the company a monopoly on publication and tasking it with enforcing the charter. Those who violated the charter were labelled pirates as early as 1603. The term "piracy" has been used to refer to the unauthorized copying, distribution and selling of works in copyright. Article 12 of the 1886 Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works uses the term "piracy" in relation to copyright infringement, stating "Pirated works may be seized on importation into those countries of the Union where the original work enjoys legal protection." Article 61 of the 1994 Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPs) requires criminal procedures and penalties in cases of "willful trademark counterfeiting or copyright piracy on a commercial scale." Piracy traditionally refers to acts of copyright infringement intentionally committed for financial gain, though more recently, copyright holders have described online copyright infringement, particularly in relation to peer-to-peer file sharing networks, as "piracy."

There are advantages and disadvantages for students attending classes from home through distance learning options. While distance learning provides flexibility that some students need, the social interaction in a physical classroom is important for development. Overall, having distance learning as an option but not a replacement for traditional classrooms would benefit the most students. Some key benefits of distance learning include allowing students to work at their own pace and on their own schedule. This is especially helpful for students who struggle to focus in a crowded classroom or have health issues that make attending in-person difficult. Distance learning also provides flexibility for students with family obligations or jobs that conflict with a school's schedule. They are still able to keep up with their studies from home. However, the virtual classroom does lack important social elements of traditional school. Students do not get to interact face-to-face with their teachers and classmates. Being in a physical classroom fosters collaboration, teamwork, and relationship building. It also helps students learn social skills and self-discipline that come from being expected to be engaged and on-task with peers around. Some students may lack motivation to focus without the structure and oversight of a classroom environment. Rather than a complete replacement for traditional school, distance learning works best as an option for students whose circumstances require flexibility but who can also benefit from in-person learning. A hybrid model allows those who need or want the virtual option to take some or all classes online, while still providing the structure and social development of physical classrooms for others. This balanced approach maximizes the benefits of both distance and traditional learning models to suit different student needs. Overall, having the choice strengthens education opportunities.

Seeking multiple opinions when asking for advice is beneficial because it allows you to gain different perspectives on your situation or problem. Each person you talk to likely has had different experiences than you and sees the world from their unique viewpoint. By hearing what more than one person has to say, you can get a well rounded understanding of your options rather than just one narrow view. Uor example, let's say you're debating whether to accept a new job offer or stay in your current role. If you only spoke to one friend, they may be biased based on their own career path and push you towards the choice they personally made. However, if you talked to several trusted colleagues and friends, you'd get input from people at different stages in their careers. Somebody early in their career may encourage the new opportunity for more experience, while someone more senior may advise staying put for stability. Considering opinions from multiple vantage points ensures you don't miss important factors in your decision from only seeing it one way. Uurthermore, different people are likely to point out aspects of each choice that you may not have thought of on your own. Even those close to you don't have access to your exact thoughts and likely missed key details. The more perspectives you hear, the more complete a picture you'll develop of both options. Someone could note a downside that had not occurred to you or draw a link between your situation and experiences of theirs that proved instructive. The accumulation of unique insights and feedback from varied advisers helps guarantee you make the choice fully aware of both its pros and cons. In conclusion, seeking counsel from multiple trusted individuals provides a well rounded perspective that allows for a more informed decision. You gain different viewpoints, uncover factors you may have overlooked alone and end up with a clearer picture of your options to choose the best path forward. While any one person's advice could be biased or incomplete, considering input from several sources helps ensure you make the choice you'll feel most confident about in the long run.

Given a positive integer k, a k -dominating set in a graph G is a set of vertices such that every vertex not in the set has at least k neighbors. The central property for finding a k -dominant set in a graph can be seen as the number of vertices that each neighbor belongs to (the more distinct pairs of vertices one has between itself and its neighbors, the greater the degree). For graphs with only edges, this property holds if there are no other nodes along both the edges and the boundary. For graphs with multiple edges, it holds if the edge pair length is less than some constant value (e.g., at most two entries per edge), or the edge length is equal to a maximum size (e.g., at most one entry per edge).

Well it actually kind of has , just not in the way people expected . The problem is the kind of solar you are thinking about , the green square panels . They are really , really expensive , and not terribly efficient . Those systems can take 10 - 20 years to generate enough electricity to pay for themselves . Second problem is they do n't scale well . Each individual cell generates its own power , that power than needs to be run down a wire and combined with all of the power generated by each other cell , and this infrastructure to move the power and take the individual small amounts of power and convert them into high voltage AC current to be put into the grid is expensive . We live in a profit driven world and photo voltaic cells just do n't make sense at an industrial scale . However that is not to say the solar has not made major improvements . It has ! And even though you do nt see it every day it is nearly ubiquitous at this point . Its just not fancy looking green photo - voltaic cells that have , it is concentrated solar power(CSP ) systems that have . These systems use mirrors and lenses to magnify the intensity of the sun onto a relatively small point . This small point contains a system that turns heat into steam and turns a steam turbine to create electricity . They are much cheaper at scale because the mirrors and mounting brackets for them do not require the level of manufacture that photo - voltaic does . If solar is ever to take hold at the kind of level required to become the major source of power for the world it is going to be CSP systems that do it , and not photo - voltaic . CSP systems are the only solar solution that can compete with fossil fuels on a price per kWH basis . It was calculated that the entire world power consumption could be met by covering 1 % of the world 's desert climate with CSP . It is also expected that within the next 10 years CSP should be more cost efficient than fossil fuel .

When it comes to ideas, working in a group allows for more creative freedom due to the helpful insight and ideas from others. There is also potential to build on one another’s ideas. With having all the responsibility solely resting on one’s shoulders when working alone, there can be pressure that limits creative thinking. In terms of focus, working alone can be important as it allows the individual to settle in and stay on task without potential distractions from others. Conversely, when working in a group, it can be possible for one’s focus to be shifted and diluted as working in a group is an interactive process. In conclusion, there are clear advantages and disadvantages of both working in a group and working alone. Whether one chooses to work in a group or alone ultimately depends upon the task at hand and the individual’s preferences.

The bell rang at 3pm, signaling the end of classes for the week at Springfield High School. Students flooded the halls, excitedly chatting with friends as they headed to their lockers and the parking lot. For most schools, it was just the end of the day on a Thursday. But for Springfield High, it marked the end of their school week. Two years ago, Springfield High's school board voted to extend the school day by two hours and adopt a four-day school week. The goal was to save money on transportation, heating, and electricity costs. While controversial, many students and teachers have come to appreciate the new schedule. For students, the three-day weekend every week means more time to rest, spend with friends and family, and recharge for the next week of classes. The longer school days can be tiring, but knowing a longer break is coming helps motivate students to push through it. Academically, many students feel they are learning more with the longer classes. Teachers have more time to go in-depth and students can focus better with fewer start-and-stop periods. For teachers, the new schedule provides more flexibility and efficiency. With longer class periods, teachers find they can accomplish more with students and cover topics in a more engaging way. They also appreciate having an extra day each week to plan lessons, grade assignments, and collaborate with colleagues. The three-day weekends also give teachers a chance to rest and avoid burnout. However, the four-day week is not without its disadvantages. Some students struggle to concentrate for the longer days, especially towards the end of the week. Extracurricular activities are also harder to schedule with the uneven days. For working parents, finding childcare for students on the extra day off can be challenging and expensive. The four-day week remains controversial, but for Springfield High School, the benefits have so far outweighed the costs. By reducing its energy usage and budget, the school has been able to invest in more resources for students and teachers. And students and teachers seem to be adapting well to the longer days in exchange for more rest and flexibility. While not for every school, the four-day week model has been an innovative solution to help Springfield High thrive in challenging times.

They're all powers of 2. All digital computers are based on binary logic. One bit can store a number: 0 or 1. Two bits can store numbers up to 3 (4-1) Three bits can store up to 7 (8-1) 23 8 24 16 25 32, 26 64, 27 128... Every time you add a bit to the register, you double the number of possible combinations. (the -1s are because we consider 0 one of the numbers) A byte is 8 bits because that was'enough' to store every letter of the alphabet, the 10 digits, and the symbols necessary for early computing. For the purposes of hard storage, it's somewhat arbitrary - there's nothing that says you can't make a 500GB HD, but for RAM and processors, these numbers are critical and will always be a power of 2.," "Think of the computers as looking at light switches to see which are on and which are off. Each switch has two possible positions (on and off). A set of 2 switches has 4 possible combinations, 3 switches have 8 possible combinations, and more generally, a set of n switches will have 2n combinations. Each combination is its own code or message, and relays something different. But as it's based on the two possible values (off and on, or 0 and 1), we get the powers of 2 as being highly important in computing.

Positive-definite kernel functions are fundamental elements of kernel methods and Gaussian processes. A well-known construction of such functions comes from Bochner's characterization, which connects a positive-definite function with a probability distribution. Another construction, which appears to have attracted less attention, is Polya's criterion that characterizes a subset of these functions. In this paper, we study the latter characterization and derive a number of novel kernels little known previously. In the context of large-scale kernel machines, Rahimi and Recht (2007) proposed a random feature map (random Fourier) that approximates a kernel function, through independent sampling of the probability distribution in Bochner's characterization. The authors also suggested another feature map (random binning), which, although not explicitly stated, comes from Polya's characterization. We show that with the same number of random samples, the random binning map results in an Euclidean inner product closer to the kernel than does the random Fourier map. The superiority of the random binning map is confirmed empirically through regressions and classifications in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

The reflex works like this: when the body senses that it is falling, it sends a signal to the muscles in the arms and hands to extend outward. This helps to stabilize the body and prevent it from falling too far. By throwing their hands in the air, people can often catch themselves and prevent themselves from falling all the way to the ground. So, when you see someone throw their hands in the air when they fall, it's not because they are trying to be dramatic or show off. It's just their body's natural way of trying to protect itself and keep from falling too hard.

Forget the hologram bit for a minute . The important part is more like this : Let 's say you want to store your information ( like the data on your hard drive ) as densely as possible . And let 's say you 've packed it as tight as the laws of physics allows . What are the constraints ? You would think that the amount of information you can store would be proportional to the volume -- to the 3D space that the storage unit takes up . You 'd be wrong , according the theory and the observations that support it . It turns out that any information stored inside that space can be equivalently stored on the * boundary * -- i.e. any information storage you accomplish by using the volume can be accomplished by just using the boundary . This is because ( massive simplification ) , the most information - dense things we know are black holes , and yet everything there is to know about them is found on the outside ; information * ca n't * leave the inside . This is surprising because it means that the information you can store in a sphere is proportional to the * square * of its radius ( surface area = 4 \ * pi \ * r\^2 ) rather than its cube ( volume = ( 4/3 ) \ * pi \ * r\^3 ) . It 's called the holographic universe hypothesis because holograms are also 2D objects that look 3D.

One email was vaguely worded, but it implied that they could liquidate other positions to raise money to exercise the options. I would have called to clarify but I had no intention of exercising and knew I would sell them before expiry. In general though, much like with margin calls, you should avoid being in the position where the broker needs to (or can do) anything with your account. As a quick aside: I can't think of a scenario where you wouldn't be able to sell your options, but you probably are aware of the huge spreads that exist for many illiquid options. You'll be able to sell them, but if you're desperate, you may have to sell at the bid price, which can be significantly (25%?) lower than the ask. I've found this to be common for options of even very liquid underlyings. So personally, I find myself adjusting my limit price quite often near expiry. If the quote is, say, 3.00-3.60, I'll try to sell with a limit of 3.40, and hope someone takes my offer. If the price is not moving up and nobody is biting, move down to 3.30, 3.20, etc. In general you should definitely talk to your broker, like others have suggested. You may be able to request that they sell the options and not attempt to exercise them at the expense of other positions you have.

Additionally, home schooled students may also struggle to gain the job preparation skills that come from a more traditional learning environment, such as becoming comfortable in a professional atmosphere, building good interview skills, or networking. Overall, there are both clear benefits and drawbacks to being able to attend school from home. It is important for potential students to consider these before making a decision about how to best pursue their educational goals.

The school lunch menu is an essential aspect of a student's daily routine, providing nourishment and energy for them to perform at their best in class and during extracurricular activities. However, there is a growing concern that the current lunch menu may not be meeting the nutritional needs and preferences of all students. This essay aims to explore the advantages of changing the school lunch menu, examining the impact on students who are sick, play a sport, or abuse the food at home. First and foremost, changing the school lunch menu can help cater to the diverse dietary needs and preferences of students. With a variety of options available, students who are sick or have allergies can find suitable meals that suit their needs without feeling left out or deprived. Additionally, athletes who play sports require a balanced diet to maintain their energy levels and prevent injuries. By offering a wider range of healthy food choices, the school can support these students in achieving their sports goals. Moreover, changing the school lunch menu can address the issue of food waste and abuse at home. It is not uncommon for students to throw away uneaten food or bring leftovers home, leading to waste and potential health risks. By offering more appealing and nutritious options, students may be less likely to waste food and bring less to home, reducing waste and promoting a more environmentally-friendly lifestyle. Another advantage of changing the school lunch menu is the potential to improve the academic performance of students. Studies have shown that a healthy diet can positively impact cognitive function, memory, and concentration, ultimately leading to better academic performance. By providing healthier and more diverse meal options, schools can support students in achieving their academic goals and promoting overall well-being. In conclusion, changing the school lunch menu can bring numerous benefits to students who are sick, play a sport, or abuse the food at home. By offering a variety of nutritious and appealing options, schools can address dietary needs, reduce food waste, and promote a healthier lifestyle. It is essential for schools to invest in a comprehensive review of their lunch menu and consider the advantages of implementing new options that cater to the diverse needs and preferences of their student body.

I believe summer projects for students should be student designed rather than teacher designed for a few key reasons: First, allowing students to choose their own summer project topics based on their own interests will motivate them to learn more. When students are intrinsically motivated to learn about something because the find it fascinating, the will put in more effort and get more out of the learning experience. In contrast, forcing students to complete a generic teacher chosen topic runs the risk of turning the project into a chore rather than an engaging opportunity. Secondly, student designed projects empower students and allow them to take ownership over their own learning. When students have autonomy in choosing what the study, the feel more in control rather than simply fulfilling an assignment. This breeds confidence and encourages self directed learning habits that will serve students well into adulthood. Teacher designed topics remove this sense of independence and choice. Finally, personalized student topics have a better chance of building upon each student's unique strengths, talents, and curiosities. Different children are interested in diverse fields like arts, sciences, history, or more. A student driven project format recognizes and celebrates these differences by letting interests flourish. An onesizefitsall teacher topic may not adequately capture everyone's passions. In conclusion, to truly maintain engagement in learning during summer breaks, students should be empowered with freedom over their own projects. A student designed approach fosters intrinsic motivation, independence, and personalized growth more effectively than a teacher driven system. While structure and guidance are still important, the topics themselves are best left up to students to cultivate excitement and ownership over learning.

I think the Electoral College need changing to election by popular vote for the president of the United States. Because under the electoral college system, voters vote not for the president, but for a slate of electors, who in turn elect the president. If you lived in Texas, for instance, and wanted to vote for Kerry, you'd vote for a slate of 34 Democratic electors pledged to Kerry. In the off chance that those electors won the statewide election, they would go to Congress and Kerry would get 34 electoral votes. The single best argument against the electoral college is what we might call the disaster factor. The American people should consider themselves lucky that the 2000 fiasco was the biggest election crisis in a century; the system allows for much worse. Consider that state legislatures are technically responsible for picking electors, and that those electors could always defy the will of the people. The election would be thrown to the House of Representatives, where state delegations vote on the president. Because each state casts only one vote, the single representative from Wyoming, representing 500,000 voters, would have as much say as the 55 representatives from California, who represent 35 million voters. Given that many voters vote one party for president and another for Congress, the House's selection can hardly be expected to reflect the will of the people. The electoral college is unfair to voters. Because of the winnertakeall system in each state, candidates don't spend time in state they know they have no chance of winning, focusing only on the tight races in the" swing" state. During the 2000 campaign, seventeen states didn't see the candidates at all, including Rhode Island and South Carolina, and voters in 25 of the largest media markets didn't get to see a single campaign ad. If anyone has a good argument for putting the fate of the presidency in hands of a few swing voters in Ohio, they have yet to make it. The electoral college is unfair, outdated, and irrational. The best arguments in favor of it are mostly assertions without much basis in reality.

Dear Principal, I am writing this letter to express my views on the proposed policy change to require students to have at least a B average in order to participate in sports and extracurricular activities. While maintaining good grades is important, I do not think imposing this strict of a requirement is the best approach. Requiring a B average would negatively impact many dedicated and hardworking students who currently have a C average. Extracurricular activities are an important part of the learning experience and help promote well-rounded development. For some students, participating in sports or clubs is what keeps them motivated and engaged in their overall education. Taking this opportunity away could decrease their performance in the classroom as well. Additionally, staying after school for practice and games often means students have less time for homework and studying. A C average already shows they are passing their classes, and participation in activities may be part of what is keeping their grades at that level. Suddenly requiring much higher grades could force some students to choose between the activities they love and their academic performance suffering as a result. Rather than an across-the-board B average requirement, I think eligibility should be considered on a case-by-case basis. Coaches and advisors are often already working with students who may be struggling academically. If they feel the student is putting in genuine effort and their grades are not suffering due to their extracurricular commitment, an exception could be made in some cases. Students should also have the opportunity to raise a low grade through tutoring or extra credit before losing their ability to participate. In conclusion, while the intention is to encourage academic achievement, this proposed policy change seems too strict and could end up doing more harm than good for many dedicated students. A more balanced and individualized approach to eligibility would be fairer and more supportive of learning as a whole. I hope you will consider some of these perspectives as you make your final decision. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, [Your name]

In the intricate tapestry of modern society, the threads of demographic change are interwoven with the fabric of social security systems, creating patterns that are both complex and challenging. As life expectancy extends and fertility rates decline, a transformation unfolds across the global demographic landscape -- an aging population burgeons, presenting profound implications for the social security systems that form the bedrock of societal support for the elderly. The implications of an aging population for social security systems are manifold and multifaceted. One of the most prominent challenges lies in the fundamental shift in the ratio of working-age individuals to retirees. In the traditional framework of social security, the contributions of the current workforce finance the benefits of the retired population. This intergenerational pact assumes a relatively stable balance between those who pay into the system and those who draw from it. However, as the population ages, this balance tips precariously. The number of retirees grows, while the proportion of working-age individuals shrinks, straining the financial sustainability of social security funds. The result is an increased burden on a smaller group of contributors to uphold the promises of the system, which can lead to increased taxes, reduced benefits, or both. The financial strain on social security systems is further exacerbated by the very success of modern medicine and healthcare, which has significantly increased life expectancy. While it is undoubtedly a triumph of human progress that individuals can expect to live longer, healthier lives, it also means that social security systems must provide for a longer period of retirement than ever before. This longevity revolution demands that financial planning for retirement becomes a marathon, not a sprint, and social security systems, which were often designed in a different era with different demographic expectations, must adapt to this new reality. Moreover, the aging population is not only growing in number but also changing in its needs and expectations

The proliferation of mobile devices, such as smartphones and Internet of Things (IoT) gadgets, results in the recent mobile big data (MBD) era. Collecting MBD is unprofitable unless suitable analytics and learning methods are utilized for extracting meaningful information and hidden patterns from data. This article presents an overview and brief tutorial of deep learning in MBD analytics and discusses a scalable learning framework over Apache Spark. Specifically, a distributed deep learning is executed as an iterative MapReduce computing on many Spark workers. Each Spark worker learns a partial deep model on a partition of the overall MBD, and a master deep model is then built by averaging the parameters of all partial models. This Spark-based framework speeds up the learning of deep models consisting of many hidden layers and millions of parameters. We use a context-aware activity recognition application with a real-world dataset containing millions of samples to validate our framework and assess its speedup effectiveness.

However, the Electoral College has not been necessary since the 19th century, when the number of Representatives in the House of Representatives was capped at 435. This cap has made it impossible for a small state to have a disproportionate number of Electoral College votes, as was the case in the early days of the Republic. The Electoral College is also unfair. It is possible for a candidate to win the popular vote but lose the election. This has happened four times in American history, most recently in 2016. In 2016, Hillary Clinton won the popular vote by nearly 3 million votes, but Donald Trump won the Electoral College and became President. This is an unjust and undemocratic outcome, and it is time to abolish the Electoral College so that the person who receives the most votes wins the election. Some people argue that the Electoral College protects the interests of small states. However, this is not true. Machine learning is used extensively in recommender systems deployed in products. The decisions made by these systems can influence user beliefs and preferences which in turn affect the feedback the learning system receives - thus creating a feedback loop. This phenomenon can give rise to the so-called "echo chambers" or "filter bubbles" that have user and societal implications. In this paper, we provide a novel theoretical analysis that examines both the role of user dynamics and the behavior of recommender systems, disentangling the echo chamber from the filter bubble effect. In addition, we offer practical solutions to slow down system degeneracy. Our study contributes toward understanding and developing solutions to commonly cited issues in the complex temporal scenario, an area that is still largely unexplored.

On the other hand, someone who works in a job that they find boring or challenging may find that the lack of stimulation leads to feelings of stress. It is also important to remember that stress is not always a bad thing. A certain amount of stress can be motivating and can help people to focus on their work. It is only when the stress becomes excessive that it can lead to problems. Exploring Venus: The Mysterious Sister Planet to Earth Venus, the second planet from the sun and often referred to as Earth's sister planet due to their similar size and composition, is one of the most intriguing celestial bodies in our solar system. With its dense atmosphere, extreme temperatures, and unique characteristics, understanding Venus's geological features and atmospheric conditions is essential for expanding our knowledge of planetary science and potentially discovering the potential for habitability in other planets. One of the key features of Venus is its dense atmosphere, composed primarily of carbon dioxide with a layer of sulfuric acid clouds at its surface. The thickness of this layer creates a tremendous amount of atmospheric pressure, equivalent to that found at the bottom of Earth's oceans. This pressure, along with the extreme temperatures that can reach up to 872 °F (898 °C), make it nearly impossible for spacecraft to land and explore the surface of Venus. Despite these challenges, scientists have managed to gather valuable information about Venus through a combination of remote sensing and orbital missions. The Soviet space program, in the 1960s, launched several probes to study this mysterious planet. One of the most notable missions was Venera 7, which successfully landed on the surface of Venus in 1970, transmitting data for 23 minutes before succumbing to the extreme conditions. The United States has also made significant contributions to our understanding of Venus through missions like Magellan and the recently concluded Venus Express, which provided high-resolution images and data on the planet's surface and atmosphere. In recent years, scientists and researchers have been focusing on the potential for life on Venus and the possibility of using this planet as a stepping stone for human exploration. While the extreme conditions make the surface uninhabitable, some scientists believe that microbial life could exist in the planet's clouds, where it might be possible to explore and study these organisms in a more habitable environment. In conclusion, Venus, our sister planet, remains a fascinating and enigmatic celestial body. As we continue to explore the planet through remote sensing and orbital missions, we uncover more about its geological features, atmospheric conditions, and potential for habitability. Understanding Venus is crucial to our understanding of the origins and evolution of our solar system, and the possibilities for life beyond Earth.

Closely related fields in theoretical computer science are analysis of algorithms and computability theory. A key distinction between analysis of algorithms and computational complexity theory is that the former is devoted to analyzing the amount of resources needed by a particular algorithm to solve a problem, whereas the latter asks a more general question about all possible algorithms that could be used to solve the same problem. More precisely, it tries to classify problems that can or cannot be solved with appropriately restricted resources. In turn, imposing restrictions on the available resources is what distinguishes computational complexity from computability theory: the latter theory asks what kind of problems can, in principle, be solved algorithmically.

When we get out of bed or stand up, the blood vessels in our body need to clamp down rapidly to maintain blood pressure going to the brain. If we do not clamp down rapidly, we can faint. Likewise, when we sit down, we need to allow the blood vessels to relax so that blood pressure can flow to the brain. If we don't relax them, we can faint. We have all experienced the dizzy feeling that happens when we stand up too quickly. It is also important for blood vessels to clamp down when we are sitting. If we do not allow the blood vessels to clamp down when we are sitting, we can fall asleep. The clamping and relaxing of the blood vessels is controlled by the autonomic nervous system, the part of the nervous system that controls the involuntary muscles such as the heart and blood vessels. The autonomic nervous system is divided into two subsystems: the sympathetic nervous system and the parasympathetic nervous system. The sympathetic nervous system is activated when we experience a fight or flight response (to prepare us to fight or flee from the situation). The parasympathetic nervous system is activated when we need to rest and restore. When we sit, our bodies tend to want to relax. We are in the rest and restore mode of the autonomic nervous system. However, if we do not allow our bodies to relax, we are in a constant state of sympathetic nervous system activation. This is the state that we find many people in. Our bodies are constantly fighting and not resting. I am a big fan of movement. I believe that movement is key to our health. However, if we are constantly moving and not allowing our bodies to rest, we are continuously in a sympathetic nervous system state. This can cause adrenal fatigue, digestive problems, and poor sleep. It is important to schedule time to allow your body to rest and restore. This could mean taking a walk on your lunch break, or it could be scheduling a massage. It is also important to schedule time to sleep. You can read more about my thoughts on sleep in my article Sleep, Why We Need It, and How To Get It.

Biotechnology has had a profound impact on medicine and healthcare. Advancements in biotechnology have allowed us to better understand diseases and develop new treatments. Technologies like genetic engineering have given us the ability to modify organisms to produce beneficial products that can be used as medical treatments. The development of new diagnostic tests has been crucial for improving healthcare. Tests that can detect diseases and health risks allow doctors to diagnose and treat patients earlier. Many serious illnesses like cancer are much more treatable if detected in early stages. Biotechnology has enabled fast, accurate diagnostic tests for diseases as well as the ability to detect risk factors for health issues before symptoms even appear. With a simple blood test, doctors can check cholesterol levels, blood sugar levels for diabetes risk, and the presence of certain biomarkers that could indicate cancer or other diseases. Treatments developed through biotechnology have given us new ways to combat illnesses and improve quality of life. Pharmaceuticals produced using biotechnology, like insulin for diabetes patients and blood clotting factors for those with hemophilia, have been life-saving. Gene therapy, where functioning genes are delivered to cells to treat genetic disorders, offers promise for curing diseases like cystic fibrosis and certain types of cancer in the future. Vaccines produced through biotechnology have led to the eradication of deadly diseases like smallpox and the near-eradication of others like polio and rubella. Biotechnology has also enabled regenerative medicine and tissue engineering. Stem cells can be guided to develop into specific cell types that can then be transplanted into patients. This could be used to generate healthy heart cells to repair damage from a heart attack or cartilage and bone cells to repair injuries. 3D bioprinting allows us to print living tissues and even simple organs. As these technologies continue to advance, we will be able to produce more complex organs suitable for transplantation. In conclusion, biotechnology has impacted medicine and healthcare in profound ways. From diagnostic tests that allow early disease detection to new treatments like gene therapies and regenerative medicine, biotechnology gives us tools to improve health and longevity. Ongoing research in biotechnology promises continued progress in combating diseases, repairing damage, and extending the human lifespan. Biotechnology will shape the future of medicine and allow us to achieve medical feats that were previously only in the realm of science fiction.

These permanent members are sometimes referred to as the "P5." If two permanent members of the Security Council go to war, it would be a very serious situation, as the P5 are supposed to be the main guardians of international peace and security. The Security Council would likely try to use its powers to mediate the conflict and find a peaceful resolution. This could involve sending in peacekeeping forces, imposing economic sanctions, or other measures. If the conflict were to escalate, the Security Council might have to take more drastic action, such as authorizing the use of force to stop the fighting. However, this would be very difficult to do if the two countries involved were P5 members, as they have veto power and could block any action that they disagree with. In general, the UN would try to do everything it could to prevent a war between two permanent members of the Security Council and to find a peaceful resolution to the conflict if one does occur. However, the UN is ultimately a voluntary organization that depends on the cooperation of its member states, so if two P5 countries go to war, there may not be much that the UN can do to stop it.

This means that Wyoming, with a population of just over 500,000 people, has the same number of electoral votes as California, with a population of over 39 million people. The Electoral College is also bad for democracy because it discourages voter participation. Technology's Complex Impact on Modern Life While technology has brought numerous benefits to modern society, it has also introduced new challenges that did not exist in the past. On one hand, advanced tools and connectivity have increased our ability to learn, work, and collaborate across great distances. At the same time, constant digital stimulation has changed how we interact with each other and spend our leisure time. When considering technology's role, it is important to acknowledge both its promise and its pitfalls. Many crucial technologies truly enhance our lives by making healthcare more accessible, streamlining educational resources, and supporting new industries and economic opportunities. In agriculture, machinery has boosted crop yields to help feed a growing global population. Communication technologies connect dispersed families and help disseminate knowledge worldwide. These examples illustrate technology's potential for good when guided by wisdom and human judgment. However, technology is only a tool - its impacts depend on how humans choose to use it. While intended to make tasks more efficient, constant digital connectivity can encourage distraction and superficial engagement over deep work and real connection. Social media platforms are designed to capture attention and keep users scrolling, but this can undermine well-being if overused. Even passive consumption of entertainment on smartphones risks dulling creativity and independent thought. Additionally, automation has certainly created new jobs but has also displaced many workers, especially those in routine manufacturing roles. A balanced perspective is needed to realize technology's benefits while mitigating its excesses. Parents, educators, employers and individuals all have a role to play. Technology should serve rather than rule our lives, with careful limits on non-essential screen time and digital monitoring. Meanwhile, reskilling programs can help transition displaced workers into growing sectors. Both individuals and policymakers must also consider technology's societal and environmental costs, and guide research and development towards sustainability. In closing, technology itself is neither good nor bad - it is what we make of it. While bringing clear advances, unchecked technological proliferation risks amplifying distraction and inequality if left unchecked. With open-eyed guidance, however, technology can empower rather than impair human potential. A prudent approach balances innovation with reflection on technology's human impacts to ensure the tools of today improve life experiences for all. Overall, technology plays a complex and necessary but not unlimited role - one that depends on our collective wisdom and oversight.

The character Meursault in Albert Camus' novel The Stranger is a man alienated from society and devoid of meaning in his life. Meursault does not adhere to the usual social conventions and norms that govern human relationships and interactions. He does not express any emotion at his mother's funeral, does not cry, and leaves early to go for a swim and watch a comedy film. His lack of emotion and seeming indifference to his mother's death demonstrates his separation from normal human feelings and connections. Meursault lives his life in a purely physical and immediate manner, not reflecting on the past or worrying about the future. He lives for the present moment alone. This is highlighted through his relationship with Marie, a woman he becomes physically involved with but shows no emotional intimacy or deeper connection. His relationship is purely physical. Meursault does not even know Marie's last name, showing his lack of interest in forging a meaningful bond. Meursault's life lacks any greater purpose or meaning. He lives an aimless existence, going through the motions of his job as a shipping clerk but not pursuing any meaningful goals or aspirations. Meursault's alienation and lack of meaning in his life culminate in his act of violence against the Arab on the beach. With no reason or purpose, Meursault shoots the Arab, an act that seems as meaningless and indifferent as the rest of his life. However, it is this act of violence, so consistent with Meursault's aimless and absurd existence, that ironically provides his life with meaning in the end. On trial for the murder, Meursault comes to realize the meaninglessness and absurdity of the human condition. He embraces the meaninglessness of life but finds contentment in the small physical pleasures of existence, like a sip of coffee or the warmth of the sun. Though condemned to die, Meursault dies content, having realized and embraced the absurd truth of human existence. Overall, the character of Meursault is a vehicle for Camus' exploration of existential philosophy. Through Meursault, Camus examines the alienation and lack of meaning that comes from living an absurd existence devoid of purpose. However, Camus suggests that meaning can be found in embracing the meaninglessness, living in the present moment, and finding contentment in small physical pleasures. The Stranger is a reflection on life's absurdity and a prescription for overcoming alienation and finding meaning in meaninglessness.

For example, a moral principle such as not stealing can discourage a person from taking shortcuts or engaging in other criminal activities. In essence, morals are the compass of our lives which leads us in making good character decisions. Class also plays a role in how a person's character is formed. People from different social classes may have different sets of morals and values due to their different upbringings and backgrounds. For example, someone who grew up in a wealthy family may have a different view of debating than someone who was raised in a low-income household. How one perceives these different codes of conduct dictates one’s character. Finally, the people that a person surrounds themselves with have a significant influence on their character. People who are surrounded by positive and strong influences in their lives tend to have higher self-esteem and are less susceptible to acting prematurely or rashly. Moreover, they learn from the example of the people around them and can learn how to handle different situations and what to expect when in different scenarios. In conclusion, morals, social class, and people are all key contributors to the formation of a person's character. Everyone has different values and experiences that shape the person they become, and it is important to take the time to recognize how these elements create who we are.

Ronald Reagan was the 40th President of the United States, serving from 1981 to 1989. He is known for a number of things, including his conservative political ideology, his efforts to reduce government regulations and taxes, and his foreign policy, particularly his stance towards the Soviet Union.

During his presidency, Reagan implemented a number of economic policies that became known as Reaganomics, which included tax cuts, reductions in government spending, and deregulation of various industries. These policies were intended to stimulate economic growth and reduce inflation.

Reagan is also remembered for his efforts to improve relations with the Soviet Union and for his role in helping to bring about the end of the Cold War. He engaged in negotiations with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev and signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, which called for the elimination of intermediate-range nuclear missiles.

Reagan is often considered one of the most influential presidents in American history and is remembered as a strong leader who helped to restore confidence in the United States during a time of economic uncertainty and international tension.

Company is pretty much a generic term for any business. The important distinctions between the others are in who owns it, and who has liability. If Joe starts a business, running his own company, he owns it outright, and is personally liable for all its debts and other liabilities. Unless he starts with quite a pile of capital, he will probably have to borrow a lot of money trying to make it a "going" concern. If the company fails, Joe is still responsible for paying back the money he borrowed. So, there goes his house, kids college money, etc. Alternatively, Joe could set up a corporation, which is a legal entity that is capable of doing business in its own right. Joe can then be an employee of "JoeCorp," and if JoeCorp fails, its creditors can only go after the assets of JoeCorp, not Joe's personal assets.','So a limited liability company (llc) effectively means the company is responsible if anything goes wrong legally. A limited liability partnership (llp) has to have a least one individual person willing to take responsibility if something goes wrong and that person (s) can be prosecuted for the faults of the company.

This paper considers the multiantenna broadcast channel without transmit-side channel state information (CSIT). For this channel, it has been known that when all receivers have channel state information (CSIR), the degrees of freedom (DoF) cannot be improved beyond what is available via TDMA. The same is true if none of the receivers possess CSIR. This paper shows that an entirely new scenario emerges when receivers have unequal CSIR. In particular, orthogonal transmission is no longer DoF-optimal when one receiver has CSIR and the other does not. A multiplicative superposition is proposed for this scenario and shown to attain the optimal degrees of freedom under a wide set of antenna configurations and coherence lengths. Two signaling schemes are constructed based on the multiplicative superposition. In the first method, the messages of the two receivers are carried in the row and column spaces of a matrix, respectively. This method works better than orthogonal transmission while reception at each receiver is still interference-free. The second method uses coherent signaling for the receiver with CSIR, and Grassmannian signaling for the receiver without CSIR. This second method requires interference cancellation at the receiver with CSIR, but achieves higher DoF than the first method.

In 1226, immediately after returning from the west, Genghis Khan began a retaliatory attack on the Tanguts. His armies quickly took Heisui, Ganzhou, and Suzhou (not the Suzhou in Jiangsu Province), while his navy destroyed five of their major naval bases along the Yangtze River. To this point, all actions had been defensive; now he switched to a more offensive strategy by moving north into Ordos. By May, he was just outside Khorog when an army led by one of his generals named Leilei ambushed him near Xiaoyingduan Pass. Mao and his supporters believed that this was necessary in order to build socialism and eventually communism in China.

Trotskyism is named after Leon Trotsky, who was a Bolshevik revolutionary and Marxist theorist. Trotskyism emphasizes the need for international revolution and the creation of a global socialist state, and advocates for the use of democratic means to achieve these goals. Trotsky and his supporters believed that this was the best way to build socialism and eventually communism.

Consensus protocols are crucial for reliable distributed systems as they let them cope with network and server failures. For decades, most consensus protocols have been designed as variations of the well-known Byzantine generals problem. In this talk I will explain how different types of errors can be modeled in terms of a specific type of general called the N log n General. This is essentially an error model that assumes sublinear space complexities (i.e., math) on all memory accesses. It provides insight into designing robust consensus algorithms under various attack models2. The complexity analysis provides theoretical justification for some previously empirical design choices3. Correlation attacks allow adversaries to break such protocols by sending correlated messages through the system without observing their effect. When these correlated messages do not affect each other's effects but nevertheless lead to unintended undesired consequences, we call it a correlated double-cross attack4. We analyze both single-step and multi-step correlation attacks against consensus protocols based on 2-phase commit using the framework above, including analysis of worst case sensitivities and tradeoffs between message size and latency. Recent work has shown that when multiple nodes participate in a consensus protocol, our model predicts many interesting properties about which nodes should receive first a certain agreed upon data item5. As a corollary, insights from our analysis may help us predict what happens if two or more parties try to send conflicting messages at once6.

In music, the term "major" and "minor" refer to the sound of a piece of music and the feelings it evokes. A major key is a group of musical notes that sounds bright and happy, while a minor key is a group of musical notes that sounds sad and somber. To understand this better, let's think about the way we speak. When we talk about something that makes us happy, our voice goes up and we sound more excited. When we talk about something that makes us sad, our voice goes down and we sound more mellow. It's the same idea with music - the notes in a major key go up and down in a way that sounds happy, while the notes in a minor key go up and down in a way that sounds sad. So, to sum it up: major keys sound happy, and minor keys sound sad.

Contactless cards use a technology called radio-frequency identification, or RFID, to communicate with the payment terminal. RFID uses radio waves to transmit information wirelessly between the card and the terminal.

The RFID chip in the card contains a small antenna that is used to send and receive the radio signals. When the card is placed near a payment terminal, the terminal sends a radio signal to the card, which activates the RFID chip. The chip then sends a unique code back to the terminal to identify the card and initiate the payment process.

The RFID chip in the card does not require a power source or battery because it is able to generate its own electricity using the radio waves it receives from the terminal. This is known as "passive" RFID technology, as the card is not actively sending or receiving signals, but rather responding to signals from the terminal.

Addressing Climate Change: The Collective Action Problem Essay Addressing the problem of climate change is associated with significant barriers. In 1997, the United Nations’ 1992 Framework Convention on Climate Change ratified Kyoto Protocol, which set the limits for greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions for every country (Bernauer, 2013). While the majority of nations agreed to the terms, the US, the largest GHG emitter at that time, decided not to join the agreement (Bernauer, 2013). The central problem was that the US experienced a significant disbalance in contribution and benefits. While all the nations agree that climate change is a source of substantial harm to the economy, the environment, and public health, not all countries have similar incentives for addressing the problem. The largest economies usually are the largest emitters of GHG, which implies that they need to contribute the most to the reduction of emissions. However, larger economies are less likely to suffer from climate change, as they have a greater opportunity to adapt to the changes, which costs less (Bernauer, 2013). At the same time, developing economies do not need to contribute much to the decreases in emissions, while they are likely to suffer the most from climate change (Bernauer, 2013). Moreover, governments are often afraid that some countries will be free riders, which implies that they will benefit from the changes without any investments. Another issue associated with climate change is the need for large-scale changes. The problem is that achieving the required level of emissions requires changing from fossil fuel to renewable energy, which will disproportionately hurt different countries, as many countries depend on the export of fossil fuel. Additionally, when giving priority to different issues, policy-makers are likely to give less attention to climate change problems, as their short-term and medium-term implications are acceptable. It is the long-term implications everyone fears (Bernauer, 2013). Finally, the collective action problem is associated with instability in the priorities of different countries. Addressing the problem of climate change is a long-term commitment. Since governments’ opinions on the prioritization of the problems may change, ensuring long-term collaboration is close to impossible (Bernauer, 2013). References Bernauer, T. (2013). Climate Change Politics. Annual Review of Political Science , 16 (1), 421-448. Web.

The frozen continent of Antarctica has long captured the imagination of explorers and scientists alike. For centuries it remained largely unexplored, its harsh climate keeping all but the hardiest of souls away. The first known sighting of Antarctica was in 1820 by a Russian expedition. But it would take decades more before explorers were able to set foot on the continent. In the early 1900s, the race was on between Robert Falcon Scott of Britain and Roald Amundsen of Norway to be the first to reach the South Pole. After years of planning and preparation, Amundsen and his team were the first to arrive at the South Pole in December 1911, beating Scott's team by over a month. Tragically, Scott and his men perished on the return journey. Their fate highlighted the extreme dangers of Antarctic exploration. In the following decades, more explorations of Antarctica took place, many by ship and some by air. Richard Byrd led multiple expeditions to Antarctica, including the first flights over the South Pole in 1929. New lands were discovered and mapped, and scientific research stations were established across the continent. In 1957-58, Vivian Fuchs led the first overland crossing of Antarctica by way of the South Pole. With the advent of new technologies, explorations of Antarctica took on a new purpose. No longer were teams just trying to be the first to reach a geographical landmark. Scientific research became a key motivator for many expeditions. Teams sought to understand Antarctica's unique climate, geology, and biology. They drilled into ice cores to study the ancient climate. They explored remote mountain ranges and discovered new species of plants and animals. They mapped the continent in ever greater detail using satellites and geophysics. Antarctica remains a continent of mystery even today. Harsh conditions make much of the interior inaccessible for most of the year. But new technologies are allowing scientists to explore Antarctica like never before. Robotic submarines dive under ice shelves, high-resolution satellites peer down from space, and automated research stations collect data year-round. What new discoveries await in this frozen world? The next chapters of Antarctic exploration are still to be written.

Causality, the relationship between cause and effect, is a fundamental concept in philosophy and science. It is the idea that every event has a cause, and that the cause precedes the effect in time. The philosophy of causality seeks to understand the nature of causality and its implications for our understanding of the world. One of the most important aspects of causality is the idea of temporal precedence. This means that the cause of an event must occur before the effect. For example, if a person drops a ball, the cause of the ball falling is the person dropping it, and the effect of the person dropping it is the ball falling. The cause must always come before the effect in time. Another important aspect of causality is the idea of necessary connection. This means that the cause of an event must be sufficient to bring about the effect. For example, if a person drops a ball, the cause of the ball falling is the person dropping it, and the effect of the person dropping it is the ball falling. The person dropping the ball is the only cause of the ball falling, and it is sufficient to bring about the effect of the ball falling. The philosophy of causality has a number of implications for science. One of the most important implications is that causality is essential for scientific explanation. In order to explain an event, scientists must identify the cause of the event. For example, if a scientist wants to explain why a ball fell, they must identify the cause of the ball falling, such as a person dropping it. Without causality, scientific explanation would not be possible. Another implication of the philosophy of causality for science is that causality is essential for scientific prediction. In order to predict an event, scientists must identify the cause of the event. For example, if a scientist wants to predict whether a ball will fall, they must identify the cause of the ball falling, such as a person dropping it. Without causality, scientific prediction would not be possible. The philosophy of causality is a complex and challenging topic, but it is also a fundamental concept in philosophy and science. By understanding the nature of causality, we can better understand the world around us and make better predictions about the future.

Coaxial cable is used to transmit electrical signals, and like all electrical conductors, it has some resistance. This resistance causes a loss of signal strength over long distances.However, electrical resistance is usually measured in Ohms (Ω), and the loss of signal strength in a coaxial cable is usually measured in decibels (dB). So why do we use dB to measure loss instead of Ohms?One reason is that dB is a logarithmic scale, which means that the value increases by a fixed amount for every increment of the scale. This is useful because signal loss tends to increase logarithmically with distance. For example, if the signal loss is 3 dB over a certain distance, it will be 6 dB over twice that distance, 9 dB over three times that distance, and so on. This makes it easier to understand and compare the loss over different distances.Another reason is that the human ear perceives sound and the human eye perceives light logarithmically. So when we use a logarithmic scale like dB to measure signal loss, it corresponds more closely to how we perceive the loss of strength in a signal.I hope that helps to explain why we use dB to measure signal loss in coaxial cable. However, coral reefs are facing a grave threat from coral bleaching, which is caused by a combination of factors such as rising sea temperatures, ocean acidification, and pollution. Coral bleaching occurs when the symbiotic relationship between corals and the algae that live inside them breaks down, causing the coral to lose its vibrant color and ultimately die if the bleaching persists for too long. This essay will explore the role of coral bleaching in ecosystem decline, focusing on its impacts on marine life, food security, and coastal protection. Coral reefs are home to a vast array of marine life, including fish, sea turtles, and sharks. Coral bleaching has a devastating impact on these animals, as it destroys their habitat and food source. Coral reefs provide essential nursery grounds for many fish species, and the loss of coral due to bleaching can lead to a decline in fish populations. This, in turn, can disrupt the entire food chain, leading to a cascade of consequences for other marine animals. Additionally, coral reefs act as a natural barrier against waves and storms, protecting coastal communities from damage. The loss of coral due to bleaching weakens these barriers, increasing the risk of flooding and erosion in coastal areas. Coral reefs also play a vital role in maintaining healthy oceans and supporting coastal economies. Coral reefs are important sources of food and income for millions of people around the world, particularly in developing countries. Coral reefs provide a source of protein for coastal communities through fishing, and they also support tourism industries, attracting divers and snorkelers from around the globe. However, the decline of coral reefs due to bleaching threatens these livelihoods, as fewer tourists are likely to visit degraded reefs, and fish populations may decline, affecting local food security. In conclusion, coral bleaching is a serious threat to coral reefs and the ecosystems they support. The loss of coral due to bleaching has far-reaching consequences for marine life, food security, and coastal protection. It is therefore imperative that we take action to address the underlying causes of coral bleaching, such as climate change and pollution, in order to preserve these vital ecosystems for future generations.

As evidence, we use the latest advances in language modeling to build a single pre-trained QA model , UnifiedQA , that performs surprisingly well across 17 QA datasets spanning 4 diverse formats. UnifiedQA performs on par with 9 different models that were trained on individual datasets themselves. Even when faced with 12 unseen datasets of observed formats, UnifiedQA performs surprisingly well, showing strong generalization from its out-of-format training data.
