Schools could also look into reapportioning the longer December-March break or shifting towards a four-day school week. The world around us is filled with beauty and wonderment. A simple walk through a park can reveal breathtakingly vibrant flowers, while a journey to a vast, untouched forest can lead you to discover an array of unique plant and animal species. But what if I told you that there is an even more fascinating realm waiting to be explored right under our feet? That's right, I'm talking about the world of fungi! Fungi are amazing organisms that belong to their own kingdom, separate from plants and animals. They come in a wide variety of shapes and sizes, ranging from tiny microscopic spores to massive, tree-like mushrooms. In fact, the largest known fungus in the world, called "Armillaria ostoyae," covers an area of 2,200 square miles in the Malheur National Forest in Oregon. That's larger than the city of New York City! But it's not just their size that makes fungi so captivating. They also play a vital role in our ecosystems. For example, certain types of fungi called mycorrhizae form mutually beneficial relationships with plants. These fungal networks help plants absorb water and nutrients from the soil, while the plants provide fungi with carbon and energy. In turn, this relationship supports a thriving community of other organisms like insects, animals, and even other plants. Fungi also have a fascinating reproductive strategy. While most organisms rely on sexual reproduction to create offspring, fungi can also reproduce asexually through the production of spores. These tiny, lightweight structures allow them to spread far and wide, colonizing new habitats and establishing new populations. In fact, some fungi can produce up to 10 billion spores in a single day! But perhaps the most intriguing aspect of fungi is their incredible diversity. Scientists estimate that there are approximately 14 million to 8.6 million species of fungi on Earth, while only about 5% of them have been identified. This means that there are still countless mysteries waiting to be discovered about these fascinating organisms. So the next time you step on a mushroom or brush past a patch of mold, take a moment to appreciate the world of fungi that surrounds us. From supporting our ecosystems to captivating our imaginations, these amazing organisms truly are a wonder of nature.

The internal iliac artery is a large artery that originates from the common iliac artery and supplies blood to the pelvic region, including the pelvis, pelvic organs, and lower limbs. It is a branch of the aorta, the main artery of the body.

The internal iliac artery is located in the pelvis, on the inside (medial) side of the hip bone (ilium). It divides into two smaller arteries, the anterior and posterior branches of the internal iliac artery, which supply blood to different parts of the pelvis.

The external iliac artery is another branch of the common iliac artery that arises from the aorta. It is located on the outside (lateral) side of the hip bone and runs down the leg. The external iliac artery supplies blood to the lower limb and the muscles of the hip and thigh. It eventually divides into the deep and superficial femoral arteries, which supply blood to the lower leg and foot.

Both the internal and external iliac arteries are important blood vessels that play a crucial role in the circulation of blood to the lower body.

The Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is a method used to categorize and analyze human facial expressions by identifying the underlying muscle movements. The FACS was developed by Dr. Paul Ekman and Dr. Walter K. Friesen in the late 1970s, and it has been widely adopted in various fields, including psychology, neuroscience, and the film and animation industry. The FACS consists of a set of 43 facial movements that can be grouped into seven primary facial expressions: happiness, sadness, surprise, fear, disgust, anger, and contempt. These expressions are further broken down into more specific facial actions or "action units" (AUs). Each AU represents a distinct muscle movement or facial feature. For example, an AU might be raising the eyebrows (AU4), tightening the lips (AU10), or narrowing the eyes (AU42). The FACS is particularly helpful in understanding human emotion and nonverbal communication. Researchers and psychologists use the FACS to study the facial expressions of individuals in different situations, such as during emotional or stressful events. In the film industry, the FACS is used by animators, actors, and makeup artists to create more realistic and expressive characters in animated films, movies, or video games. In summary, the Facial Action Coding System is a valuable tool for analyzing and categorizing human facial expressions. It helps researchers and artists better understand emotions and create more realistic representations of emotions in different mediums.

The facial action coding system (FACS) is a set of standards that categorizes and describes facial expressions. Developed by Dr. Paul Ekman and his colleagues in the 1970s, it has been widely used by researchers, psychologists, and actors to study human emotions and understand the complexities of facial expressions. The FACS consists of two main components: the Action Units (AUs) and the Action Description Authentication (ADA) system. Action Units are the fundamental building blocks of facial expressions, representing the specific movements and actions of facial muscles. There are 43 different AUs that cover a wide range of emotions, including happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, and surprise. Each AU represents an individual facial movement or action, such as raising the eyebrows (AU4), tightening the lips (AU14), or squinting (AU12). The second component, the Action Description Authentication (ADA) system, is a set of guidelines that help researchers and actors standardize and authenticate the descriptions of facial expressions. This system ensures that everyone is referring to the same AUs and using consistent terminology when discussing or categorizing facial expressions. The FACS has played an essential role in advancing our understanding of human emotions and their manifestations on our faces. It has been applied in various fields, from psychology to acting, and has contributed to the development of emotion recognition technology. By breaking down facial expressions into their fundamental components, the FACS provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing and interpreting the subtle cues that our faces reveal, helping us better understand ourselves, others, and the complex nature of human emotions.

The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was one of the most significant pieces of legislation ever passed in the United States. It outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in employment and public accommodations. The Act had an enormous impact on American society and politics that still resonates today. Prior to the Act, discrimination and segregation were rampant in many areas of public life. Racial minorities faced discrimination and segregation in employment, education, public facilities, and accommodations like hotels and restaurants. The Civil Rights Act banned such discrimination and segregation, opening up opportunities for minorities in education, the workplace, and leisure activities that had previously been denied to them. It gave minorities a legal tool to fight against discrimination. The passage of the Act also showed the triumph of the Civil Rights Movement and its efforts to raise awareness of racial injustice and push for change. The movement had gained momentum throughout the 1950s and early 1960s with events like the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the Greensboro sit-ins, and the March on Washington. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was a major victory that validated the Movement's goals and strategies. It indicated that grassroots movements and nonviolent protest could enact legislative change. Politically, the Act split both major parties to some extent. Southern Democrats in particular opposed civil rights reforms and saw them as a federal overreach. The Act exacerbated an ideological split within the Democratic party that contributed to the political realignment of the South. Over time, white voters in the South shifted to supporting the Republican party. At the same time, the Act cemented the support of minorities for the Democratic party that championed civil rights. The effects of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 have endured and shaped America in fundamental ways. It banned discrimination and opened up public life to minorities, accelerating their social and economic mobility. It gave moral force to the Civil Rights Movement and demonstrated the power of grassroots political activism. And it reshaped the political landscape, contributing to the rise of the modern Republican party in the South. The Act was a pivotal moment that redefined what it meant to be an American and moved the nation closer to fulfilling the promise of equality enshrined in its founding documents.

Essay: The Importance of Imagination vs. Knowledge Imagination and knowledge are two concepts that are often seen as opposites, but they are actually complementary and essential for our Growth and development. Imagination can also help us find new solutions to problems, and to apply knowledge in creative ways. In conclusion, imagination and knowledge are both important, but they serve different purposes. The two are interconnected, and they are essential for our Growth and development. So, let us embrace both imagination and knowledge, and use them to create a better future for ourselves and for Generations to come.

The organizers of the Olympiad have created a new division for "machine learning" systems, which will be pitted against the human students. The goal is to see whether these artificial intelligence (AI) systems can solve the problems as well as, or better than, the humans. The competition is open to any type of AI system, including those based on neural networks, evolutionary algorithms, and traditional rule-based systems. So far, no AI system has been able to beat humans at the Olympiad, but the organizers are hopeful that this will change in the future. "We believe that the participation of machine learning systems in the Olympiad will help to promote research in this area, and ultimately lead to better AI systems," said a spokesperson for the organizers. The first round of the competition will take place on May 18-19, with the final round taking place on July 16-17.

The state-of-the-art approaches in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are able to learn a mapping function from one image domain to another with unpaired image data. However, these methods often produce artifacts and can only be able to convert low-level information, but fail to transfer high-level semantic part of images. The reason is mainly that generators do not have the ability to detect the most discriminative semantic part of images, which thus makes the generated images with low-quality. To handle the limitation, in this paper we propose a novel Attention-Guided Generative Adversarial Network (AGGAN), which can detect the most discriminative semantic object and minimize changes of unwanted part for semantic manipulation problems without using extra data and models. The attention-guided generators in AGGAN are able to produce attention masks via a built-in attention mechanism, and then fuse the input image with the attention mask to obtain a target image with high-quality. Moreover, we propose a novel attention-guided discriminator which only considers attended regions. The proposed AGGAN is trained by an end-to-end fashion with an adversarial loss, cycle-consistency loss, pixel loss and attention loss. The world we live in is becoming increasingly digitized, and many people question if libraries still have a significant role to play in society today. As a student in grade 7, I am aware of the vast amount of information available online, but I strongly believe that libraries remain essential institutions in the digital age. In this essay, I will argue in favor of libraries, discussing why they are still crucial for communities and individuals. Libraries offer free access to these materials, allowing people from all backgrounds to access information and knowledge. Additionally, libraries provide access to computers and the internet, which is essential for those who do not have access to such technology at home. Secondly, libraries serve as community hubs where people can come together and learn, share ideas or simply relay. They offer a safe and quiet space for students to study, and they often host events such as book clubs, author talks, and workshops that bring communities together. These events promote social engagement and intellectual curiosity, which are essential for personal growth and development. Thirdly, libraries have a vital role to play in promoting literacy and reading among children and young adults. Libraries offer age appropriate books and reading programs that help to foster a love of reading in young people. Studies have shown that children who read for pleasure perform better academically, and libraries play a crucial role in providing access to reading materials and encouraging a reading culture. Finally, libraries are essential institutions in promoting information literacy. In the age of misinformation and fake news, libraries provide a safe and reliable source of information. Librarians are trained professionals who can guide people to find accurate and trustworthy information, helping to combat the spread of falsehoods and propaganda. In conclusion, I argue that libraries remain crucial institutions in the digital age. They provide access to resources that might not be available otherwise, serve as community hubs, promote literacy, and are essential for promoting information literacy. As we continue to navigate the digital landscape, libraries will continue to play a vital role in our communities, providing access to information and knowledge for all.

In the tapestry of human entertainment, few spectacles boast the rich and colorful history of the circus. Its evolution is a fascinating journey through time, culture, and the relentless pursuit of wonder. The circus, as a concept, has transformed from ancient Roman chariot races to a grandiose display of acrobatics, exotic animals, and clowning that captivates audiences worldwide. The story of the circus begins in ancient Rome, where the Circus Maximus, a grand arena, was erected for the public's enjoyment. Here, chariot races, gladiatorial combat, and staged animal hunts satisfied the Roman appetite for spectacle and thrill. It was a far cry from the modern circus, yet the seeds of spectacle and crowd-pleasing feats were sown. As the Roman Empire declined, so too did the grand circuses of old, but the human lust for spectacle did not. Traveling performers, minstrels, and troubadours carried the torch of entertainment through the medieval period. These were the progenitors of the modern circus performer, showcasing feats of skill and strength in town squares and at fairs. Jugglers, acrobats, and magicians became the day's stars, drawing crowds with their daring and artistry. The circus, as we begin to recognize it, took shape in the 18th century. It was in 1768 that an Englishman named Philip Astley, a former cavalry sergeant-major turned showman, established what is considered the first modern circus. In a ring, he showcased equestrian tricks, a format that proved popular and was imitated across Europe and beyond. Astley's Amphitheatre in London became the epicenter of this new form of entertainment, combining horse riding displays with acrobatics and clowning. The circus ring, a circle 42 feet in diameter, was not an arbitrary choice. The size was determined by Astley's discovery that a horse galloping in a circle of this diameter naturally fell into a trot that was manageable for performing stunts. This insight became a standard in circuses worldwide, a dimension still used in circuses to this day. As the 19th century dawned, the circus continued to evolve. This paper describes the NTNU ASR system participating in the Interspeech 2020 Non-Native Children's Speech ASR Challenge supported by the SIG-CHILD group of ISCA. This ASR shared task is made up of two subtasks: a bilingual ASR task and a monolingual ASR task. For the bilingual ASR task, our system is based on the hybrid deep neural network (DNN) hidden Markov model (HMM) architecture. Our acoustic model is a convolutional recurrent neural network (CRNN) consisting of four convolution layers, two bi-directional long short-term memory (LSTM) layers, and one fully connected layer. The CRNN is trained with mean-variance normalized log Mel-filterbank energies extracted from audio clips. We also use an LSTM language model for decoding. For the monolingual ASR task, we use a DNN-HMM system with features extracted from the same audio clips as in the bilingual ASR task. For the DNN, we use a five-layer time-delay neural network (TDNN) with rectified linear unit activations. To improve accuracy, we perform data augmentation by using SpecAugment and elastic time warping (ETW). We train an n-gram language model for decoding. Experimental results show that our system achieves top performances in both tasks among all participants in the challenge.

A national DNA database is a collection of DNA samples and associated identifying information that is maintained by a government or other organization. There are a number of reasons why a national DNA database might not be established in a particular country. One reason is that such a database could raise concerns about privacy and the potential for abuse of personal information. DNA contains a great deal of sensitive and personal information, including information about an individual's ancestry, medical history, and susceptibility to certain diseases. Some people may be concerned that a national DNA database could be accessed by government agencies or other organizations for purposes beyond those for which it was originally intended, such as for employment or insurance decisions. Another reason that a national DNA database might not be established is that there are significant logistical and technical challenges involved in collecting and maintaining DNA samples from every person in a country. DNA samples must be collected, stored, and analyzed in a way that is accurate and reliable, and this requires specialized equipment, trained personnel, and secure facilities. A researcher from the Swiss research institute EMPA has developed an invisible lock system that uses conductive ink on a transparent polymer film to create invisible buttons. The result is a "soft touch" surface, which could be used for everything from touchscreen computers and cellphone displays to smart packaging. After five years of intensive development work by a group led by Bernhard Vollbrecht at EMPA, the scientists have succeeded in developing a new type of two-dimensional (2D) locking technology - one based on extremely thin layers of intermetallic compounds rather than magnetic materials or optical films. Individual metallic elements are embedded between sheets of polymers during production; these are then firstly heated up using thermocouples until they separate in order to reveal their internal structure as individual components - like tiny tubes filled with coloured liquid. These parts can later be connected again when required through laser welding. This method makes it possible to produce 2D structures whose complexity outstrips anything previously achieved. In addition to this technical breakthrough, making visible electronic modules in thin form means not only being able to incorporate them into products but also to combine different functions within one module - that is to say, for example, imaging sensors combined with electrical contact strips without any additional connection methods. So far, very few researchers are pursuing the use of metal nanostructures in electronics since such applications remain largely unexplored: however, Professor Vollbrecht believes his approach will open up entirely novel areas of application. Indeed, he predicts there will soon be no need for conventional mechanical contacts whatsoever if all we want is to transmit information over complex networks. They would simply become visual signals. Likewise, conventional display covers would lose much of their function. He points out that nobody today wants light bulbs anymore because fluorescent lighting is so commonplace that people don't see its lack of aesthetics. Why should contactless data transmission not be regarded in exactly the same way? What we dream about now is something completely different! Lady Macbeth is one of the most complex and fascinating characters in Shakespeare's play Macbeth. When we first meet Lady Macbeth, she is portrayed as a ruthless and ambitious woman who will stop at nothing to get what she wants. Upon receiving a letter from Macbeth informing her of the witches' prophecy that he will become king, she is immediately determined to make sure it comes true. She calls upon the spirits to "unsex me here, / And fill me from the crown to the toe top-full / Of direst cruelty!" so that she can convince Macbeth to kill Duncan. She knows her husband is "too full o' the milk of human kindness" to do what needs to be done, so she takes charge of the situation. However, as the play progresses, Lady Macbeth's character changes dramatically. After Macbeth kills Duncan and becomes king, Lady Macbeth becomes increasingly paranoid and guilt-ridden over their crimes. While at first she was the driving force behind Macbeth's actions, she starts to unravel and goes mad with guilt. Her sleepwalking scene in Act V poignantly shows her descent into madness. The doctor observes that she is "troubled with thick-coming fancies, / That keep her from her rest." The blood on her hands is a physical manifestation of the deep guilt she feels over her role in Duncan's murder and the other bloodshed that followed. Tragically, it seems that Lady Macbeth was not as ruthless as she first appeared and was ultimately unable to handle the consequences of her actions. In many ways, Lady Macbeth is a deeply tragic figure. While at the beginning of the play she appears to be in control and determined, by the end she has crumbled under the weight of her guilt and gone mad. Her story shows that ambition and the desire for power can have devastating consequences. Lady Macbeth serves as a warning for those who try to act against their own human nature and moral conscience. She is a complex and captivating character who adds a great deal of depth and poignancy to Shakespeare's famous tragedy. Overall, Lady Macbeth's compelling character arc from a seemingly heartless woman to one filled with remorse and guilt makes her one of Shakespeare's most memorable and haunting characters.

The electoral college is a unique system used in the United States for the election of the president and vice president. It is designed to balance the power between the states, with the idea that smaller states have a stronger voice in the election process. However, this system has been criticized and questioned for its efficacy. The electoral college works through the allocation of votes based on the number of representatives each state has in Congress. States with more representatives have more electoral votes to allocate. When citizens vote in a general election, they are essentially voting for a group of electors who will represent their chosen candidate. The electoral college process has two main phases: the general election and the electoral college vote. During the general election, citizens cast their vote for the presidential candidates, and the popular vote is counted. In this phase, the electoral college system is not yet implemented. Following the general election, the electoral college vote takes place. Each state then sends a group of electors (usually the same number as representatives in Congress) who will cast their vote for the presidential candidate their state has chosen. The electors meet in their respective states and cast their votes. The votes are then sent to Congress, where they are counted. If a candidate receives over 270 electoral votes, they win the presidency. One of the primary concerns with the electoral college is that a candidate can win the presidency without winning the popular vote. This happened in the elections of 1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016. The electoral college system has been criticized for allowing this discrepancy, as some argue that it goes against democratic principles. Another criticism of the electoral college is that it gives undue influence to smaller, less populated states, as they have the same number of electoral votes as larger states. This can lead to the election of candidates who are less popular among the general population. In conclusion, the electoral college system does work in the sense that it functions as it was designed and has been used in presidential elections. However, its effectiveness is debatable, as it can lead to a disconnect between the popular vote and the outcome of the election. As a result, some people argue for changes to the electoral college system or for its complete abolition.

The 45 rpm discs also came in a variety known as extended play (EP), which achieved up to 10-15 minutes play at the expense of attenuating (and possibly compressing) the sound to reduce the width required by the groove. EP discs were cheaper to produce, and were used in cases where unit sales were likely to be more limited or to reissue LP albums on the smaller format for those people who had only 45 rpm players. LP albums could be purchased 1 EP at a time, with four items per EP, or in a boxed set with 3 EPs or 12 items. The large center hole on 45s allows for easier handling by jukebox mechanisms. EPs were generally discontinued by the late 1950s in the U.S. as three- and four-speed record players replaced the individual 45 players. One indication of the decline of the 45 rpm EP is that the last Columbia Records reissue of Frank Sinatra songs on 45 rpm EP records, called Frank Sinatra (Columbia B-2641) was issued on December 7, 1959. The EP lasted considerably longer in Europe, and was a popular format during the 1960s for recordings by artists such as Serge Gainsbourg and the Beatles.

The foundation of Northwestern University is traceable to a meeting on May 31, 1850 of nine prominent Chicago businessmen, Methodist leaders and attorneys who had formed the idea of establishing a university to serve what had once been known as the Northwest Territory. On January 28, 1851, the Illinois General Assembly granted a charter to the Trustees of the North-Western University, making it the first chartered university in Illinois. The school's nine founders, all of whom were Methodists (three of them ministers), knelt in prayer and worship before launching their first organizational meeting. The changing roles and representations of ethnicity and race in American literature and film over time have been a reflection of the evolving social and cultural landscape of the United States. From the early works of literature to contemporary films, the portrayal of different ethnicities and races has undergone significant transformations, reflecting the progress, challenges, and struggles of marginalized communities. In early American literature, the representation of ethnicity and race was often rooted in stereotypes and prejudices. Native Americans were often depicted as savages or noble savages, emphasizing their perceived backwardness or romanticizing their connection to nature. African Americans, on the other hand, were frequently portrayed as subservient and inferior, perpetuating the racial hierarchy of the time. These representations reflected the dominant white perspective and reinforced racial biases that were prevalent in society. However, as the United States progressed and underwent significant social and political changes, so did the portrayal of ethnicity and race in literature and film. The Harlem Renaissance, a cultural movement in the 1920s and 1930s, marked a turning point in African American literature and art. Authors such as Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston presented a more nuanced and authentic depiction of African American life, challenging the prevailing stereotypes and showcasing the richness of their culture and experiences. Similarly, in the aftermath of the Civil Rights Movement in the 1960s, there was a surge of literature and films that explored the African American experience and highlighted the struggles for equality and social justice. Works like Ralph Ellison's "Invisible Man" and films like Spike Lee's "Do the Right Thing" delved into the complexities of racial identity and the systemic oppression faced by African Americans. The 21st century has seen a further evolution in the representation of ethnicity and race in American literature and film. There has been a greater emphasis on diverse narratives and voices, with authors and filmmakers from various ethnic backgrounds sharing their experiences and perspectives. This shift has led to a more inclusive portrayal of different ethnicities and races, challenging traditional narratives and providing a more accurate reflection of the diversity of America.
